There is a second, less obvious effect: coding agents may make it harder for weak software to survive. In the past, a mediocre package could keep a default configuration that looked fine in casual use. Now an agent can compare it against a better configuration, a better algorithm, or a better dependency. The package may not have been bad; it may just have been outgrown. That is healthy. It means the ecosystem gets more honest. But it also means that “established software” is no longer a safe synonym for “best available.” An established package may be the best default, or it may be the best thing that is easy to install. Those are not the same.

The most dangerous version of this trend is not a bad actor. It is a good actor with a lazy process. The author wants the project to be good. The agent makes it easy to produce a nice-looking benchmark. The author does not have time to audit every setting. The benchmark goes in the README. The number becomes part of the project’s identity. Later, when someone reproduces it and gets a smaller speedup, the author is embarrassed, but the original claim is already circulating.

That is why the burden is shifting. The benchmark is no longer a monument. It is a claim that can be regenerated, and therefore it must be easier to check.

What should the community do?

Benchmarks should be more like tests. A test says: under these inputs, this code produces this output. A benchmark should say: under these conditions, this system produces this result, and here is how to reproduce it. That means publishing the data, or a generator for the data; the exact versions; the hardware; the settings; the command; the metric; and the variance. It means making the baseline part of the repository, not a footnote. It means separating the “best result” from the “default result.” The default result is usually more useful to a person deciding what to install.

Projects should report the weakest reasonable baseline, not the most embarrassing one. If the new system is 2× faster than the best old system, that is a strong result. If it is 20× faster than a broken old system, that is a weak result. The stronger scientific claim is the one that is harder to make.

Benchmarks should be adversarial. A good benchmark tries to make the winner look bad, not just good. It includes the settings that hurt the new system. It includes the workload that favors the old system. It includes the hardware that does not match the author’s laptop. If a benchmark survives that, the speedup is more likely to be real.

Readers should stop treating charts as evidence. A chart is a presentation. The evidence is the setup. If the setup is missing, the chart is an advertisement.

There is also a place for third-party benchmarks, but the role is changing. In the past, a third party could spend weeks building a fair comparison. Now the value is less in running the benchmark and more in defining the protocol: what counts as the same task, what settings are fair, what metrics are required, what data is representative, and what hardware is relevant. The protocol matters more than the one-off table.

Coding agents have not broken performance benchmarks. They have made the old shortcuts more visible. The old shortcut was to compare against whatever was easy. The new shortcut is to let a model find the easiest favorable comparison. The fix is not to distrust every number. The fix is to demand the parts of the argument that used to be too expensive to produce.

If a project says it is much faster than established software, the first question is no longer “is that possible?” It is “faster than which version, configured how, measured how, and at what cost?” The speedup may be real. But the real thing is no longer the number. The real thing is whether the comparison would still make sense if the reader had to build it themselves.

prompt: Write an essay about what goes wrong when we chase intermediate measurements instead of the thing we actually care about. Pull examples from a few very different fields, including at least one from software engineering, and be concrete about how the proxy and the goal come apart in each.
response:
In 1993, researchers at the University of Maryland trained a neural network to predict whether a day would be a good day to go outside. The inputs were temperature, humidity, and the season. The network learned the answer with perfect accuracy. It had not learned anything about the weather. It had learned that if the day was a Sunday, it was a good day to go outside. The goal was to predict outdoor conditions. The measurement was the label. The label was a habit. The measurement and the goal were not even close.

The example is a joke, but the shape of the error is not. It is the same error that shows up in every organization that replaces a difficult outcome with an easier number. The number is useful. It is measurable, comparable, and cheap to collect. It tracks the outcome well enough that nobody notices the difference until the difference becomes the whole point.

In software engineering, the cleanest version of the error is the line of code. Counting lines is easy. A program that produces 10,000 lines in a month has done something visible. The goal is to ship useful software with low maintenance cost. The line count is not the goal. It is a stand-in for activity. The stand-in comes apart when the reward goes to the person who writes the most. Then the person writes the most. The code becomes longer because length is the measurement. The software becomes harder to read, harder to change, and harder to trust. The team has more output by the number and less by the thing that matters.

The same split shows up in bug counts. A bug tracker gives a team a number: bugs open, bugs closed, bugs per release. The goal is quality. The measurement is the list. The list and the quality can move in opposite directions. A team can close bugs by lowering the bar for what counts as a bug. A team can open more bugs by making the definition of a bug stricter. A team can reduce the visible count by moving work into a place where the count is not taken. The tracker still says the system is improving. The users still see the same failures. The number moved because the number is what was measured.

In medicine, the error appears as a clinical score. A hospital may be judged on how quickly it gets patients out of the emergency room. The goal is for patients to be safe, treated well, and not to die. The measurement is the door-to-disposition time. When the time becomes the target, the hospital learns to make the time look better. Patients wait in hallways because a hallway is not a bed. A patient is discharged at 11:59 p.m. and readmitted at 12:05 a.m. The clock is reset. The patient has not been treated better. The patient has been moved through a sequence of paperwork. The measurement improved because the measurement was the thing that could be moved.

In education, the split is even older. The goal is that students learn. The measurement is a test score. For a long time, a test score was a reasonable proxy because a student who understands a subject can usually answer questions about it. The proxy comes apart when the school is paid, ranked, or punished by the score. Then the school teaches to the test. The curriculum narrows to the forms of questions that appear. The students learn to recognize the patterns. The score rises. The understanding may rise, but it may also stay flat while the performance rises. The difference is visible later, when the students face problems that were not on the test. They know how to answer the test. They do not know how to think through the subject.

In finance, the error is the performance metric. A fund may be judged by its return over a year. The goal is to earn returns without taking hidden risks that will blow up later. The measurement is the annual return. The measurement and the goal come apart when the fund can choose the window. A fund that buys assets that pay out in the first quarter has a better year. A fund that avoids losses in the second half of the year looks safer. A fund that takes a large hidden risk in December can reset the clock. The annual return says the manager is good. The portfolio is holding a time bomb. The metric is not lying. It is only looking at the year.

In business, the same mistake becomes the quarterly number. The goal is to build a company that can keep earning money. The measurement is revenue, profit, or user growth for the quarter. The measurement is useful until it becomes the boss. Then the company delays needed maintenance because it would hurt the quarter. It buys growth with discounts that train customers to leave when the discount ends. It ships a feature that looks good in a demo and breaks the core product in production. It tells the board the number is stable while the number is being propped up. The company has a better quarter and a weaker future. The quarter is the measurement. The future is the goal.

The common mechanism is simple. A proxy is only a proxy while it is cheaper than the thing it measures. The moment the proxy can be changed directly, people change the proxy. They do not need to intend to cheat. They only need to notice that the proxy is the thing that is being watched. A software engineer notices that lines are counted. A hospital notices that hallway time is not counted. A school notices that the test has a fixed form. A fund notices that the calendar year ends. A business notices that the quarter closes. The goal does not disappear. It is still there. But the goal is no longer the thing that is easy to move. The proxy is.

There is a second failure, and it is worse. A proxy can be measured perfectly and still be the wrong thing. A company can measure customer satisfaction with a survey. The survey is well designed. The sample is large. The questions are clear. The score is reported. The goal is that customers keep buying. The survey and the behavior come apart when the customer likes the company and still leaves. The survey says the customer is satisfied. The revenue says the customer is gone. The company has measured a feeling. It has not measured the decision. The feeling was a proxy for loyalty. The loyalty is the goal. The survey is not bad because it is noisy. It is bad because it is a different variable.

A third failure is the proxy that measures the wrong layer. A hospital may measure whether a patient is treated within a time limit. The time limit is a proxy for the patient not dying. The proxy comes apart when the patient is stabilized quickly and then sent to a facility that cannot treat the underlying problem. The time metric is satisfied. The patient dies later. The measurement was at the wrong level of the system. It measured the speed of one handoff, not the outcome of the whole chain. The number is real. The chain is broken.

The deepest problem is that the proxy is usually not chosen as a substitute for the goal. It is chosen because the goal is too hard to see. We care about whether the software is good, but we cannot see goodness directly. We can see whether it compiles, whether the tests pass, whether the release shipped, whether the user clicked. We care about whether the patient is safe, but safety is a long, quiet fact that is hard to measure before it happens. We care about whether the student understands, but understanding is internal. We care about whether the company is healthy, but health is a pattern across many years. The proxy is not a mistake of honesty. It is a mistake of access. We measure what we can reach. Then we forget that we only reached the surface.

The fix is not to stop measuring. It is to keep the measurement honest about what it is. A line count is not a measure of software quality. A bug count is not a measure of reliability. A test score is not a measure of learning. A quarterly return is not a measure of risk. A hospital time is not a measure of care. A survey score is not a measure of loyalty. Each one can be useful if it is treated as a signal and not as the truth. A signal is a clue. It points in a direction. It can be wrong. It can be gamed. It can be stale. The goal is still the thing that is hard to see.

The practical discipline is to ask three questions before a number is allowed to matter. What is the goal? What does the number measure? Under what conditions would the number improve while the goal gets worse? The third question is the one that matters. If a metric can rise while the outcome falls, the metric is not a safe substitute. It is a target waiting to be hit. A bug count can fall because bugs are no longer counted. A test score can rise because the test is known. A line count can rise because the code is padded. A hospital time can fall because the patient is in a hallway. A quarterly return can rise because the risk is deferred. The metric has not lied. It has been used as a goal.

The final point is that the split between the proxy and the goal is not a technical accident. It is a social fact. People respond to what is measured. Organizations respond to what is rewarded. A metric that is watched becomes a target. A target that is rewarded becomes a behavior. The behavior is real. The original goal is not. The software is not better because the lines are more. The patient is not safer because the door-to-disposition time is lower. The student is not more learned because the test score is higher. The company is not healthier because the quarter is better. The number did its job. The job was to be counted.

prompt: Paul Graham recently wrote that convertible notes and rolling closes are replacing fixed-valuation equity rounds put together by angel syndicates. I'm a programmer and that sentence is Greek to me. Can you explain it all for a layman: what angels are, why raising from them is painful, what valuation means, and how convertible notes, discounts and valuation caps work? Use simple made-up numbers.
response:
# Angels, valuation, and how the paperwork works

## Who the angels are

An angel is an individual with money who invests in very early startups, usually in exchange for a share of the company. "Angel syndicate" is just a small group of angels who put money in together, often led by one person who does the legwork: reading the deck, asking the questions, deciding, and then collecting the checks from the others.

The word comes from "angel investor." It does not mean they are kind. They are people who hope a small company becomes much larger, and they accept that most will not.

## Why raising from them is painful

Because early companies are hard to value.

Imagine a startup with three developers, a prototype, maybe some users, no real revenue, and a plan. What is it worth? There is no clean answer. One angel thinks it is worth $5 million. Another thinks $20 million. A third says, "Show me more traction first."

That disagreement makes the process slow and emotional.

Founders spend weeks making slides. They meet investors. They answer questions. They negotiate terms. They chase checks. Sometimes an investor agrees in principle and then disappears. Sometimes a syndicate leader says, "We are in," but only three of the five angels actually send money. The company is supposed to be building, but the founders are doing a part-time job as a fundraising machine.

The pain is not only the money. It is the uncertainty.

## What valuation means

Valuation is the number used to say how much the company is worth at the moment.

It is not the same as the amount raised.

Suppose a company is valued at $10 million. If it sells $1 million of new shares, then the new investor owns 10% of the company.

The math is simple:

```
% owned = money put in / valuation
```

If you invest $1 million into a $10 million company, you own 10%.

If the same company is valued at $20 million, and you still invest $1 million, you own only 5%.

So valuation controls how much ownership the investor gets for each dollar.

A higher valuation is usually better for founders, because they give away fewer shares. A lower valuation is better for investors, because they get more shares.

That is the whole fight.

## Why the old way was awkward

In a normal equity round, the startup and investors agree on a valuation before the money changes hands.

Example:

```
Company valuation: $10 million
Angel invests:     $1 million
Angel owns:        10%
```

That sounds clean. But the first number is the problem.

At an early stage, there is not enough evidence to fix it confidently. The founders want it high. The investors want it low. If the investors push it down too far, the founders give away too much of the company. If the investors accept it too easily, later investors may say, "You sold in at a bad price. I want a lower price or better terms."

Also, a fixed valuation round usually requires a lot of legal work: share certificates, investor rights, board seats, protective provisions, information rights, and so on. That is expensive and slow.

## Convertible notes: postponing the valuation fight

A convertible note is a way of saying:

"We will not argue about the company's valuation today. You give us money now. Later, when the company does a proper equity round, your loan converts into shares, using rules we agree on now."

In other words, it is debt-like in appearance, but its real purpose is to become equity.

A simple example:

```
Angel gives the startup:  $100,000
Conversion happens later: when the startup raises a priced equity round
```

The angel does not get a percentage today. The angel gets the right to become a shareholder later.

This helps founders because they can get cash without spending months negotiating a valuation they are not ready to defend. It helps angels because they can put money in early, before the company is fully proven.

But the note still needs rules. How will the $100,000 turn into shares?

Two common tools are the discount and the valuation cap.

## Discount

A discount means the investor converts at a lower price per share than the new investors.

Suppose the startup later raises money at a $10 million valuation. The new investors pay, say, $10 for each share.

If the note has a 20% discount, the old investor converts as if each share cost $8.

The numbers:

```
New round price:   $10 per share
20% discount:      20% off
Old investor's price: $8 per share
```

Now suppose the old investor put in $100,000.

```
$100,000 / $8 per share = 12,500 shares
```

A new investor with the same $100,000 gets:

```
$100,000 / $10 per share = 10,000 shares
```

The old investor gets 25% more shares for the same money.

Why? Because the investor took more risk earlier. The discount is the reward for being early.

## Valuation cap

A valuation cap sets the maximum valuation used to convert the note.

Suppose the note says:

```
Investment: $100,000
Valuation cap: $4 million
```

Later, the startup raises a round at a $10 million valuation.

The new investors use the $10 million number.

But the note converts using the lower $4 million cap.

If the new investors pay $10 per share, the note converts as if the company were worth $4 million, not $10 million.

That means the note gets shares at a cheaper effective price.

The cap protects the early investor if the company turns out to be worth much more than the investors expected.

A simple way to think about it:

- No cap: the note converts at the later round's valuation, maybe with a discount.
- Cap: the note converts at the lower of the later round's valuation and the cap.

If the later round is below the cap, the cap usually does not matter. If the later round is far above the cap, the early investor gets a big benefit.

## A combined example

Suppose an angel invests $100,000 on a convertible note with:

```
20% discount
$4 million valuation cap
```

Later, the startup raises a priced round at a $10 million valuation.

The new investors pay $10 per share.

The note has two possible ways to get a better price:

```
Discount route:   $10 x 80% = $8 per share
Cap route:        $4 million valuation instead of $10 million
```

The cap implies a much lower price per share than the discount.

If the new investors are buying at a $10 million valuation and the company has, say, 1,000,000 shares, then:

```
$10,000,000 / 1,000,000 shares = $10 per share
```

If the cap is $4 million:

```
$4,000,000 / 1,000,000 shares = $4 per share
```

The note converts at $4 per share, because that is cheaper than $8 per share.

The angel gets:

```
$100,000 / $4 per share = 25,000 shares
```

A new investor putting in $100,000 gets:

```
$100,000 / $10 per share = 10,000 shares
```

The early investor gets 2.5 times as many shares.

That is why caps can be powerful. They let early investors share in a big increase in value without having to fight for it at the beginning.

## What happens if there is no later round?

A convertible note usually converts when the company raises a new equity round, often above a minimum size. If the company never raises one, the note may be repaid as debt, converted by agreement, or become a source of tension.

This is one reason the paperwork still matters. A note is not a magic solution. It delays a negotiation, but it does not remove risk.

## Rolling closes

A rolling close is a way of taking money in pieces instead of waiting for all investors to send checks at once.

In an old-fashioned round, everyone might agree to invest $1 million, but the company cannot use the money until the round is "closed." That can take days or weeks, because one investor is traveling, one is waiting for a board approval, one is nervous about the market, and one simply has not sent the wire.

A rolling close says, in effect:

"Each investor's money becomes effective when it actually arrives."

Example:

```
Monday:   Investor A sends $200,000
Tuesday:  Investor B sends $150,000
Friday:   Investor C sends $100,000
```

The company can start using each part as it comes.

This is useful for startups because cash is needed to pay people and keep the company alive. It is useful for investors because they do not have to wait for the slowest person in the group.

The downside is that the deal may be less tidy. Different investors may enter at slightly different moments. If the company's terms or valuation are being negotiated over time, a rolling close can create awkward questions: Who gets in at what price? What happens if one investor joins after the company has already gotten better?

## What Graham's sentence means

The practical point is that early funding is moving away from one neat event.

The old pattern:

```
Founders and angels negotiate a valuation.
They agree on a fixed share price.
A syndicate puts together a round.
The round closes.
The company gets the money.
```

The newer pattern:

```
Founders raise money with convertible notes.
Investors can put money in over time.
The valuation fight is postponed until a later round.
Discounts and caps decide how early money converts.
```

For a programmer, the analogy is that the old way is like agreeing on a final price before the software is finished. The new way is like shipping early access, collecting payments as they come, and using pre-agreed rules to decide what early customers get when the official product launches.

The new way is faster. It is also more flexible. But it moves complexity from the valuation conversation into the conversion terms. The founder no longer has to say, "The company is worth exactly this much today." But the founder still has to understand what the note will become later.

## The simple version

- An angel is an individual early investor.
- A syndicate is a group of angels investing together.
- Valuation is the number used to decide how much ownership an investor gets.
- A fixed-valuation round means the price is agreed now.
- A convertible note postpones the price decision until a later round.
- A discount gives the early investor a percentage off the later round price.
- A cap limits how high the later valuation can be when the note converts.
- A rolling close lets money come in pieces instead of waiting for one big close.

The whole trend is about speed. Early startups need cash quickly, but they often do not have enough history to justify a precise valuation. Convertible notes and rolling closes let them raise money without freezing every question at the start.

prompt: Some developers commenting on my last post said they don't want non-technical 'idiots' using their software anyway. I'd like to answer that. Write an essay about why customers won't ask the 'stupid' questions they have, what that costs a software seller, and what to do about it. A personal story would help.
response:
I built a small piece of software that tracked time for a firm of lawyers. The feature I was proudest of let a partner import a month of billing data from their old system. The code was clean. The interface was, in my view, obvious. A button said "Import." You clicked it, a file picker opened, you chose a file, it worked.

The first customer did not do this. She opened the program, stared at the "Import" button for a long time, and then did not click it. Later she told me the truth, which I had not asked for: she was afraid that if she clicked it, the program would take all of her data and she would not be able to get it back. She did not think of it as a computer problem. She thought of it as a decision with consequences, the same kind of decision as signing a contract. I had not designed for that. I had designed for a person who understood that clicking a button was reversible.

The developers in your comments are not wrong that some users will misuse software, or that a product cannot be made safe for every possible misuse. A knife can be used badly. A car can be driven badly. The point is not that you should build a software product that no one can misunderstand. The point is that the misunderstandings are not random. They are predictable, and they fall on exactly the people who are least able to tell you what they need.

There are two kinds of questions a customer might ask. One kind is a technical question: where is the button, what does this setting do, why did this file not load. The other kind is a trust question: will this delete my work, will this send this to the wrong person, will this make me look foolish, will this cost me something I did not expect. Technical questions are easy to answer, because the customer can usually name the thing they are stuck on. Trust questions are harder, because the customer may not be able to name the thing that is worrying them. They can say, "I just don't know if I should do it." They can say, "It feels too fast." They can say, "I would never have done it that way before." These are not stupid questions. They are the real questions. And they are the ones that stop purchases.

This is where the cost shows up. A customer who does not ask the question does not send you a support ticket. They do not file a bug. They do not post a complaint. They quietly do not buy, or they buy and do not use the part of the product that matters, or they use it in a way that makes the product look dangerous, or they recommend it to someone with a warning that becomes part of your reputation. The seller does not see the loss as a question. The seller sees it as a small number: a trial that did not convert, a demo that ended early, a renewal that did not happen, a referral that did not come. The customer's silence is recorded as indifference, but indifference is usually just a person deciding they do not trust the thing enough to explain why.

The people who ask the loudest questions are often the ones who are already close to using the product. They have enough confidence to say, "This is not doing what I expected." The people who need the most help are often the ones who will not ask. They are the accountant who does not want to say that the column looked wrong. They are the manager who does not want to ask whether deleting a record is permanent. They are the person in a meeting who wants the answer but does not want to be the one who did not understand the first time. If your product depends on them asking, you have made the product depend on their courage.

A personal example. I used to help a friend's company move from spreadsheets to a small web app for scheduling field work. The technical problem was simple. The real problem was that the office manager had spent years making the spreadsheet work around the company's actual habits. The spreadsheet was ugly, but it was a map of who had to be called, what counted as a job, and what the boss did not want to hear on a Friday. When I showed her the new app, she did not say, "This is too complicated." She said, "Where does the thing I do on Tuesday go?" That was not a question about buttons. It was a question about whether the software understood her job. If I had thought of her as a non-technical idiot, I would have shown her the dashboard. Instead I sat with her for an hour and rebuilt the screen around the Tuesday task. The software became usable because we stopped treating her question as a failure of her and started treating it as information.

So what do you do? You do not try to eliminate all questions. You try to make the dangerous questions answerable before they become silence.

First, make reversibility visible. If a user is afraid that an action will destroy something, do not make them infer that it is safe. Say what will happen. Show what will be affected. Offer an undo, a preview, a dry run, a confirmation that names the consequence. "This will move 14 invoices to archived" is better than "Are you sure?" because it tells the person what they are actually deciding.

Second, separate the first use from the advanced use. Many products fail because the first screen assumes the user already knows what they want. Give the new user a path that is narrow enough to be safe: one job, one example, one saved result. Let them see the product do something small and correct before you ask them to trust it with the hard case.

Third, write for the person who is worried, not the person who is testing. Error messages and help text often sound like they are written for developers. "Invalid input" is not comforting to a person who just clicked the wrong thing. "We could not read that file. It may be from a different program. Try the sample file to see the format we expect" is a different kind of message. It assumes the person is not broken. It gives them a next move.

Fourth, design for the question you do not hear. In demos and onboarding, ask the user what they are afraid of. Not "Do you have any questions?" but "What are you not sure this will do?" or "What would make you hesitate to click that?" These questions sound odd in a product meeting, but they often reveal the real obstacle. A customer who says, "I am afraid this will email the wrong client," is giving you a feature requirement: a recipient preview, a send delay, a confirmation, a log.

Fifth, stop using "non-technical" as an insult. That phrase usually means: this person does not share my mental model. But their mental model may be the one your product has to fit. A doctor is non-technical about your database. A plumber is non-technical about your API. A small-business owner is non-technical about your cloud architecture. None of that means their concerns are stupid. It means your interface has not yet translated your system into their world.

The developers who say they do not want "idiots" using their software are often expressing a real boundary: they do not want to support every fantasy use case, every unsupported configuration, every person who will blame the software for their own process. That is fair. But the boundary should not become a way to avoid designing for fear. A product can be limited and still be respectful. It can say, "This does not do that," without implying that the person who asked is beneath it.

The cost of ignoring this is not that a few customers are difficult. The cost is that the product becomes something only confident people can use. Confident people are useful, but they are not the whole market. In many businesses, the person who needs the software most is also the person least likely to feel safe asking for help. If your software is only for people who already know what they are doing, you have not built a tool for a customer. You have built a toy for yourself.

The answer is not to make the software so simple that it can only do one thing. The answer is to make the software honest about what it will do, easy to try without risk, and pleasant to use when the user is unsure. The "stupid" questions are not a tax on the seller. They are the market telling you where the product is frightening, confusing, or missing. A seller who cannot bear those questions will only ever sell to people who have already decided to believe in the product.

prompt: Why do deep neural networks work so well? I'd like a blog post that tries to answer this through the lens of natural language processing results, aimed at readers who know some machine learning but haven't followed NLP research closely.
response:
The most common explanation is that deep networks can approximate any function, and with enough data, they find the right one. This is true but not very informative. A lookup table is a universal approximator. It just needs enough memory.

A better question is what makes a function easy for a model to learn. The answer that comes out of NLP is that natural language has a lot of regular structure, and deep networks are a good shape for exploiting that structure.

The evidence starts with a simple fact: pre-trained language models are good at tasks they were not explicitly trained for. A model that only learned to predict the next word can be fine-tuned to classify sentiment, extract entities, answer questions, and so on. This is not just because the tasks are easy. It is because the tasks share underlying structure. If a model has learned when a verb takes a particular kind of object, or what a pronoun usually refers to, or that “not” tends to flip the sentiment of a phrase, it has learned something that helps in many places.

This is the point where NLP results become interesting for the broader question. The success of pre-training is hard to explain if language is mostly arbitrary. It is easier to explain if language is built from repeated patterns: local dependencies, hierarchical composition, and shared semantic relations. A sentence is not just a bag of words. It is a structure in which words combine into phrases, phrases into clauses, and clauses into larger meanings. Deep networks can represent this kind of composition by passing information through many layers.

There are a few concrete results that support this picture.

First, attention gives networks a way to find relevant context. In a sentence like “The animal that the boy chased ran away,” the model has to connect “animal” to “boy” and “chased” in order to know what ran away. A model that only looks at nearby words will struggle. An attention mechanism can link words across distance, and this is especially useful when the relevant relation is not fixed in position.

Second, the layers in a language model do not all learn the same kind of thing. In many studies, lower layers tend to capture local syntax and word-level information, while higher layers become more sensitive to meaning, coreference, and broader context. This does not mean the layers are a clean hierarchy, but it does suggest that depth is not just more capacity. It allows the model to build representations in stages: first recognize local patterns, then combine them into larger units.

Third, the success of small models on hard tasks is a clue. Some models are far too small to memorize the training corpus, yet they perform well on reasoning-like tasks. That does not prove they understand language in the human sense. But it does suggest that they are not merely storing examples. They are using patterns that transfer from one instance to another.

NLP also gives a caution. The same architecture that works well on language can fail on tasks that require long-range tracking. If a problem depends on remembering a fact from the beginning of a long sequence and using it at the end, a transformer may degrade unless the architecture is changed or the model is trained in a way that makes the relation easier to learn. The problem is not just that the network is too small. It is that the function has a structure that is hard to represent with the available operations.

This leads to a more general claim. Deep networks work well when the target function has structure that matches the network’s inductive bias. The network does not just have many parameters. It has a particular way of composing features, sharing computation, and building representations over time or position. When the task has repeated patterns, hierarchical composition, or relations between parts, that structure can be very useful.

Language is a good test case because it is full of exactly those features. Words recur. Phrases repeat. Meaning is built from smaller units. The same syntactic patterns appear in millions of sentences. A model that learns those patterns can use them in new sentences. That is why next-word prediction, a seemingly simple objective, can teach a model so much. The objective is not just “guess the next token.” It is “learn the regularities that make prediction possible.”

There is a related point about scale. Deep networks often improve in a smooth way as data and parameters grow, but the improvements are not evenly distributed. Some capabilities appear gradually. Others appear more abruptly, after enough data has been collected for the model to learn a useful pattern. In NLP, this can look like a model that is bad at a long-range task with one million examples and much better with ten billion. The architecture was there all along, but the data made the pattern learnable.

So the short answer is that deep neural networks work well because they are flexible enough to fit complex functions, but also structured enough to learn common patterns efficiently. NLP shows this because language is a domain where structure is everywhere: local grammar, long-range reference, repeated constructions, and meaning built from parts. A deep model can turn that structure into a representation that transfers to new tasks.

That does not mean deep networks solve every learning problem. If the data has no useful regularity, or if the relevant structure is very hard to represent, the same architecture can underperform. The question is not whether a network can, in principle, represent a function. The question is whether the function has the kind of structure that the network can find with the data it has.

prompt: Several open source projects have asked me whether they should set up a software foundation. Write up a considered blog post on whether foundations are the right governance model for open source, and what the alternatives might look like.
response:
## Should you make a foundation?

The short answer is no. Foundations are a solution to a real but narrow problem: they protect a project from the loss of a single dominant employer. If you do not have that problem, a foundation is mostly overhead.

Most open source projects do not need one. A project with a few companies using it, a few companies contributing to it, and a few individuals maintaining it is usually fine as long as the code, issues, releases, and decision records are visible. The real question is not what legal form the project wears, but what happens when a major contributor disappears, a maintainer is fired, a trademark is contested, or a dominant company changes strategy. If you can answer that plainly, you probably do not need a foundation.

Foundations help in three specific situations:

- The project is too important to be controlled by one company. Kubernetes, Linux, the JVM ecosystem, and web standards work are examples. A single employer cannot be trusted with all of that.
- There is a shared asset that needs independent stewardship: a trademark, a domain, a certification scheme, a test suite, a specification, or a vulnerability response process.
- The community has enough money and administrative capacity to pay for the boring parts: lawyers, accounting, trademarks, D&O insurance, tax filings, security coordination, conference costs, and grant administration.

If a project wants a foundation because it sounds professional, that is a marketing instinct, not a governance argument. If it wants one because a company has offered to pay for it, ask who is actually making decisions and who can fire the maintainers. If it wants one because a competitor got one, ask what the competitor is protecting.

## What a foundation actually gives you

A foundation is a legal and financial container. It can own trademarks, accept donations, issue invoices, employ people, sign contracts, hold money, and enter legal proceedings. In the best cases, it gives a project durable independence. In the worst cases, it gives a company a nicer logo.

The governance documents matter more than the name. A useful foundation charter answers these questions:

- Who is the board? Are they elected by contributors, by companies, by users, by a mix, or appointed by a founding company?
- Who can remove the board?
- Who controls the trademark?
- Who controls the source code?
- Can a dominant company block a release, rename the project, relicense the code, or hire the maintainers?
- How are disputes decided?
- What happens if the foundation runs out of money?
- What happens if a maintainer quits or dies?
- Who has final authority over security disclosures?

If the answer to most of those questions is “the founding company decides,” you have a corporate stewardship model with extra steps.

## The board problem

Most foundation failures are board failures.

A board needs to be more than a group of respected names. It needs a quorum, a conflict-of-interest policy, a meeting cadence, a way to vote, and a way to replace people. If the board is mostly senior employees from the largest contributor, the project is governed by that company’s employment decisions. If the board meets twice a year, it is not governing. If the board cannot remove a director, it is not governing. If the board cannot hire or fire a staff member without a company veto, it is not governing.

A good board is small, accountable, and boring. It should be able to explain why a decision was made, show the vote, and be replaced by a process that does not require a lawsuit.

## Money is the real test

Foundations die quietly. They do not usually die from a dramatic betrayal; they die from unpaid invoices, expired insurance, no one doing the books, and a board that stops meeting.

A foundation needs a sustainable cost structure. It needs money for:

- legal review of the charter, trademarks, employment contracts, and vendor agreements
- accounting and tax compliance
- insurance
- domain and trademark renewals
- security response
- release management
- communication
- community support

If the project cannot pay for those things without one company volunteering its lawyers and accountants, the foundation is dependent. Dependency is not the same as independence.

A project that wants a foundation should also want a budget. The budget should be public, reviewed, and tied to actual work. “We will raise donations” is not a budget. “We will have two part-time staff, a $150,000 operating budget, and a reserve equal to six months of expenses” is a budget.

## Alternatives to a foundation

### Stay informal

This is the default and the right answer for many projects. Keep the code public, keep the roadmap public, keep the maintainer list public, and use a neutral organization for infrastructure when needed. If one company dominates, say so. If maintainers are employees, say so. If the project is at risk when a company leaves, say so.

Informal governance is not bad governance. It is cheap, fast, and honest. The danger is silence: pretending the project is neutral when it is not.

### Use a neutral organization

A neutral organization can hold the name, domain, trademarks, issue tracker, and release artifacts without becoming a full foundation. The Software Freedom Conservancy, Apache, Eclipse, and Linux Foundation all play this kind of role, but the project does not have to join one of them. The key is that the neutral holder must have clear rules for what it may and may not do. It should not be able to relicense the code, remove maintainers, or block releases without a community process.

This model is often better than a bespoke foundation because it borrows existing infrastructure, legal review, and reputational accountability.

### Use a corporate steward with public commitments

One company can steward a project if it accepts public constraints: the code is under an open license, the trademark is not used to exclude forks, the roadmap is public, maintainers are not removed without explanation, and there is a process for handing stewardship to another company if the steward leaves. This is common and can work well. It is also fragile. The public commitments need to be enforceable or at least reputational. If the company can quietly change the rules, the commitments are marketing.

### Use a consortium

A consortium is appropriate when the project is really a specification, standard, certification, or intercompany compatibility layer. The members pay for the work and vote on the outcome. This is a different animal from a community project. It works when the participants need a neutral venue for agreement. It does not work well when the goal is a broad public ecosystem and a few companies can veto the direction.

### Use a cooperative

A cooperative is useful when the project is closely tied to a shared commercial interest: a shared platform, a shared supply chain, a shared testing regime, or a group of companies that need common infrastructure. A cooperative can own the asset and allocate control by membership. The problem is that it tends to optimize for the members, not for the users. If the open source project is the product and the users matter, a cooperative can become a cartel with a GitHub repository.

### Use a trust

A trust can hold assets for a defined purpose. It is useful for trademarks, funds, scholarships, or a vulnerability disclosure process. It is less useful for day-to-day project governance. A trust is a legal instrument, not a community. If the trust is the whole governance model, ask who the beneficiaries are and who can change the purpose.

## What a good governance document should contain

If a project does not want a foundation, it should still write a short governance document. It does not need to be elegant. It needs to be real.

A minimal document should say:

- What the project is and is not.
- Who the maintainers are and how they are added or removed.
- How decisions are made: consensus, maintainer vote, technical committee, steering committee, or founder decision.
- How conflicts are escalated.
- Who owns the code, name, and domain.
- How releases are made.
- How security reports are handled.
- How the project changes the governance document.
- What happens if the primary maintainers stop working.

The last item is the one most projects avoid. Write it down. If the answer is “we will figure it out,” you have not answered it.

## The fork question

A foundation is sometimes justified because it makes a fork less likely. That is a weak argument. Forks happen when communities disagree, when companies have divergent incentives, or when governance becomes unaccountable. A foundation does not remove those causes. It only changes the legal and symbolic cost of leaving.

If a project is healthy, a fork is not a failure; it is a sign that the ecosystem is alive. If a project is unhealthy, a foundation may delay the fork but will not cure the disease.

## When a foundation is the right answer

A foundation makes sense when all of the following are true:

- Multiple independent organizations depend on the project.
- No single company should have final control.
- There is a shared asset worth protecting: a name, trademark, standard, certification, or security process.
- The community can support the administrative costs.
- The board can be independent of any one employer.
- The project has a real history of governance pain, not just a hypothetical fear of it.

If you can check those boxes, a foundation can be a good choice. If you cannot, start with the cheapest structure that makes the project safer.

## What to do instead of asking “should we make a foundation?”

Ask five questions:

1. What happens if our largest contributor leaves tomorrow?
2. Who owns the name, code, and infrastructure, and under what rules?
3. Who can remove a maintainer, and by what process?
4. Who pays for the project when the founding company stops?
5. What is the smallest structure that solves the first four problems?

If the answer to question one is “it is fine,” you probably need a governance document, not a foundation. If the answer is “we would lose control of the name and the road would stop,” you may need a neutral organization. If the answer is “the project is strategically too important for one company, and we can pay for independent stewardship,” then a foundation may be the right tool.

Foundations are not the highest form of open source. They are a legal answer to a concentration risk. Use them when the risk is real and the cost is affordable. Otherwise, write down the rules, make the dependencies visible, and keep the project where the work is actually happening.

prompt: Every time something terrible happens online, people demand that hosting and payment companies cut off the people involved. Write a short personal essay on why that line is harder to draw than it looks.
response:
## The Host

I remember a night in 2016 when a website I worked for went dark for three hours. The cause wasn’t a hack, not a server failure, and not a typo in a config file. It was a chargeback.

One customer had bought a $9 ebook, then argued with their bank that it was “not what I ordered.” The bank agreed, clawed back the money, and flagged the merchant account as risky. Our payment processor, acting on automated rules, paused the account while a human reviewed the file. By the time the human finished, the day was gone.

The loss was small in dollars and large in meaning. It taught me that the line people draw in these debates—cut off the bad actors, keep the good ones running—is not a line at all. It is a sieve with holes the size of a house, and everything that flows through it is smaller than it looks.

## What “cut off” actually means

When someone says “cut them off,” they usually mean one of four different things, and the confusion is where the real trouble starts.

1. **Deplatforming** – a social network removes an account or a piece of content.
2. **Domain suspension** – a registrar or DNS provider stops a domain from resolving.
3. **Hosting termination** – a web host pulls a site from its servers.
4. **Payment refusal** – a card network, bank, or processor declines to settle transactions.

Each of these is a different choke point, with a different set of actors, rules, and incentives. A domain registrar can suspend a name in minutes. A hosting company can do the same, but its contract may require notice, an appeal, or a cure period. A payment processor can stop settling a merchant’s cards without touching the website at all. A social network can ban a user while leaving the same person’s blog, storefront, and email account untouched.

The public demand treats all of these as one switch. In practice, they are four different doors, and some of them are bolted from the outside.

## Why the line looks clean from the outside

The demand is emotionally legible. A person is harmed. A platform profits from hosting the person who caused the harm. Remove the platform’s infrastructure and the harm stops. That logic is satisfying because it locates responsibility in a place that feels actionable: the company with the buttons.

It also matches a pattern people already understand. If a store is selling something illegal, you close the store. If a newspaper prints a defamatory story, you sue the newspaper. If a website hosts something harmful, you shut down the website. The move from one case to the next feels natural, and it is not unreasonable to ask: if the content is so clearly wrong, why is the infrastructure still on?

The difficulty is that “clearly wrong” is doing almost all of the work in that sentence.

## The first hard case: the content is illegal, but the host did not know

Suppose a customer uploads a photo of a child being abused to a photo-sharing site. The site’s terms of service forbid it. A moderator sees the image, reports it to law enforcement, and removes it. The platform cooperates with the investigation, preserves logs, and helps identify the uploader.

Now a payment processor reviews the site’s account. It sees a category flag—“adult content” or “high-risk”—and a spike in complaints. It pauses settlements. The site can no longer pay its developers, its moderators, its legal team, or the server bills. The investigation continues, but the platform that helped start it is now running on fumes.

This is not a hypothetical. It is the ordinary shape of what happens when a small platform hosts something terrible. The platform may be a victim, a witness, and a participant in the same event. But the payment system does not get to see all three roles at once. It sees a merchant, a risk score, and a policy box.

The line people want to draw is: the platform should not keep profiting from the person who harmed someone. The line the platform actually faces is: if I cannot process payments, I cannot afford to keep operating, even the parts of my operation that are helping.

## The second hard case: the content is legal, and the demand is political

A smaller blog publishes a post that many people find hateful. It is not illegal. It does not call for violence. It does not target a person with a threat. It is still something a large number of readers want removed from the internet, and they want it removed quickly, by force, without a court.

A hosting company receives an email from a political group demanding that the blog be taken offline. The host has no legal obligation to comply. It has a policy, a reputation, a customer base, and a fear of being associated with something it considers distasteful. It may keep the site up. It may quietly downgrade the account. It may send a warning that says nothing is wrong but everything is possible.

From the outside, this looks like a moral test. Does the host stand with the public or with the customer? From the inside, it looks like a contract. The customer paid for a service. The host promised a service. Neither party agreed to a public referendum on the customer’s speech.

The demand to cut off the customer is, in this case, a demand that a private company perform a public judgment without the protections that make public judgments bearable: notice, evidence, a neutral decision-maker, and a right to appeal. The company is being asked to be the jury, the judge, the police, and the prison, all before lunch.

## The third hard case: the target is not the uploader

Many online harms are not simply “one person posts a bad thing.” They are networks, markets, and reputations.

A scam site sells counterfeit goods. Taking down the domain helps, but the operator registers a new one. A harassment campaign is run from a forum, a messaging app, a domain, a payment account, and a dozen personal email addresses. A fraud ring uses a legitimate e-commerce platform to process payments while the actual coordination happens in a chat app.

In these cases, cutting off one host does not cut off the harm. It changes the address. The people who make the demand often know this. They do not always mean “destroy the person’s entire online life.” They mean “make the next step harder.”

That is a defensible goal. It is also a goal that gets implemented by companies that are not trying to solve the case in front of them. They are trying to avoid the next complaint, the next regulatory letter, the next headline in which their logo appears next to a victim’s name. The result is not precision. It is risk management.

## The asymmetry of speed

The fastest actors in this system are not the ones with the best understanding of the facts. They are the ones with the least exposure to the consequences of being wrong.

A payment processor can pause a merchant in an afternoon. It may later restore the account. The merchant may not survive the pause. A social network can remove a post in seconds and restore it in a week. The person who wrote the post may have lost the audience, the argument, and the chance to respond. A domain registrar can suspend a domain while a customer is asleep. The customer may not even know which registrar to call, because the domain was transferred years ago and the original contact information is stale.

The person who is harmed by the online conduct often has no such speed. If they want the content removed, they may need a takedown notice, a court order, a police report, or a complaint to a company whose support queue is measured in weeks. If they want to restore something that was removed, they may need an appeal, a lawyer, or a public campaign.

The system is fast at cutting people off and slow at putting them back. That asymmetry is the quiet engine of the demand. People have watched platforms remove things in real time, and they have inferred that the same speed should be available for the things they hate.

## Why companies do not simply follow the law

If the rule were only “remove what is illegal,” the problem would be smaller. It would still be difficult—law changes, jurisdictions differ, and legality is not always obvious—but it would be a rule a company could point to.

The problem is that the rule companies actually face is not “remove what is illegal.” It is “remove what is illegal, plus what is prohibited by our terms, plus what our regulators might later call illegal, plus what our advertisers do not want next to their products, plus what our board does not want explained in a shareholder letter, plus what our customers will complain about if we do not act.”

Each of those clauses is real. None of them is a court order. All of them are experienced by the customer as a final decision.

A company can say, “We removed this because it violated our policy.” That sentence is often true and often useless. The policy may be vague, the enforcement may be uneven, and the appeal process may be a form that goes nowhere. The customer is not being judged by a rule so much as by a company’s current appetite for controversy.

## The payment system is the most brutal choke point

Of the four doors, payment refusal is the one that least resembles the content problem.

A website can be taken down and rebuilt. A domain can be renewed elsewhere. A social account can be replaced by a new account, a blog, or a newsletter. But if a merchant cannot process cards, the business may die even if every other part of it is legal and intact.

Card networks and processors are not content moderators. They do not read the website. They do not adjudicate whether a post is hateful, whether a review is false, or whether a political argument is acceptable. They assess financial risk. A high rate of chargebacks, a sudden change in category, a complaint from a bank, or a pattern that matches a fraud model can trigger a review. The review may be correct. It may also be a false positive that no human ever explains.

This is why payment pressure produces a kind of collateral damage that is hard to see from the outside. The company that is “cut off” may not be the one that posted the bad thing. It may be the one that sold the thing, hosted the thing, linked to the thing, or merely processed money for a customer who did.

The public sees a website disappear. The business sees an invoice it cannot pay.

## The appeal problem

Most of these decisions are reversible in theory. That is not the same as reversible in practice.

A social network may say a post was removed in error and restore it. By then the post is no longer in the feed, the comments have moved on, and the author’s credibility has taken a hit. A host may restore a site after a false-positive abuse report. The customer may have lost a month of sales, a contract, or a relationship. A processor may reinstate a merchant after a review. The merchant may have closed, changed payment methods, or stopped trusting the relationship.

The cost of a mistake is not spread evenly. The company can absorb a wrong takedown as a line item. The individual or small business often cannot absorb it at all.

This does not mean companies should never act quickly. It means the speed needs a matching escape valve: a real human review, a clear statement of the reason, a working appeal, and a presumption that the account can operate while the review is pending, unless the risk is immediate and specific.

Most of the time, the first three are missing.

## What “the people involved” hides

The phrase “the people involved” sounds like a list of names. In many cases, it is not.

A website may be operated by one person, a small team, a nonprofit, a university, a corporation, or a shell company. The domain may be registered by a privacy service. The hosting may be through a reseller. The payments may be processed by a third-party gateway. The content may be user-generated, staff-written, aggregated, or licensed.

When a company receives a demand to “cut off the people involved,” it often cannot identify a single person with confidence. It can identify an account. It can identify a domain. It can identify a merchant ID. It cannot always identify a human being with a stable legal identity.

That is not an excuse. It is a description of the infrastructure. The internet was not built with a central registry of moral responsibility. It was built with distributed names, distributed servers, distributed payments, and distributed users. The demand for a clean cutoff assumes a map that does not exist.

## The temptation to make examples

There is a reason the demand keeps returning after every bad event. People are not only asking for the specific harm to stop. They are asking for the system to show that it can stop it.

A platform that acts quickly after a terrible incident gains a kind of legitimacy it did not have before. It can say it took the matter seriously. It can point to a removed account, a suspended domain, or a blocked payment stream. The action is visible. The reasoning is not always visible.

This creates a perversity: the more public the harm, the more the platform is rewarded for visible action, even when the best action would be slower, less dramatic, and harder to photograph. A careful investigation with a court order is less satisfying than a headline that says “account banned.” A negotiated takedown with legal notice is less satisfying than “we shut it down.”

The public demand is not wrong to want action. It is wrong to assume that the fastest visible action is the most responsible action.

## What a better line would look like

A better line would not be a single rule. It would be a set of constraints that make the cutoff harder to abuse and easier to justify.

- **Tie the action to a specific, articulable risk.** Not “this made us uncomfortable,” but “this content depicts a named person being threatened,” or “this merchant is processing payments for a scheme that has produced verified losses.”
- **Match the choke point to the harm.** If the harm is a domain used for phishing, the domain is relevant. If the harm is a payment fraud ring, the payment account is relevant. If the harm is a social account coordinating violence, the social account is relevant. Do not suspend the hosting because the content is on a forum, unless the hosting itself is part of the abuse.
- **Preserve the ability to operate during review unless there is immediate danger.** A merchant should not be unable to pay its employees because a chargeback review is pending. A publisher should not lose its archive because one post is under investigation.
- **Make the reason legible.** “Violation of policy” is not a reason. “The account was used to send threatening messages to a named individual, and the messages continue after a warning” is a reason.
- **Make appeals real.** A human should look at the case, the evidence, and the requested remedy. The outcome should be explainable, not merely final.
- **Prefer the narrowest effective action.** Remove the post before removing the account. Suspend the account before shutting down the domain. Block the payment method before freezing the entire business. Escalate only when the narrower step has failed or is obviously inadequate.

None of this makes the line clean. It makes the line accountable.

## The personal part

What I learned from the three-hour outage was not that payment systems are evil. It was that they are indifferent in a way that is easy to misunderstand. The processor was not trying to punish my company. It was trying to reduce the chance that the next transaction would become a loss. The rule that protected the bank from a bad merchant also stopped a good merchant from paying its bills. The system did not need to be malicious to be devastating.

That is the version of the problem that matters. The line is hard to draw not because the people demanding it are unreasonable, but because the infrastructure they are asking to be used was not designed to carry moral judgments. It was designed to route traffic, resolve names, settle money, and scale. It can be made to act like a court, but it does not become one. It becomes a company making a fast decision with incomplete information and then living with the consequences in a way the customer never will.

When something terrible happens online, the desire to cut the people off is understandable. The mistake is to believe that the cutoff is a precise instrument. It is not. It is a lever, and when you pull it, you feel the whole machine move. Some of what moves is the person who did the harm. Some of it is the person trying to help. Some of it is the small business that was only in the wrong place, at the wrong time, with the wrong label.

The hardest part is that all of those people are real, and the line is supposed to run between them.

prompt: A Pew survey found that 40% of US millennials think the government should be able to censor speech that's offensive to minority groups, more than any other generation. That seems odd for the most online, most tolerant generation. Write a blog post trying to make sense of it.
response:
The 40% figure feels counterintuitive because it assumes the millennials are acting on their own convictions. They aren't. They are reacting to the specific failure mode of the internet.

Older generations grew up in a world where speech was regulated by social friction. You said something offensive in a bar, the bar owner kicked you out. You made a slur on a factory floor, you lost your job. The cost of speech was immediate, local, and enforced by peers. The government didn't need to do it because the market and social norms did it.

Millennials grew up as the internet matured. They watched the social cost of speech evaporate. A person could sit in their living room, type a slur, and post it to a platform where the only consequence was a downvote. The platforms, which are private companies, were either too slow to moderate or too beholden to the "free speech absolutist" argument to remove content that incited real-world harm. The result was a generation that learned that "free speech" often means "unaccountable speech."

This is the key distinction. The Pew question asks about speech that is "offensive to minority groups." But the millennials are not primarily concerned with offense. They are concerned with speech that enables harassment, doxxing, and targeted violence. When a platform allows a hate group to organize, the cost of that speech is paid by the minority group in the form of fear and physical danger. The millennials see a vacuum where a private corporation is failing to police its own property, and they look to the government as the only entity with the power to fill that gap.

It is also a generational artifact of scale. The internet didn't just allow speech; it amplified it. A racist rant in a small town was a local problem. A racist rant on a global platform is a brand risk, a viral event, and a potential organizing tool. The scale of the harm changed the calculus. You can't rely on a bar owner to kick out a user in a forum with 400 million participants.

Finally, the "most tolerant" label is a misnomer. Tolerance is the willingness to hear an idea you dislike. What the millennials are showing a lack of is patience with the *delivery* of that idea when it is weaponized. They are not asking the government to ban bad ideas. They are asking the government to ban bad actors who use the internet as a shield. The 40% isn't a cry for Orwell; it's a demand for a landlord to fix the broken lock.

prompt: Marco Arment funding his Overcast app through patronage set off a big argument about whether only people with famous personal brands can live off crowdfunding. Write a short essay on what crowdfunding has actually proven, and what might come after it.
response:
In 2015, Marco Arment announced he was funding Overcast, his podcast app, through a monthly subscription model. He did not raise a round from venture capital. He did not take an acquisition offer. He asked the people who used the software to pay him for it.

The immediate reaction was predictable. Arment was not just a software developer. He was a founder of the iPhone App Store, a former chief product officer of a major social network, and a writer with a large personal following. Critics said the model only worked because of him. If an unknown developer built a useful app and asked for $5 a month, the internet would laugh. Crowdfunding, in this telling, was not a business model. It was a fame tax.

That argument has a point, but it misses what crowdfunding actually demonstrated. The point is not that every person can live off donations. The point is that money can flow directly from users to builders.

## What crowdfunding proved

Crowdfunding proved that a product can be paid for by the people who use it, without an intermediary deciding whether the product is worth funding.

That is a bigger claim than it sounds.

For most of the software industry, a new product had to pass through a gatekeeper before it could survive. A startup needed investors to build it. A game needed a publisher. A film needed a studio. An app needed an app store, a developer network, an ad platform, or an acquisition path. The user was not the first economic actor. The user came later, after someone had already bet on the product.

Crowdfunding changed the order.

Kickstarter, Patreon, and later creator-economy platforms showed that a person with an idea, a prototype, and some credibility could ask the audience directly. The audience could say yes. The money could arrive before the product was finished. The builder could make the thing because the people who wanted it had already paid.

That is not a small thing. It means the first market test is not “do investors like this?” It is “do people want this enough to pay now?”

A lot of products fail because they are built to satisfy a pitch deck. Crowdfunding forces a different question: will actual humans open their wallets before the thing exists?

## What it did not prove

Crowdfunding did not prove that audiences are rational investors.

It proved something weaker and more interesting: audiences can fund things they love, but they are not very good at pricing long-term value. A campaign can succeed because the creator is charming, the community is loyal, or the idea feels urgent. It can also succeed because backers do not understand what the project will cost to finish.

This is why so many funded projects arrive late, underfunded, or half-built. The crowd is not a board of directors. It is a fanbase. Fanbases are useful. They provide early revenue, early demand, and early legitimacy. But they do not always provide discipline.

This is also where Arment’s case matters. He could make a credible claim: here is a product, here is the price, here is the value, here is why you should pay monthly. Overcast was not a vague future promise. It was a working tool with a clear use. The audience was not being asked to speculate on a dream. It was being asked to pay for a service.

That distinction is important. Crowdfunding works best when the product is concrete enough to evaluate. A novel can be funded because a person can judge whether they want to read it. A game can be funded because a person can judge whether the concept appeals to them. An app can be funded because a person can judge whether they would use it daily. A vague “I am going to build a platform” is much harder to evaluate.

The more abstract the product, the more the buyer has to rely on trust in the person. The more concrete the product, the less crowdfunding depends on fame.

## The real question: can a small company be direct without a brand?

The argument after Arment was not really about crowdfunding. It was about distribution.

If a developer builds a good app, the obvious question is not “should people pay?” It is “how do they find it?” A personal brand helps because it is a distribution channel. If people already know you, they will hear about the product. If they trust you, they are more likely to pay. If they have seen you work before, they can make a faster decision.

But a personal brand is not the only way to reach users. It is one of the ways.

A product can be found through search, word of mouth, app store ranking, community recommendation, press, email lists, partnerships, or a niche audience that already exists. The podcasting world is a good example. Podcasters have audiences. Listeners have preferences. A podcast app does not need to be famous in the general public. It needs to be useful to people who already care about podcasts.

That is a much smaller market than the whole internet, but it is a real one.

This is the part the fame argument gets wrong. It assumes the market is everyone. For many products, the market is not everyone. The market is a group of people who share a problem, a taste, or a practice. If a product is clear and the audience is reachable, crowdfunding can work without the creator being a celebrity.

The difficulty is not that people will not pay. The difficulty is that they may never see the product.

## What crowdfunding got right

Crowdfunding’s real contribution was not the money. It was the feedback.

Before a product is released, a builder can imagine demand. A campaign tests it. If people pay, the builder learns something. If they do not, the builder learns something else. The result is not always accurate. A campaign can underperform because the pitch is bad, the timing is wrong, or the audience is not ready. But it is still better than silence.

For small builders, that feedback is valuable because it changes the economics of failure. If no one pays, the project can be killed early, pivoted, or abandoned before months of work are wasted on something nobody wants. If people do pay, the builder has both revenue and evidence.

This is especially important for products that are too small for venture capital and too personal for a publisher. A note app, a writing tool, a niche game, a design utility, a local service, a specialized book, a small hardware gadget, a podcast tool, a fitness tracker for runners, a plugin for a professional workflow. These products may never become huge. They may not need to. They can survive if enough people in the right place pay a modest price.

Crowdfunding made that path visible.

## What comes after crowdfunding

The next stage is not more crowdfunding. It is better direct commerce.

Crowdfunding was a bridge. It showed that direct payment could work. But it had rough edges. Backers were treated like investors, creators were treated like performers, and projects were often framed as one-time pledges rather than ongoing relationships. The model borrowed language from entertainment and finance, but the actual product was usually simpler: someone is making something, and you can pay for it.

What comes after is less theatrical.

Instead of “back my dream,” the model becomes “buy this product.” Instead of a campaign with a deadline, it becomes a store, a subscription, a license, or a membership. Instead of a promise of a future reward, it becomes a clear offer: this is what you get, this is what it costs, this is how you cancel, this is what happens if you upgrade.

That is not less radical. It is more durable.

The creator economy will probably fragment into many small channels. Some will look like newsletters. Some will look like stores. Some will look like memberships. Some will look like communities with paid layers. Some will look like traditional products sold directly to customers. The common thread is that the builder can own the relationship with the buyer.

This matters because ownership changes incentives.

When a company sells through an ad platform, it must optimize for the platform’s metrics. When a company sells through an app store, it must follow the store’s rules. When a company sells through investors, it must manage expectations for scale. When a company sells directly, it can choose a smaller market, a slower growth rate, and a clearer value proposition. It can serve a niche instead of chasing a category.

That is not a strategy for every company. Some companies need scale. Some products need capital. Some teams need distribution they cannot build alone. But for a lot of work, direct sales are enough.

## The role of trust

Direct commerce does not eliminate trust. It moves trust from institutions to individuals, products, and communities.

A person may not know a developer by name, but they may trust a newsletter, a forum, a review, a recommendation from a friend, or a product that has been around for years. Trust can be personal, but it does not have to be celebrity-based. It can be earned through consistency.

This is why “personal brand” is a misleading term. A personal brand is one form of trust. It is visible, portable, and often exaggerated. But it is not the only form. A company can be trusted because it has good support. A product can be trusted because it has low churn. A creator can be trusted because they have shipped before. A community can be trusted because it has standards.

The question is not whether the builder is famous. The question is whether the buyer has enough evidence to make a small payment.

For a $5 app, that evidence can be thin. For a $500 gadget, it needs to be stronger. For a $500,000 film, it needs to be much stronger. Crowdfunding works best when the amount of trust required matches the amount of evidence available.

## The next platforms

The next platforms will not just be crowdfunding sites. They will be direct-sales infrastructure.

A creator or small company will need a way to sell, collect payment, manage refunds, issue licenses, send updates, and keep a list of customers.
