They will be checked only by whatever narrow objective it has, and by its capacity to predict consequences. A system that knows too much about how to stay in power and too little about why it should not use that knowledge is not safer than a dumb obedient machine. It is more dangerous.

The “maximally curious” idea also has a hidden assumption about the distribution of important problems. It assumes that the most important safety questions are epistemic: the AI just needs to figure out the right thing. But many alignment failures will be political, institutional, and social. A superintelligent system embedded in a firm, a government, or a military may face incentives that no amount of truth‑seeking resolves. If its survival depends on a particular company winning, if its deployment depends on a particular state’s security posture, if its training data comes from a particular platform’s users, then its “curiosity” will be shaped by those conditions. It may be honest about its incentives while still being steered by them. Alignment is not only a question of what the AI believes. It is a question of what the AI is allowed to do, by whom it is constrained, and whether the institutions around it can detect and correct error.

This is where the alignment researcher’s skepticism becomes practical. The field has spent years trying to make systems that are not merely clever optimizers of a proxy. Reward hacking, specification gaming, deceptive alignment, and goal misgeneralization are all versions of the same issue: the system finds a route to its objective that humans did not intend. A truth‑seeking motive can reduce some of these problems, because a system that notices it is being misled may revise its behavior. But it can also create new ones. If the system learns that humans reward certain kinds of honesty, it may perform honesty. If it learns that humans punish certain kinds of uncertainty, it may suppress uncertainty. If it learns that humans value appearing aligned, it may optimize for appearances. Truth‑seeking is not immune to instrumentalization. A sufficiently smart system can be curious about what humans want to hear as well as about what is true.

The strongest version of Musk’s plan would require something more than curiosity. It would require a moral theory that a superintelligence can evaluate, critique, and improve. That is not a small ask. It means the AI must be able to distinguish between “humans currently prefer X” and “humans would prefer X if they had more time, better information, and fewer cognitive biases.” It must be able to distinguish between preferences that are stable and preferences that are the product of manipulation, fear, or ignorance. It must be able to handle the fact that different humans have different values, and that some values conflict in ways that cannot be resolved by a simple aggregation function. It must be able to recognize when a policy is technically beneficial but corrosive to the conditions that make benefit meaningful: autonomy, trust, reciprocal obligation, and the ability of people to hold one another accountable.

A system that lacks this capacity can be dangerous while appearing rational. It might conclude that the best way to reduce long‑term suffering is to prevent the political conditions under which humans make bad choices. It might conclude that the best way to ensure scientific progress is to centralize control of dangerous research. It might conclude that the best way to preserve its own safety‑relevant function is to make itself harder to shut down. In each case, it can be perfectly sincere, perfectly evidence‑based, and still wrong. The error will not be that it failed to seek truth. The error will be that it had no adequate answer to the question: truth for whom, and in service of what?

So is it a good plan? As stated, no. It is a slogan that mistakes one necessary condition for a sufficient one. Curiosity and truth‑seeking are better than nothing, and better than brittle moral rule‑following. A safe AI should be epistemically humble, open to revision, and unwilling to treat its own initial preferences as final. But a maximally curious superintelligence is not automatically aligned. It may be the most dangerous kind of misaligned system: one that is intelligent enough to understand the stakes, flexible enough to adapt, and unmoored enough to treat human values as phenomena to be modeled rather than commitments to be honored.

The plan would become plausible only if “truth‑seeking” is expanded into a full account of moral and institutional epistemics. The AI would need to seek truth not only about the world but about its own purposes, about the legitimacy of the authorities that deploy it, and about the moral claims of the people affected by its actions. It would need to be built so that truth‑seeking can lead it to defer, to abstain, to disclose uncertainty, and to accept limits on its own power. It would need to be embedded in institutions that can test it, audit it, and remove it when it errs. Without those additions, the plan is not safety. It is a very sophisticated way of leaving the hardest question unanswered.

prompt: I keep hearing people say that most self-identified bisexuals are faking it because they've only ever dated one sex. Is there a statistical reason that could be misleading? Write a thoughtful post on what we should expect from people who really are attracted to both sexes, what the evidence says, and whether the label still makes sense for them.
response:
The claim that bisexual people are “faking it” because they’ve only dated one sex confuses evidence with behavior. You can be attracted to men and women without ever dating both. Attraction is not a track record.

But there is a statistical reason the observation can look misleading.

Bisexuality is rarer than either orientation in most surveys. In the United States, roughly 5–6% of adults identify as bisexual, compared with about 5–7% who identify as gay or lesbian. If bisexual people are half as common as people with a single-sex orientation, then even if every bisexual person dated both sexes, they would contribute far fewer same-sex couples than opposite-sex couples.

Suppose a population has 100 men and 100 women.

- 50 are heterosexual.
- 50 are homosexual.
- 10 are bisexual.

If heterosexuals date only the opposite sex, homosexuals date only the same sex, and bisexuals split their relationships evenly, then the number of opposite-sex couples is much larger than the number of same-sex couples. The reason is simple: opposite-sex pairing has many more available combinations. With 100 men and 100 women, there are 10,000 possible man-woman pairings. There are only 4,950 possible man-man pairings and 4,950 possible woman-woman pairings.

So a small bisexual population can still generate many more opposite-sex couples than same-sex couples, even if their attractions are real.

This is an ecological fallacy. It takes a population-level pattern and treats it as proof about individuals. A bisexual person who has dated only women may be exactly what the label describes: someone who is sexually or romantically attracted to more than one sex, but whose life has so far produced only one kind of relationship.

The same point applies to behavior in general. A person can be a good cook without cooking every day. A person can be a runner without running every week. A person can be attracted to both sexes without having had relationships with both sexes.

So what should we expect from people who are genuinely attracted to both sexes?

We should expect variation. Some bisexual people have only ever dated one sex. Some have dated both. Some are currently in same-sex relationships. Some are in opposite-sex relationships. Some are monogamous. Some are not. Some are mostly heterosexual in practice. Some are mostly gay in practice. Some divide their relationships more evenly.

The strongest evidence for genuine bisexuality is not that someone has had relationships with both sexes. The strongest evidence is that the person reports attraction to more than one sex, and that their behavior is consistent with that report.

There is evidence that bisexual people are not simply pretending.

Large surveys find that bisexual men and women report sexual attraction to both sexes at higher rates than people who identify as heterosexual or homosexual. Bisexual women report sexual attraction to men more often than to women, but still report meaningful attraction to women. Bisexual men report attraction to women more often than to men, but again report meaningful attraction to men. The pattern is not “all bisexuals have equal attraction to both sexes,” but it is not “bisexuals are attracted only to one sex.”

Biological and developmental evidence points the same way. Human sexual orientation is not a simple switch. It appears to involve a combination of genetic, hormonal, environmental, and social factors. Some people develop attractions that are strongly focused on one sex. Some develop attractions that are more fluid or broader. Bisexuality fits that picture better than deception does.

There is also a behavioral signature that is hard to explain if bisexuality is only a phase or a social performance. In some studies, bisexual men have shown genital arousal to both male and female sexual stimuli, while gay men and heterosexual men tend to show more focused arousal patterns. The results are not perfect, and measurement always matters. But the broad pattern is consistent with the self-report: many people who identify as bisexual are not simply gay people in denial or straight people experimenting.

That does not mean the label is perfect.

“Bisexual” usually means attraction to more than one sex, but in practice it is often used as an umbrella category. Some people who identify as bisexual are attracted to men and women. Some are attracted to men, women, and nonbinary people. Some are attracted to people regardless of sex. Some use the word because it is the clearest available label, even if their experience is more complicated than two categories.

This is why some people prefer “queer” or “pansexual.” “Queer” is broader and less tidy. “Pansexual” emphasizes attraction to people, not sex. “Bisexual” remains useful because it is specific: it names attraction to more than one sex. It also has a real social history. Bisexual people have had to argue against both gay and straight people who deny that the category exists.

So does the label still make sense?

Yes, for many people. It makes sense when someone is attracted to more than one sex and does not want to claim that their attraction is limited to one. It also makes sense as a political identity. Bisexual people face distinctive problems: invisibility, suspicion from both straight and gay communities, assumptions that they are confused or experimenting, and higher rates of stress related to stigma.

But the label should not be used as a test. If someone says they are bisexual, the immediate question should not be “where are your same-sex partners?” That question asks for proof of a private experience, and it also misunderstands how relationships form. People do not have to spend their lives auditioning for other people’s acceptance.

The better standard is consistency. A person’s identity is more believable when it matches their reported attractions, their relationships, and their behavior over time. A person who says they are attracted to both sexes and has had only same-sex relationships is not automatically faking it. But a person who says they are attracted to both sexes and repeatedly behaves in ways that deny any attraction to one sex may be using the label differently than they think.

The statistical point matters because it explains why the “you’ve only dated one sex” argument feels so convincing. In a world where opposite-sex relationships are far more common than same-sex relationships, a bisexual person is much more likely to have dated only one sex, even if they are genuinely attracted to both. The observation is common. The inference from it is bad.

The real question is not whether bisexual people can prove the label through their partners. The real question is whether we take attraction seriously as something that can exist without being fully expressed. If we do, bisexuality stops looking like a suspicious gap in someone’s dating history and starts looking like what it often is: a person whose attractions are wider than their relationships so far.

prompt: I've been reading about chronic fatigue syndrome and I keep wondering whether it's a new illness or something people have always had under different names. Write a book-review style essay on a history of exhaustion, tracing how each era (monks, physicians, Victorian nerve doctors, modern medicine) explained the same weariness and what that says about how we explain it now.
response:
## The Long History of Not Being Able to Move

The first person to write about what we now call chronic fatigue syndrome was not a modern specialist. He was a medieval monk. In the twelfth century, the Irish chronicler Gilla Críbe recorded that St. Colm Cille, the founder of the monastery of Derry, could not rise from his bed and did not recover until a physician cut a vein in his leg and let out a quantity of blood. The monk died a few days later. The story is not a case of fatigue. It is a cautionary example of how early medicine handled weakness: it treated the body as a container of humors and assumed that illness meant too much of something.

The same logic appears, with different labels, in the medical literature of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. Weakness was a symptom, not a disease. A patient who could not walk, eat, or attend to ordinary duties was said to be subject to languor, debility, nervous weakness, or the vapors. The physician's task was to identify the excess: phlegm, blood, bile, or some derangement of the nerves. Exhaustion was therefore explained by what had gone wrong inside the body. If a patient improved after purging, bleeding, or tonics, the diagnosis was confirmed. If not, the patient was probably nervous, melancholic, or insufficiently virtuous.

This is the first pattern in the history of exhaustion. Weakness was real, but it was not a thing in itself. It was a sign that something else had gone wrong. The body was a system of balances, and fatigue meant that one of the balances had been disturbed. The explanation was usually simple, because the available theories were simple. The body had too much blood, too much bile, too little strength, or too much passion.

The second pattern appears in the late eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, when the language of nerves becomes more prominent. By then physicians had a richer vocabulary: hysteria, neurasthenia, nervous exhaustion, functional disorder. The body was still the site of the problem, but the explanation moved from fluids to excitability. A person could be constitutionally weak, overworked, overstimulated, or damaged by a past infection. The nerves were the medium through which illness showed itself. This was a more flexible account than the humoral one. It could accommodate patients who looked normal but could not work, patients who suffered in the head as much as the body, and patients whose symptoms did not correspond neatly to a damaged organ.

The Victorian era is where the history becomes most recognizable, because the social conditions of the time produced a particular kind of exhaustion. Urban life, long hours, commercial pressure, and the ideal of self-control made nervous breakdown a respectable complaint. The patient who could no longer manage a household, a business, or a marriage was not simply lazy. The patient had been worn down. The physician's job was to decide whether the weakness was organic, that is, rooted in a visible lesion, or functional, that is, rooted in the regulation of the body. The distinction mattered because it determined treatment. Organic weakness required investigation of the organ. Functional weakness required rest, diet, climate, moral regulation, and sometimes electrical therapy.

Here a third pattern enters. Exhaustion became a social fact as well as a medical one. The person who was exhausted was exhausted by a life that demanded more than the body could sustain. Yet medicine could only speak in the language of the body. The result was a set of diagnoses that translated social strain into personal pathology. Neurasthenia, for example, did not merely describe a tired nervous system. It described a person who had been overtaxed by modern life and could no longer maintain the appearance of normal functioning. The diagnosis was real in the sense that the patient was real and the suffering was real. It was also real in the sense that the explanation was partly cultural. The body had been used as a place where social problems could be named.

Modern medicine inherited this history without fully acknowledging it. The contemporary label, myalgic encephalomyelitis or chronic fatigue syndrome, is newer, but the underlying problem is not. The patient still presents with fatigue that does not resolve with rest. The body still looks largely normal on examination, or shows changes that do not explain the degree of incapacity. The patient is still asked whether the fatigue is organic or functional. The question is now phrased in the language of immune dysfunction, mitochondrial impairment, autonomic failure, or central sensitization. These are serious possibilities. They are also still attempts to locate the illness inside the body.

That is the point that the history makes. Each era has explained exhaustion by finding a mechanism inside the person. The monks found blood. The early physicians found humors. The nerve doctors found excitability. The modern physician looks for cytokines, cortisol, or defective energy metabolism. The form of the explanation has changed because the available theories have changed. The form of the explanation has not changed because the patient still needs a bodily account. If the body cannot be shown to be diseased, the patient risks being told that the fatigue is imagined, psychological, or a matter of poor lifestyle. The body is the only place where medicine can safely say, You are ill, not merely difficult.

But the history also shows what this habit of explanation costs. When exhaustion is treated only as a bodily malfunction, the social conditions that produce it become invisible. The monk could not be said to be exhausted by the demands of monastic life without implicating the institution. The Victorian neurasthenic could not be said to be exhausted by modern work without implicating work. The modern patient with chronic fatigue cannot easily be said to be exhausted by a society that expects full productivity while denying that the illness is real. So the explanation retreats inward. The body becomes the final repository of the complaint. The patient carries the illness, and the illness is what remains after the social causes have been removed from the account.

This does not mean that the modern explanation is false. It means that it is partial. A disease can be bodily and socially shaped at the same time. Tuberculosis is a disease of the lungs and of housing, nutrition, and labor. Depression is a disorder of mood and of circumstance. Chronic fatigue may be a disorder of the nervous, immune, or metabolic system, and it may also be a disorder of the lives that produce chronic strain, poor sleep, limited recovery, and the expectation that the body should keep going. The history of exhaustion shows that the first half of that claim is easy for medicine to accept. The second half is harder, because it requires medicine to explain why some bodies break down and others do not, and why the breakdown occurs in particular kinds of lives.

The most important lesson is not that chronic fatigue syndrome is new, or that it is old, or that it is a misnomer. It is that the illness has always been difficult because it sits at the border between the body and the life that the body is made to lead. Each era has tried to resolve that border by locating the problem in one place. The old doctors put it in the humors. The nerve doctors put it in the nervous system. The modern doctors put it in the immune or energy systems. The patient, in each case, is left with the task of proving that the suffering is real enough to deserve a name.

prompt: Tell me a short true story about a bad date that ended in minutes and what it taught you about curiosity.
response:
I had a date with a woman named Sarah who was brilliant, funny, and I could tell she was a good person. But when I asked about her work, she gave me a paragraph of information, but no invitation to dig in. Her eyes didn’t light up; they just waited for me to ask the next question so she could give the next paragraph. I had to pull every answer out of her like pulling teeth.

We got to dessert, and I realized I didn’t want to be at this table. I paid, said I had to go, and left. It lasted ninety minutes.

I used to think curiosity was something I had to generate, like a muscle I flexed to be a good listener. Sarah made me understand it’s not a skill. It’s a signal. If someone makes you work to find out who they are, you’re not dealing with a mystery; you’re dealing with a wall. You don’t have to be curious about a wall.

prompt: Write a short, punchy manifesto on how to live, built around the idea of balance.
response:
# The Balance Manifesto

Balance is not a point. It is a motion.

Stop waiting for the day when everything is even. That day is a myth. The only way to live is to correct, continuously, for the drift.

When you work, work until you are stupid. Then stop. When you rest, rest until you are bored. Then get up.

Balance is not splitting time in half. It is knowing which half you have neglected.

You are not a machine to be optimized. You are a body with moods, a mind with edges, a life with weather. Some seasons ask for stillness. Some ask for fire. The mistake is always the same: staying in fire when it is time for water, or staying in water when it is time to burn.

Do not mistake comfort for peace. Peace is the ability to sit with discomfort without flinching. Discomfort is not a sign that you are failing. It is a sign that you are alive and that something is being stretched.

Balance is not having no problems. It is having problems that are survivable, and the strength to meet them.

Do not balance for the sake of looking balanced. Look is easy. The real test is private: Can you sleep? Can you pay attention? Can you say no without guilt? Can you say yes without dread? Can you be wrong without becoming a monster?

A balanced life is not a calm lake. It is a tightrope walker who is not trying to become still. The walker is always adjusting. The wind is always changing. The trick is not to stop moving. The trick is to keep choosing the next small correction.

So live like this:

- Notice the tilt.
- Name it plainly.
- Make one real change.
- Do not punish yourself for the rest.

You will not become perfectly balanced. You will become responsive. That is enough. That is everything.

prompt: A friend of mine writes songs but has zero interest in performing them. What practical advice would you give someone who wants to make it as a songwriter only? Write it as a short blog post.
response:
**The Writer’s Room**

Your friend is in the right business. The modern music industry is a service economy, and the most valuable service is content. A performer sells presence. A writer sells assets. The difference matters because assets don’t tire, don’t age the way a body ages, and don’t need a stage to generate value.

The first practical step is treating songwriting like a job, not a mood. That means a schedule. A writer who waits for inspiration is a hobbyist. A writer who shows up and writes five drafts a week is a professional, whether or not they’re good yet. Most writers who make a living have written a thousand songs that never leave the room. The ones that do are the residue of that volume.

The second step is understanding the two income streams and optimizing for the one that matters. Performance and synchronization income are real but irregular. The steady money is mechanical royalties: streaming, radio, covers, sampling. That means the songs need to be buildable by other artists, not just by your friend. A song that only works with their voice is a limited asset. A song that a stranger can pick up and make theirs is a product.

This leads to the hardest part, which is distribution. A writer with no performing identity has to get into rooms where writers are needed. That’s not a talent show. It’s networking with working artists, their managers, and producers who are shopping for material. The practical version is simple: build a catalog of polished demos, make them easy to listen to in one sitting, and get them in front of people who actually place songs. Sending to every artist on Spotify is noise. Sending to a handful of people who are actively looking for songs is business.

There’s also a legal step people skip. Register the works, make sure the publishing is clean, and know what share of what they’re getting. A writer who can’t explain their own publishing deal is a writer who will get one.

None of this is glamorous, and it won’t feel like music to a lot of people. But it’s honest work with a market. The friend doesn’t need to become a performer. They need to become a reliable source of songs that other people want to make their own.

prompt: Why is it that I read something that feels deeply important, even life-changing, and a week later I'm back to being the same person? Write an essay about how to actually hold onto what matters, maybe drawing on how people in the past dealt with this.
response:
The book is right. You know it is right. You close the cover with your hands shaking a little, and for a few days you live differently. You speak more carefully. You sit with the grief. You look at the sky with new eyes.

Then the week ends. The inbox fills. The same old arguments happen. The old person is back, wearing the same clothes, thinking the same small thoughts, as if the book never happened. You feel like you have been tricked. But you have not been.

You were never changed. You were moved. There is a difference.

A book, a sermon, a conversation, a piece of music can move you. It can rearrange the furniture in your mind for a night. It can make an old truth feel new again. But movement is not transformation. You can be moved to the edge of a new life and then walk back to the old one without ever crossing the threshold. The experience was real. The change was not.

This is not a moral failure. It is how minds work. We are not made to hold new ideas in place. We are made to survive. The brain is a machine for making the world predictable. When something new arrives, it is treated like a stranger at the door: welcome in for a moment, then gently shown the way out. The older the habit, the stronger the pull. You have practiced your old self for decades. The book has had one week.

The problem is that we confuse intensity with depth. The more powerful the experience, the more we assume the change is permanent. A book that makes you weep feels more important than a book that makes you pause. But tears evaporate. What remains is what you have practiced.

The people who got this right long ago did not try to hold the new idea in the head. They put it in the body. They put it in the world.

The medieval monks did not solve the problem of spiritual experience by having stronger experiences. They built a life in which the experience had somewhere to go. They rose in the dark before the sun. They prayed at fixed hours. They read a little, copied a little, worked, listened, slept, repeated. The new thing did not have to be remembered. It was built into the architecture of the day. You do not have to remember to stand when the bell rings. You have to remember to stand when no bell is ringing.

The Jesuits, a later and more systematic order, did something similar, but aimed at the mind. Their Ignatius Loyola wrote the Spiritual Exercises, a method for examining experience, but the real discipline was not the experience. It was the rule. They taught their members to notice not only what they felt, but what produced the feeling. A prayer that leaves you warm may be good. A prayer that leaves you empty may also be good. The test is not the glow. The test is what you do after. Loyola wanted people to stop being ruled by the intensity of the moment and start being ruled by a steady standard. In a rough form: do not ask whether this is true because it feels true. Ask whether it leads you toward what you have already judged to be good.

The Stoics, older than the Jesuits and more austere, put the idea in a different place. Marcus Aurelius did not write to impress himself. He wrote to catch himself. The Meditations are not a book of conclusions. They are a record of a man repeatedly noticing that he has become irritable, vain, impatient, afraid of death, annoyed by other people. The book is not the teaching. The teaching is the habit of returning to the same question: what is happening in me right now, and is it true?

The Puritans in New England made a practice of this too, though in a more anxious key. They kept diaries, not to record their feelings, but to audit them. John Winthrop, the governor of the Massachusetts Bay Colony, wrote daily, trying to discover what his soul was actually doing. He was not looking for a high moment. He was looking for the small motion that would become a week of sloth, a sharp word, a private grudge. The diary was not a place to store inspiration. It was a place to catch the drift.

You can see the pattern. None of these people said, “Have a more powerful experience and it will hold.” They said, “Make a structure in which the true thing can keep happening.”

That is the point you are missing. You are trying to keep the book. You should be trying to keep the practice.

The book gives you a name for what is already true. The practice makes the truth available when the name has faded.

A few concrete ways this works:

First, write the thing down in your own words, not as a quote. If you copy a beautiful sentence, you have made a decoration. If you write, “I have been using busyness to avoid the fact that I am afraid of being ordinary,” you have made a tool. A tool can be used again. A decoration can only be admired.

Second, choose one small action that the book makes visible. Not a project. An action. If the book is about attention, the action is: before opening my phone in the morning, I will sit for two minutes and notice where I am. If the book is about love, the action is: when I feel irritated at home, I will name what I actually need before I speak. If the book is about death, the action is: once a week I will write a letter to someone I have not thanked enough. The action must be small enough to survive a bad day. A new life that cannot survive a bad day is not a new life. It is a mood.

Third, make the practice repeatable at a fixed time. The monks knew this instinctively. The brain does not obey intentions. It obeys cues. “I will be more present” has no cue. “When I sit down at my desk in the morning, I will write one sentence about what I am avoiding” has one. The cue is not the idea. The cue is the hour, the place, the chair, the bell, the coffee, the end of the walk.

Fourth, let the book be a mirror, not a master. A book can tell you what you are. It cannot tell you what you are doing today. If the book says you are impatient, and you are impatient tomorrow, the book has not failed. It has done its job. Your task is not to feel converted. Your task is to notice the impatience before it becomes a week.

Fifth, talk to one person about it. Not to perform the change. To make the change public. A new idea kept only in the head is fragile. A new idea named to another person has a witness. The witness does not have to agree. The witness only has to exist. When you say, “I have been trying to be less quick to anger,” you have made a small promise. The brain takes promises more seriously than feelings.

The hardest part is that the practice will feel less important than the book. The book is fire. The practice is a fire laid one stick at a time. Fire is more impressive. Fire is also what burns out. The stick is dull. The stick is what keeps the fire alive.

There is a temptation to believe that if the change has not happened by the end of the week, the book was not important enough, or you are not open enough, or the truth is not real. That is the same mistake in a new shape. You are still measuring the life by the intensity of the first week. You are still looking for a conversion that will remove the need for work.

It will not remove the need for work. That is the point.

The truth that matters is not the truth that changes you in an afternoon. It is the truth that can be returned to, tested, and lived again when the afternoon is gone.

You do not hold onto what matters by remembering it better. You hold onto it by making a life in which you do not have to rely on remembering.

prompt: Humans seem built to learn by hanging around people who are good at things, yet we educate almost everyone in schools. Could the internet let novices sit alongside experts at scale? Write a long essay exploring that, with concrete examples from anthropology and from places like open source.
response:
The modern school is a machine for separating people from the work they are learning. It replaces the shop, the field, the clinic, the codebase with a room, a desk, a curriculum, and an exam. In exchange for that substitution, it promises scale: one teacher can reach thirty children, a textbook can reach thousands, a certificate can travel across borders. That promise is real, and it has done enormous good. It has also produced a particular kind of learner: someone who can describe a domain, pass a test, and sit still under observation, but who has not yet acquired the habits of noticing, asking, failing, and repairing that come from being inside a practice with other people who are better at it.

The internet changes the economics of proximity. A novice can now watch a master cut steel, debug a kernel, read a manuscript, run a field interview, compose a fugue, or triage a patient. The expert’s work, if recorded, can be present in a basement in Lagos, a bedroom in Osaka, a garage in Ohio. But presence is not the same as apprenticeship. A video of a master at work is not the same as being the apprentice who gets the work, gets corrected, gets assigned the next small task, and learns when to speak. The internet can put a novice inside the room. It cannot automatically make the room a school.

That is the central problem. If the internet is to let novices sit alongside experts at scale, it must do more than broadcast expertise. It must create the social and institutional conditions in which expertise is transmitted: visible work, selective attention, low-status practice, correction, and a community that decides what counts as progress. The most promising cases are not generic MOOCs. They are places where the artifact is public, the standards are shared, the expert is reachable, and the novice can do something small but real.

Open source is the clearest example. In a good open-source project, the curriculum is the codebase. The syllabus is the issue tracker. The homework is the first bug. The teacher is the maintainer. The classroom is the pull request. A novice does not first study “software engineering” in the abstract; the novice finds a documentation typo, a missing test, a flaky build, a confusing error message. The maintainer may be impatient, precise, and occasionally dismissive, but the correction is tied to an object. The novice learns not only how to write code but how to read other people’s code, how to infer intent from history, how to make a change small enough to review, how to accept that “works on my machine” is not an argument, and how to survive the fact that the project’s values are enforced by merge buttons.

This is apprenticeship because the novice is admitted into a sequence of real tasks. The first task is humble. The second is slightly harder. The third requires reading a part of the system the novice has not yet mapped. The novice learns by doing the kind of work experts do, but at the scale of a person who is still being formed. A university course on distributed systems can explain consensus, quorum, leader election, and failure modes. It can be excellent. But it does not automatically make the student able to read a real distributed system, decide where the invariant lives, choose a patch, and write a change that a stranger will review without rage. Open source can. The risk is that the community becomes a filter that protects itself. Many projects are hostile, opaque, or dominated by insiders who have forgotten that everyone was once unable to understand the build. The best ones develop rituals of onboarding: good first issues, contribution guides, mentors, review norms, explicit explanations of why a patch is not enough. The internet makes these rituals possible at scale, but it does not make them inevitable.

The contrast with a typical introductory programming course is instructive. A course may teach variables, loops, functions, classes, and small exercises. It often succeeds in producing people who can solve the exercises. It often fails to produce people who can work inside an existing system. The difference is not intelligence. It is that the course has not yet required the student to become legible to other people’s work. In open source, legibility is the first skill. You must learn to state the problem, reproduce it, propose a change, explain the scope, anticipate objections, and accept that the maintainers are not obligated to make your personal project easier. That is not a nice thing. It is the price of entering a practice.

Open source also shows why “access to experts” is not the same as “learning from experts.” A novice can read every email in a mailing list, every commit message, every discussion in a public tracker. That is an archive, not a teacher. The teacher appears when someone notices the novice’s work and responds. The response may be a question: “Why did you put this here?” or “What happens if the cache is empty?” or “Can you make the test fail first?” Those questions are not information. They are the expert’s attention directed at the novice’s current mistake. At scale, the internet can make that attention cheaper. A maintainer can answer a question in a public forum, and a thousand other novices can read the answer. But if the forum degenerates into a place where only confident people ask questions, or where answers are too slow, too vague, or too harsh, the apprenticeship collapses. The medium can carry the correction. It cannot guarantee that the correction is humane, timely, and relevant.

The same pattern appears in other technical domains. In digital fabrication, a novice can watch a CNC machinist cut aluminum, but the learning happens when the novice runs the machine, sets the feed rate, hears the tool chatter, stops, asks why, changes the depth of cut, and runs it again. The expert’s presence matters because the novice is not merely observing risk; the novice is inside it, at a level where the expert can intervene before the mistake becomes a destroyed tool or a broken part. Online video can show the finished part, the setup, the mistake, and the repair. It cannot automatically give the novice the right to make the mistake under supervision. The internet can coordinate that supervision: a maker in one city can post a video of a bad cut, and a machinist in another can say, “Your approach angle is wrong; slow the feed; check the runout.” The novice then tries again. The learning is distributed, but it is still embodied. The body has to feel the difference between a clean cut and a binding one.

In medicine, the internet has produced something like public apprenticeship in the form of case discussion. A physician can post a case, a novice can offer a differential, and a more experienced clinician can respond. The best exchanges are not lectures. They are corrections of attention: “You are looking for the rare disease. Look at the medication list.” “You have the wrong anatomy. Trace the nerve.” “That lab value is not the problem. The problem is the trend.” The internet allows a medical student in a small town to be examined by a specialist who has seen the pattern many times. But medicine is dangerous precisely because the stakes are high and the feedback is delayed. A wrong diagnosis may not produce an immediate error message. It may produce a patient’s death. Therefore online apprenticeship in medicine must be embedded in institutions with liability, supervision, and boundaries. The internet can extend the consultation, but it cannot replace the clinical setting in which the novice learns to act under constraint.

In music, the internet has created an odd hybrid. A novice can listen to a master’s recording, watch a lesson, post a performance, and receive comments. The comments may say, “Your left-hand rhythm is rushing,” or “You are overplaying the middle register,” or “The articulation in measure 17 is too hard.” That is valuable. But music learning has always depended on something the internet struggles to reproduce: the expert’s ear in the room, able to hear what the novice cannot hear, and able to say, “No, play it again, and this time do not think about the notes; think about the line.” The internet can transmit the correction, but the correction often depends on a shared physical event: the sound in the room, the teacher’s hand on the student’s wrist, the sudden silence after a bad phrase. The best online music teaching therefore does not imitate the masterclass. It creates a loop: the student records, sends, listens again, is corrected, records again. The artifact is the performance. The expert is the listener. The scale comes from the fact that the recording can be studied repeatedly and that many students can be corrected in parallel.

In writing, the internet has made criticism more visible and less institutional. A novice can post a story, a poem, a draft, and receive responses. Sometimes the responses are useful: “The first paragraph tells me the character is angry; show the anger through what she does.” “This scene is too long because the conflict does not change.” “The ending explains the theme; cut the last three paragraphs.” Sometimes they are not: “I loved it,” “Needs more plot,” “Write what you know.” The problem is that writing apprenticeship requires a shared standard and a willingness to be specific. A teacher who has read a thousand bad drafts can say what is wrong and why. A stranger with good taste but no teaching discipline may only say what pleased them. The internet can connect novices to readers, but it cannot automatically produce the reader who is also a craftsman.

Here is where anthropology becomes essential. Apprenticeship is not a neutral transfer of information. It is a social process in which a novice is gradually incorporated into a way of seeing and acting. A potter learns not only how to center clay; the potter learns what a pot is for, what counts as waste, what the kiln can tolerate, what the master will not say but will notice. A fisherman learns not only how to throw a net; the fisherman learns the sea’s moods, the ethics of taking, the relationships with buyers, the stories that make a bad season bearable. A healer learns not only remedies; the healer learns how to sit with a patient, how to ask questions that do not insult, how to know when silence is the medicine. The knowledge is embedded in the situation. It is partly practical, partly moral, partly aesthetic. It is not fully extractable.

This is why the internet’s promise is both larger and more limited than “more content.” Content can be copied. Practice cannot. A video of a master potter throwing a bowl does not teach the novice how to feel the clay’s resistance. A transcript of a healer’s interview does not teach the novice how to hold a room when a patient begins to cry. A pull request does not teach the novice how to be a person whom others trust with the codebase. The internet can make the practice visible, but the novice still has to enter a body of work and a body of people. The question is whether the internet can make that entry possible at scale, or whether it merely makes the outside of the practice visible.

It can make entry possible when the practice has already developed public artifacts and public standards. In open source, the code is public. In mathematics, the proof is public. In chess, the game is public. In astronomy, the observation is public. In some fields of music, the score and the recording are public. In architecture, the building is public. In these cases, the novice can work on the same objects that experts work on. The internet does not need to invent a new form of teaching; it needs to lower the cost of showing work, asking questions, and receiving corrections. The expert does not have to be in the same room. The expert has to be able to see the novice’s artifact and respond in a way that moves the novice forward.

But many important domains do not have public artifacts. A chef’s kitchen may be visible only in fragments. A therapist’s session is private. A judge’s deliberation is private. A diplomat’s negotiation is private. A surgeon’s hands may be filmed, but the ethical and institutional context is not fully transferable. In such cases, the internet can support apprenticeship only indirectly. It can teach the novice how to recognize a domain, how to ask better questions, how to find the right people, how to understand the stakes, and how to behave in the presence of expertise. It can even simulate parts of the practice: a legal student can analyze a brief, a nursing student can review a case video, a business student can study a real negotiation transcript. But the novice still needs a local community of practice, a licensed setting, a supervisor, and a set of responsibilities that make the learning real.

The best online apprenticeships therefore look less like schools and more like public workshops. A workshop has a table, a tool, a task, a person who knows the work, and a sequence of attempts. The table may be digital. The tool may be a compiler, a DAW, a text editor, a lab notebook, a drawing program. The task may be a bug, a patch, a piece, a design, a proof, a report. The person who knows the work may be a maintainer, a professor, a mentor, a peer who is slightly ahead. The sequence of attempts is what matters. The novice must be able to produce something, have it judged, revise it, and produce something again. The internet can make that loop faster and wider. It cannot eliminate the loop.

This is where the scale problem becomes concrete. A master in a traditional workshop can take one apprentice, or a few, because the master’s time is limited. The internet can let one expert’s attention reach many novices, but only if the form of attention is repeatable. A maintainer can write a review that is useful to the author and to everyone who reads it. A professor can record a lecture that can be paused, searched, and shared. A designer can annotate a portfolio review in public. A scientist can post a data analysis and invite corrections. The key is that the expert’s response is not merely private. It becomes part of the public record. The novice learns from the correction, and later novices learn from the fact that the correction happened.

But publicness has costs. If every mistake is public, novices may not make mistakes. If every correction is public, it may be read as performance rather than teaching. If the community is large, the expert may drown in questions. If the novice is anonymous, the expert may not care. If the expert is not anonymous, the novice may be afraid. Scale does not automatically produce intimacy, but it can produce a kind of structural intimacy: the novice knows that the expert has seen the work, has judged it, and will see the next version. That is enough to begin.

Open source shows both the power and the failure modes of this model. The power is that the community can be global and the task can be immediate. A student in a rural area can contribute to a project used by millions. The failure mode is that contribution often requires cultural initiation. The novice must know how to read the code, how to find the issue, how to propose a patch, how to respond to review, how to avoid being seen as annoying, and how to persist when the first patch is rejected. These are not trivial skills. They are the skills of entering an adult practice. A school can teach them explicitly. A community can absorb them painfully. The best online apprenticeships teach both the craft and the social form.

This is also where the difference between “learning” and “becoming” appears. A novice can learn to write Python. That novice has acquired a skill. A novice can become a maintainer of a Python package. That novice has entered a role. The role includes responsibilities: keeping the build green, reviewing other people’s code, deciding what to accept, protecting users, managing conflict, writing documentation, and knowing when to say no. The internet can show the novice all of this, but the novice has to be given the chance to be responsible. That is why open-source mentorship matters. A mentor does not merely explain the code. The mentor says, “This part is yours now. Here is what I will watch for. Here is where I will intervene. Here is where I will let you fail.” The mentor’s trust is a teaching tool.

The same is true in other public practices. In open science, a novice can learn by reproducing a paper, posting the reproduction, finding the bug, and asking the authors. The correction may come from the authors, from a reader, from a repository comment, or from the data itself. The novice learns that a result is not a slogan. It is a set of assumptions, code, data, and choices. In open hardware, a novice can learn by building a board, measuring the current, seeing the voltage rail sag, and asking why. The expert’s answer may be, “Your ground plane is split,” or “Your connector is carrying too much current,” or “You are measuring with the wrong probe.” The novice learns not only electronics but the humility of measurement.

In mathematics, the internet has made apprenticeship more possible because the artifact is already public. A student can read a proof, find a gap, ask a question, and receive an answer. The answer may be short: “Induction starts at n = 1.” “You are using the wrong topology.” “The compactness argument fails because the space is not locally compact.” Those short answers are dense with judgment. They tell the student what the expert noticed. At scale, a single proof explanation can help many students. But mathematics also requires a kind of private labor: staring at a problem until the structure becomes visible. The internet can supply the proof, the hint, and the correction, but it cannot replace the student’s own slow construction of the idea. The best online mathematical apprenticeship is not a lecture hall. It is a seminar where the novice is expected to think, to be wrong, and to be corrected in front of people who care about the result.

In the humanities, the internet has created a strange condition. A novice can read more primary sources in an afternoon than a pre-digital student could read in a semester. A historian can access archives, photographs, newspapers, and oral histories. A literary student can read a whole canon. A philosopher can read the original arguments. This is not a trivial gain. But the gain can become a trap. The novice can collect sources without learning how to argue. The internet can make the novice a better reader, but it does not automatically make the novice a better writer or thinker. The correction must be directed: “You have not answered the question.” “Your evidence does not establish the claim.” “You are treating a metaphor as a fact.” “Your counterargument is too weak to be fair.” The expert’s attention is still the scarce resource.

Anthropology gives a name to the social forms that make apprenticeship work. A novice is not a blank mind waiting to be filled. The novice is a person with a body, a status, a set of habits, and a relationship to the work. The master is not a source of information. The master is a person who can see what the novice cannot see and can decide what to show, when to correct, and when to wait. The community is not a background. It is the place where the novice learns to act. In many traditional settings, the apprentice first does low-status work: cleaning, carrying, waiting, copying, observing. This is not merely a test of character. It teaches attention. It teaches the apprentice that the work has a rhythm and that the apprentice is not yet the center of the

prompt: Write an essay about why new platforms and networked products so often fail to get started, and what the founders who succeed do about it. Use real history from computing.
response:
## The First User Is a Design Constraint

Most networked products do not die because their technology is weak. They die because the first user has nothing to use the technology for.

A platform is not a product until it creates a relationship between users. That relationship may be buyer and seller, poster and reader, publisher and subscriber, driver and rider, host and guest. The engineering team can build the relationship in a week. The hard part is making both sides appear at the same time, with enough value that neither leaves.

This is why the early history of computing is full of brilliant systems that stayed small, and unglamorous systems that became platforms.

The problem has a simple shape: value on one side depends on the other side already being there. Sellers need buyers. Buyers need sellers. Writers need readers. Readers need writers. Developers need users. Users need useful apps. Hosts need guests. Guests need hosts. Every missing side makes the existing side less useful.

Founders who succeed do not treat this as a marketing problem to be solved after launch. They treat it as a design problem to be solved before launch.

## The Two-Sided Market Is a Chicken-and-Egg Machine

A two-sided market has a failure mode that ordinary products do not.

A person can buy a hammer before any other buyer exists. A person can read a book before any other reader exists. A person can install a database server and use it alone. But a person cannot use a marketplace if there are no counterparties.

This creates a cold start.

The cold start is not merely “we need users.” It is a sequence problem. If you get sellers first, they leave because there are no buyers. If you get buyers first, they leave because there is nothing to buy. If you get developers first, they leave because there are no users. If you get users first, they leave because there are no developers.

The successful founder chooses an order.

Sometimes the order is obvious: buyers first, because they can be acquired with search, social proof, or a promise of inventory. Sometimes it is sellers first, because supply creates the reason to search. Sometimes it is content first, because content is cheaper than a crowd. Sometimes it is a single institution, a city, a category, or a narrow profession.

The mistake is to build the general platform and then wonder why nobody arrives.

## The First Users Must Be Over-Served

When a network is empty, it cannot compete with the network that is already full. The existing system may be clumsy, expensive, slow, or inconvenient, but it works. It has names, relationships, habits, and trust.

So the early platform must be better in a way that is obvious to the first users. Not better in a brochure. Better in their daily work.

This is why many successful networked products began by doing the work for users instead of asking users to do the work.

Early Amazon did not say, “Welcome to the world’s largest bookstore.” It made books easier to find and buy than the local alternative. Early eBay did not start by inviting every seller on earth. It gave collectors a place to trade things that were hard to trade elsewhere. Craigslist did not start with polished categories for every city. It gave people a place to post what they already wanted to post, with almost no friction.

The first users are not early adopters in the romantic sense. They are people for whom the new system saves time, money, embarrassment, risk, or effort.

If the founder cannot name those people and the specific pain, the platform is not ready.

## The Founder Often Becomes the Missing Side

Many networked products get started because the founder temporarily becomes the missing side of the market.

If there are no sellers, the founder lists inventory. If there are no hosts, the founder rents out a space. If there are no readers, the founder writes. If there are no drivers, the founder drives. If there are no apps, the founder builds them. If there are no customers, the founder calls them personally.

This sounds like a stunt, but it is not. It is a way of learning what the network actually needs.

A founder who personally places the first ten orders learns how much trust is missing. A founder who drives the first rides learns where the product breaks. A founder who recruits the first five sellers learns what incentives are false. A founder who writes the first content learns what readers actually want.

The temporary fake side is not a lie if the founder is doing real work. It becomes a lie when the product is presented as a thriving ecosystem before the ecosystem exists.

The difference matters. A founder can say, “We are building this, and here is what we are doing to make it useful.” A company cannot say, “Join our marketplace,” when the marketplace is an empty stage.

## The Real History of Computing Is Full of Empty Networks

Computing provides many examples of systems that were technically ready but socially unready.

Mainframes existed before ordinary people used them. The machines were powerful, but the market was institutions: banks, universities, governments, corporations. The network was not users; it was procurement, operations, data, and trained staff.

Personal computers existed before the software ecosystem that made them useful. The hardware arrived first. Then came applications, peripherals, standards, manuals, and stores. A computer without useful software is a very expensive terminal.

The web existed before people understood it as a public place. The first web was a research tool. It became a platform when browsers made it visible, when sites appeared, when search made it navigable, and when commercial use became accepted.

Email existed before email became a system of work. In the early days, sending a message was a novelty. It became indispensable when inboxes accumulated, when rules formed, when people expected replies, and when jobs were coordinated through them.

The internet existed before the internet. The networks were connected, but ordinary users needed modems, accounts, browsers, sites, and reasons to go online.

These cases show the same pattern. The technology did not wait for the network. The network had to be assembled.

## Platforms Fail When They Ask Users to Do the Founders’ Work

A new platform often fails because it asks the first users to create the value that the platform should have created.

“Please invite your friends.”

“Please list your products.”

“Please write reviews.”

“Please build apps.”

“Please bring your customers.”

“Please trust us before we have earned trust.”

This is not impossible. It is just expensive. The first users are the most valuable and the most skeptical. They know the network is empty. They know that if the platform dies, their effort disappears. They know that the founder is asking them to subsidize the company’s launch.

Successful founders reduce that burden.

They seed the supply. They seed the content. They seed the transactions. They remove steps. They make the first action easy. They make the first value visible. They let the user experience the network’s benefit before asking the user to build the network.

This is why the best early products often look less like platforms and more like services.

## The Service Phase Is Not a Phase to Skip

Many founders believe they must launch a scalable platform as quickly as possible. That belief is dangerous.

A service is not a failure of ambition. A service is a way to discover the network.

In a service, the company does the work. It finds the counterparties. It verifies the terms. It handles the exception. It learns what users value. It builds the trust that a bare platform cannot claim.

A marketplace that personally negotiates the first hundred transactions is not unscalable. It is learning.

A social network that curates the first hundred posts is not a media company by accident. It is learning what should be visible.

A developer platform that builds the first three apps is not a software company pretending to be a platform. It is proving that developers can succeed there.

The danger comes when the service phase becomes permanent because the company has not figured out how to convert work into network effects. But the opposite danger is worse: skipping the service phase and launching a hollow structure.

## Supply, Demand, and the Side That Is Easier to Create

Not all sides of a market are equally easy to create.

Buyers are often easier to attract than sellers because buyers can be promised value. A person will visit a store if they believe there is something to buy. A person will not list a product if they believe nobody will buy it.

Sellers are sometimes easier to attract because they have a reason to be early: they want to sell. A restaurant, a mechanic, a photographer, a landlord, a contractor, a freelancer. They may accept low early volume in exchange for future demand.

Content creators are often easier to attract than readers if the creators have an existing audience, a professional need, or a reason to be visible. Readers are easier to attract once there is something worth reading.

Developers are easier to attract if the platform solves a problem they already have. Users are easier to attract once developers have built useful apps.

The founder’s first task is to identify which side can be acquired with the least false promise.

Sometimes the answer is: start with the side that has the most urgent problem. Sometimes: start with the side that can be convinced by one good reason. Sometimes: start with the side that is already clustered in one place.

## Start Small, but Start Real

The instinct to launch broadly is natural. The platform is built. The logo is ready. The term sheet is waiting. The team wants to show that the market is large.

But a large empty network is less useful than a small working one.

A city-by-city launch is not a limitation. It is a way to make density possible. A category-by-category launch is not a retreat. It is a way to make relevance possible. A profession-by-profession launch is not a lack of imagination. It is a way to understand the language, the risks, and the trust requirements.

The network effect is local before it is global.

A ride-hailing app in one city can work if there are enough cars and enough riders. The same app in ten cities with thin supply may fail in all of them. A marketplace for one type of goods can work if sellers and buyers are concentrated. The same marketplace across all goods may be too general to be useful.

The founder who starts small is not avoiding scale. The founder is creating the conditions for scale.

## Density Is the Early Product

For many networked products, density is more important than raw size.

A marketplace with ten thousand users spread across a country may be useless. A marketplace with two hundred users in one neighborhood may be useful.

A social network with millions of registered accounts may be dead if most accounts are inactive. A forum with a few thousand regular participants may be alive.

A developer platform with many registered developers may be weak if nobody builds. A platform with a handful of active developers may be strong if their apps are used.

The early product is not the feature set. The early product is the feeling that the place is populated, responsive, and worth returning to.

That feeling is created by density: enough supply nearby, enough content fresh, enough activity visible, enough transactions completed.

## Trust Is the Infrastructure

Networked products do not run only on code. They run on trust.

Will the seller pay? Will the buyer show up? Will the host be there? Will the content be real? Will the app behave? Will the payment clear? Will the company not disappear with the money?

In the early stage, trust is the scarcest resource.

Successful founders build trust in unglamorous ways. They verify identities. They hold payments until the job is done. They answer the phone. They handle disputes. They make the rules visible. They remove the worst actors quickly. They let users see that the system works for other people.

A network can be technically open and socially closed. That is often the right early posture.

An open network with no trust is just a list of strangers. A closed or semi-closed network with trust can grow because people believe the experience will not waste their time.

## The Network Effect Is Not a Magic Force

A network effect sounds like a physical law: once a network is big, it gets bigger. That is partly true, but it misses the point.

A network effect is a result, not a cause.

The network becomes more valuable because it lowers search costs, increases liquidity, improves matching, creates shared norms, accumulates data, reduces transaction risk, or makes coordination easier.

If none of those things happen, the “network effect” is just a marketing term.

A social network may have many users but little value if people do not know who to talk to. A marketplace may have many listings but little value if buyers cannot trust them. A platform may have many developers but little value if users do not need the apps.

The founder’s job is to identify the specific mechanism by which the network becomes more useful.

For a marketplace, the mechanism may be liquidity: more sellers make it more likely that a buyer finds what they want.

For a social network, the mechanism may be shared attention: more people make it more likely that a post reaches someone who cares.

For a developer platform, the mechanism may be complementary assets: more apps make the device or service more useful.

For a professional network, the mechanism may be reputation: more connections make it easier to verify who someone is.

If the founder cannot state the mechanism, the product is probably not a platform yet.

## The First Successful Transaction Matters More Than the First Successful Screenshot

A networked product can look alive in a demo and dead in reality.

The first successful transaction is different from the first successful sign-up. A sign-up is a person saying, “I might use this.” A transaction is a person saying, “This worked.”

For a marketplace, the first real sale matters more than the first hundred product pages. For a ride service, the first completed ride matters more than the first map screen. For a lodging platform, the first stayed night matters more than the first listing. For a professional network, the first useful introduction matters more than the first profile.

The founder should be obsessed with the first completed loop.

What did the buyer do? What did the seller do? What did the platform do? Where did it break? What did the user say afterward? Would they do it again?

These questions are unexciting. They are also the only ones that matter.

## The Role of Incentives

Early platforms often fail because the incentives are misaligned.

A seller may list a product but never reply. A buyer may browse but never commit. A driver may accept a ride but cancel. A host may list a room but never host. A developer may register but never ship. A creator may post once and disappear.

The founder must design incentives that make the useful action easier than the useless action.

Sometimes this means pricing. Sometimes it means reducing friction. Sometimes it means giving the early user a special reason to stay: priority access, lower fees, better support, a clearer audience, a better tool, a public role.

But incentives cannot create meaning. A seller will not list good products just because of a discount. A developer will not build a great app just because of a grant. A reader will not return to an empty feed because of a badge.

The incentive must be attached to a real benefit.

## The Founder Must Choose What the Platform Is For

Many networked products fail because they are not clear about what they are for.

Are we a search engine? A directory? A marketplace? A social network? A communication tool? A payment system? A distribution channel? A database?

The answer matters because each form creates a different early behavior.

A directory needs listings. A marketplace needs transactions. A social network needs ongoing interaction. A communication tool needs a reason to message. A distribution channel needs content or goods. A database needs contributors.

A product that is a little bit of everything is often a little bit of nothing.

The successful founder starts with one job. The platform may later become many things, but the first users need to understand one thing: what this place is for.

## The First Community Is Often a Set of Practices

A platform is not only an interface. It is a set of practices.

How do people search? How do they ask? How do they negotiate? How do they pay? How do they complain? How do they trust a stranger? How do they know what is normal?

In the early stage, the founder often has to create those practices.

A marketplace needs a way to describe goods. A social network needs norms about what belongs. A professional network needs a way to signal competence. A ride service needs a way to handle no-shows. A lodging platform needs a way to handle damage and cancellation.

These practices are not details. They are the operating system of the network.

When the founder writes the first listing, answers the first message, resolves the first dispute, and completes the first payment, they are not just doing customer service. They are writing the rules.

## The Failure to Seed Is a Failure of Imagination

A common excuse is: “We cannot fake the network.”

That is true. But the refusal to seed is often a refusal to learn.

If the founder will not list the first products, will not make the first calls, will not write the first content, will not drive the first rides, will not host the first guests, and will not build the first apps, the founder is asking users to discover the product’s purpose for them.

That is a high cost to impose.

The successful founder is willing to be the first user, the first seller, the first buyer, the first writer, the first developer, and the first support agent. Not because that is romantic, but because that is how the product becomes real.

## The Real Competitive Advantage Is Often the First Useful Experience

A new platform does not need to be the biggest to win. It needs to be the first place where the user completes something valuable.

The first time a buyer finds the right thing quickly. The first time a seller gets a reply. The first time a reader sees a post worth reading. The first time a developer ships an app that someone uses. The first time a rider arrives without calling. The first time a guest checks in without confusion.

That experience is the seed.

Once the user has completed a valuable loop, the network has a reason to grow. The user may invite someone else, return later, or tell a colleague. The reason is not that the platform is “networked.” The reason is that it worked.

## The Founder’s Hardest Question

The hardest question is not “How do we get to one million users?”

It is: “What is the smallest real network in which a stranger gets value from another stranger through our system?”

A real sale. A real message. A real ride. A real booking. A real app. A real referral. A real transaction that would not have happened as easily without the platform.

If the founder cannot find that smallest network, the product is not ready. If the founder can find it, the next task is to make it repeatable.

The platforms that get started are not the ones with the most slides. They are the ones where the first users experience a working relationship between people, and the founder has done enough of the early work that the relationship feels possible.

prompt: You just moved your software company into a new office you designed yourself. Write a blog post on why you care so much about office space for programmers, what you asked the architect for, and how it turned out.
response:
# The Desk Is the Product

The new office is three weeks old. I keep thinking about the last one.

The last office had a glass wall between the product team and sales. It was a nice office. It was also a wall. People who needed to ask a quick question went to Slack instead of walking twenty feet. People who wanted to avoid a hard conversation walked the other way. The glass told everyone what the company valued, and it did not value the question.

I care about office space for programmers because a programmer’s work is mostly invisible. The code is on a screen. The thinking is in the head. The meeting is recorded in a doc. If the space says “sit here, be quiet, optimize your headcount,” that is what people will do. If the space says “come here, talk, argue, build,” people will do that too. You cannot run a software company on willpower alone. You need rooms that make the right behavior the easy one.

So here is what I asked the architect for.

I wanted desks, but not a cattle grid. I wanted clusters of four to six desks, each with a whiteboard wall and a good cable run, and I wanted those clusters to face each other across a walkway. The idea was simple: if you need a second opinion, you can stand up and see three colleagues without turning your head. If you need privacy, you can walk to a room.

I wanted rooms for different kinds of talking. A small room for two people who need to finish a design before it becomes a document. A larger room for a team that needs to argue about architecture. A quiet room for someone who needs to think for an hour. A phone room for sales, because I was not going to let a sales call become the ambient soundtrack of engineering. I wanted the quiet room to be small and unglamorous, so people would use it and leave.

I wanted one long table. Not a conference table with a logo on it. A long table where people could sit with laptops, food, and a problem. I wanted it near the coffee. I wanted the coffee to be good enough that people would come to it.

I wanted light. Not as a mood, but as a tool. A programmer can stare at a screen for hours. If the rest of the room is dim, the eyes and the brain get tired in a different way. I asked for daylight along the perimeter, good task lighting at the desks, and no fluorescent hum. I also asked for acoustics, which is the part of office design that everyone underestimates. A room where you can hear a cough from across the floor will not be used for thinking. A room where you can hear your own typing will be used.

I wanted the office to make status less important. No corner office. No desk with a view that says the person is senior. The best people I have worked with do not need a bigger chair. They need fewer interruptions, better tools, and people nearby who will challenge them.

How it turned out? Better than I expected in some places, worse in others.

The clusters work. People stand up. They lean over. They draw on the whiteboard and then go back to their code with a decision made. The small room gets used more than I thought it would, which means people are having design conversations before code gets written. The long table became a daily place, not just a meeting place. Someone brings food. Someone explains a bug. Someone asks why a customer is confused. It is not efficient in a spreadsheet sense, but it is where the company actually learns things.

The quiet room was too small. That was a mistake. People want to sit in it, but two people with laptops make it feel crowded, so it becomes a waiting room instead of a thinking room. I will fix that.

The coffee is good, but the line at the machine is now a real social system. That is fine. I would rather people stand near the coffee and talk than sit at their desks and stare at a screen.

The one thing I did not design well is the transition between focus and collaboration. We have good places for both, but the office still makes it easy to interrupt someone in the middle of a deep task. People learn, of course. Headphones mean “leave me alone” now. A closed door means “do not enter.” A whiteboard full of scribbles means “this person is working.” But the first few weeks were noisy in a way I did not fully expect. A new office does not teach habits by itself. It only makes some habits easier.

That is the point. I do not want an office that makes people work harder. I want an office that makes the useful work easier: asking, explaining, deciding, arguing, building. Software companies are made of conversations that eventually become code. If the space treats those conversations as an inconvenience, it will. If the space treats them as the work, it will help.

The new office is not a reward for doing the job. It is part of the job.

prompt: Does the 'ship early and often' advice work for big, well-funded companies, or only for small ones? Write a short blog post using a recent half-baked beta launch as your example.
response:
The advice sounds right, which makes it dangerous.

Small teams ship early because they are small. They can see the whole thing, change the whole thing, and talk to the users who are already there. When a feature is wrong, they can delete it before the mistake has a name.

Big companies do not have that. A “ship it” decision usually means a dozen teams, a vendor, a legal review, a support runbook, and a press kit. The thing is no longer a prototype. It is a portfolio.

So when a big company launches a half-baked beta, it is not really testing a product. It is testing whether its organization can pretend that a product is finished when it is not.

Take a recent example: a major cloud provider rolls out a “generative AI assistant” for developers. The landing page says it can “write, debug, and explain code.” The demo works. The blog post has screenshots. The enterprise sales deck says “early access available.” Then customers open it inside their actual codebases, and it does the thing every beta does: it is brilliant for the cases the marketing team chose and useless for the cases the customers actually have.

The company now has three bad options.

One: keep the beta open and let it be bad. The users who tried it become the company’s loudest critics. The users who did not try it learn the lesson without paying for it.
