The word “beta” is supposed to mean “we are still figuring this out,” but in a big company it often means “we are still figuring out whether this is ours.”

Two: pull it back. That is honest, but it costs credibility. The launch was not just a product update; it was a signal. The signal said: we are all in. The retreat says: we were not.

Three: declare it stable and keep it bad. This is the most common big-company move. The UI gets a few small fixes. The status page says “operational.” The support macros get updated. The product does not improve because the original promise was too large, and now the team is defending the promise instead of making the product.

Small companies can escape this because their mistake is local. A founder can say, “We were wrong, we removed it, we will try something smaller.” The user may be annoyed, but the company still has a shape. A big company cannot. Its mistake is institutional. Every department has already arranged itself around the launch. The beta becomes a permanent condition: not finished, not abandoned, too expensive to fix, too visible to admit.

The real problem is not speed. The real problem is that big companies often mistake early for small.

Ships early should mean: a small, useful thing, exposed to real users, before the company has built too much around it. Big companies usually mean: a large, unfinished thing, exposed to users after the company has already built too much around it.

A small company’s beta is a test. A big company’s beta is a commitment.

So does “ship early and often” work for big, well-funded companies? Sometimes, but only when they can make the early thing genuinely small. A limited feature for a limited group. A narrow use case with a clear boundary. A way to hear the user before the sales organization has already decided what the user needs. If the “early” thing is a platform, a brand, a roadmap, or a strategic bet, it is not early shipping. It is early exposure.

The best big-company launches do not look like betas at all. They look boring. They do one thing. They say what they do not do. They let a small number of users use it badly, then they change the product instead of changing the narrative.

The worst ones look exactly like the recent half-baked beta: confident, broad, technically possible, commercially premature, and already too large to take back.

prompt: Why do computer science students graduate from good universities without knowing how to work on a real software project, and why do their term-length team projects so often produce nothing useful? Write it as an opinionated blog post, with a suggestion for what to do about it.
response:
A good CS degree teaches students to solve well-posed problems in isolation. Real software is not that.

A real project has no specification. It has a customer who does not know what she wants, a codebase that is not yours, a deadline that will not move, and a teammate who will disappear in week four. The work is not the code. The work is keeping a shared, changing, half-understood system in a state where everyone can still make progress. That is a different skill from the one the curriculum trains, and it is not an accident.

The curriculum has to be general, and generality pushes toward problems with a clean answer. You can test a sorting algorithm. You can grade a proof. You cannot easily grade "handled a scope change without the project collapsing." So the degree optimizes for what is measurable, and what is measurable is the individual solving a contained problem. That is genuinely valuable. It is also not what software engineering is, and the student is never told the difference.

The team project makes this worse. It is usually a few weeks long, the team is new, the topic is invented by the students, and the deliverable is judged by a professor who has no stake in it. Every incentive points away from usefulness. There is no one to ship it to, so "done" is whatever the group agrees to call done. There is no consequence to a vague spec, because the spec is not going to be maintained. There is no reason to write tests or document decisions, because no one besides the team will ever read them. And because the grade is on the final artifact rather than on the process, the group optimizes for an artifact that looks complete. A demo that works on the happy path, and a report that explains why everything else is out of scope.

So the project teaches students that software is a deliverable you produce at the end, not a state you maintain. That is the opposite of how real projects work.

The fix is not more projects. It is projects that have to be true.

The single most important change is to stop making the students invent the product. Give them a real problem with a real user, ideally one the university actually has. The registrar wants a self-service degree-audit tool. The library needs better search over its special collections. A student org wants a tool that does not lose its event data. Now "useful" has a definition. The user will reject the happy-path demo. She will ask for the thing nobody thought of, which forces a spec conversation that a made-up topic never produces.

The second change is to make the project longer than a term. A term is too short to have a real architecture problem. You need a second team, or the same team across a semester break, to inherit the first group's code. Inheritance is the curriculum. The second team cannot ask the first team what a function means in a case they did not test. They have to read it, trust it partially, change it, and live with the result. That is where "working on a real project" actually gets learned.

The third change is to grade the process, not just the artifact. A working demo is necessary, but it should not be the whole grade. Grade the decisions: why this data model, why this boundary, what you punted on and why. Grade the tests that would catch a regression the next team would introduce. Grade the handoff: could a stranger run the thing, find the entry point, and change one behavior without asking you? A project that is impressive but uninheritable should score lower than a modest one that is maintainable.

The fourth change is to make the team a constraint, not a setting. Assign the groups. Rotate one person mid-project. Require written decisions in a place the whole team can see. Require a short review before a change goes in. None of this is glamorous, and all of it is the job.

The point is that the problem is not that students are not smart. They are usually very smart. The problem is that the degree teaches them a model of software in which the hard part is the solution, and the team project then confirms the model by making the solution the only thing that gets graded. Change the object of the exercise, and the skill follows.

prompt: An economist argues that mental illnesses are just unusual preferences rather than real constraints, the way a physical illness is. I think that's wrong, but I want a rigorous reply. Write a response to his latest rebuttal that offers a better way to think about what makes something a disease, with concrete examples.
response:
The "preference" framing collapses the moment you ask why the preference is there. A person who prefers to eat only chalk is expressing an unusual preference, but no one calls that a disease. They call it an eccentricity. What makes something a disease is that the preference is produced by a malfunction in the system that is supposed to produce preferences. A preference is a signal that something in the world matters to you. A disease is a defect in the signal generator.

The economist’s move works only for preferences that are stable, coherent, and track some feature of the person’s history or environment. It breaks for states that are incoherent with the person’s own evidence, that fluctuate in ways no stable preference could, and that the person experiences as foreign. A phobia is not a preference against a thing. It is a failure of the fear system to process evidence: the person has been told repeatedly, by experience, that the object is safe, and the fear does not update. The preference "I avoid spiders" is downstream of a broken learning process. Calling it a preference is like calling the needle of a broken compass a choice.

A good way to think about disease is in terms of the function the system is supposed to serve and the ways it can fail. A disease is a reliable impairment of a capacity that the organism or person is supposed to have. Hunger is a capacity: it tells you when you need fuel. Anorexia is an impairment of that capacity: the signal is present but is overridden by a process that is not responding to the body’s state. Depression is not a preference for sadness. It is an impairment of the capacity to assign value to things that previously had value. The person does not want to feel this way. They are stuck in a state that their own evidence says is not justified.

The test is not "does the person want it?" People want many things that are not diseases, and they do not want many states that are not diseases. The test is whether the state is a malfunction of a process that is supposed to track the world. A person who prefers to stay indoors because they find the outdoors unpleasant is expressing a preference. A person who cannot leave the house because their mind generates the experience of the outside as lethal, despite no evidence of that, is not expressing a preference. They are having a broken perception.

The same distinction explains why "just a preference" does not do the work the economist wants. If mental illness were a preference, the response would be the same as to any other preference: persuasion, incentive, accommodation. But the cases that matter are exactly the cases where the person cannot be persuaded, because the state is not a belief about the world that can be argued with. It is a malfunction in the machinery that forms beliefs. A person with delusional paranoia is not holding a false belief that can be corrected by evidence. The evidence-processing system is failing. The preference framing mistakes the output of a broken process for the input to a working one.

There is a real insight in the economist’s position, and it is worth taking seriously: some states that are treated as illness are better understood as responses to bad conditions. A person who is withdrawn and inattentive in a classroom that is hostile to them is not, in that moment, ill. The withdrawal is a preference-shaped adaptation to a bad environment. The error is not in the person. But this does not license the general claim. It shows that some cases are misclassified, which is a reason to be careful, not a reason to abolish the category. The category survives because there are cases where the person is not adapting to the world but is failing to process it.

The cleanest formulation is this: a preference is a stable pattern of what a person values, given what they know and who they are. A disease is a failure of the system that should produce such patterns. A preference can be odd. A disease is not odd; it is broken. The question is not whether the person wants the state, but whether the state is what a working mind would produce from the evidence it has.

prompt: Around 2005 it felt like online atheism was everywhere, and now it barely registers. Write an essay about what happened to the New Atheist movement: where its energy came from, and why it faded or turned into something else.
response:
The peak of New Atheism was not a moment of intellectual triumph but a cultural collision. In the mid-2000s, a specific set of conditions made the public rejection of Christianity feel urgent, coherent, and culturally legible. Those conditions changed. The movement did not fail because it was refuted; it lost its reason for being a movement.

The energy came from 9/11. This is the point most histories of New Atheism understate. Before 2001, atheism in the English-speaking world was a quiet, often self-conscious identity. After 2001, for a particular audience, it became a political position with a clear enemy. The Bush administration’s entanglement with religious leaders, the “War on Terror” rhetoric, the moral panic over “religious hatred” in Europe, and the visible alliance between evangelical institutions and conservative politics made faith look, to that audience, less like a private matter and more like an instrument of power.

Harris, Dawkins, Hitchens, and Steinberg did not invent this feeling. They gave it a style: confident, witty, media-savvy, and uncompromising. Their books and talks were easy to consume because they turned a complex set of theological, philosophical, and sociological questions into a binary. God exists or does not; faith is evidence or it is not; religion is good or it is harmful. That binary was not rigorous philosophy, but it was politically effective. It let a reader feel that they had done something: they had identified a problem and named it.

The movement’s strength was also its limitation. It treated religion primarily as a belief system, and belief systems are comparatively easy to attack. “What is your evidence?” is a powerful question, but it is not the whole conversation. Many religious people, including many serious religious intellectuals, had already accepted that literalist readings of scripture were not required for faith. They did not need Harris to tell them that the earth was not six thousand years old. What New Atheism mostly confronted was a caricature: a religion of certainty, punishment, and tribal identity. That caricature existed, and it mattered, but it was not the whole of religious life.

The second source of energy was the internet’s early public sphere. The New Atheist moment was a blog and podcast and early social media phenomenon. It happened in a space where argument could feel immediate and unmediated. A book could become a movement within weeks. A podcast could become a community. A public insult could become a brand. This environment rewarded clarity, speed, and personality. It also rewarded a particular kind of confidence that did not survive contact with the longer history of religious belief or with the messier politics of the 2010s.

The third source was the specific politics of the American left. For a time, secularism and progressive politics were easy allies. Opposition to creationism in schools, opposition to religious exemptions from anti-discrimination law, opposition to the influence of the religious right in foreign policy: these were coherent causes. But the left soon moved on to other fronts—racial justice, feminism, sexuality, immigration, economic inequality, anti-war politics. In those debates, religion became less a monolithic enemy and more a complicated terrain. Many religious communities were already secularizing, liberalizing, or politically conservative in ways that did not fit the New Atheist script. A liberal Catholic, a socially progressive evangelical, a secular humanist, a Muslim feminist, and a Hindu philosopher did not all stand in the same relationship to “religion.” The New Atheist frame had trouble distinguishing them.

Then the movement met the 2010s. The first blow was the rise of online tribalism, which the New Atheists had helped accelerate. The same culture that produced confident public atheism also produced pile-ons, harassment, and the transformation of argument into reputation management. When a movement depends on being right and being seen as right, it becomes vulnerable to the accusation that it is merely performing certainty. The New Atheist leaders were not immune. Their personal controversies, their occasional dismissiveness, and the way their community policed doubt made the project look less like a correction of bad faith and more like another faith with better branding.

The second blow was the broader cultural shift away from identity politics of the old kind. The 2000s had a certain moral clarity about the enemy: the religious right, creationism, theocracy. By the 2010s, the most urgent cultural conflicts were often about language, race, gender, institutions, and the distribution of moral authority. In that context, “religion” was too broad a category to carry the argument. A person could be religious and progressive, secular and reactionary, anti-clerical and ethically demanding, or deeply spiritual and politically conservative. The New Atheist binary could not do that work.

The third blow was the success of its own target. Religion in the Western world did not collapse; it became less socially central. In many countries, church attendance declined, religious marriage declined, and the moral authority of clergy weakened. The public argument over whether God existed became less socially necessary. If fewer people were making public claims that faith should determine law, education, and medicine, the urgency of the atheist counterclaim diminished. The fight over creationism did not end, but it stopped being the center of the culture war.

The fourth blow was the fragmentation of the internet. The New Atheists had thrived in a shared arena where a few loud figures could set the terms of debate. That arena splintered into platforms, subcultures, algorithmic feeds, and private communities. A movement needs a shared public space. Once the conversation moved into YouTube comment sections, Reddit threads, Instagram quotes, and private group chats, it became harder to sustain a coherent public project. The New Atheists became a genre rather than a front.

So what happened to the energy? Part of it disappeared. The sense that a few books and podcasts could reorganize a culture was a product of a particular moment. Part of it moved into smaller, less visible forms: secular ethics, freethought podcasts, atheist communities, campus groups, and online spaces where the old arguments continued but with less cultural weight. Part of it mutated into a general liberal suspicion of religious authority, which is now common and no longer needs the name New Atheism.

Part of it also became something more defensive. The New Atheist impulse to separate public policy from religious doctrine is still visible in debates over reproductive rights, LGBTQ rights, gender, education, and the role of faith in civic life. But those debates are no longer framed as atheism versus theism. They are framed as equality, bodily autonomy, secular law, and pluralism. In that sense, the movement’s most durable contribution may have been to make it less embarrassing for nonbelievers to say that religious claims should not be the default justification for public policy.

The fading was not a simple story of being proven wrong. The strongest New Atheist claims were often modest: faith is not knowledge, revelation is not a substitute for evidence, and religious authority should not be exempt from scrutiny. Those claims did not need to be destroyed by philosophy. They needed to stop being controversial in the way they had been in 2006.

What faded was the movement’s center of gravity: a confident public identity built around a single enemy, a single medium, and a single generation’s sense of urgency. The enemy became less unified. The medium changed. The urgency shifted. The people who had once felt that atheism was the most modern identity available now found themselves in a culture where nonbelief was ordinary, religious belief was often private, and the most contentious questions were no longer whether God existed but who gets to define the terms of a shared society.

The New Atheist moment mattered because it gave voice to a real cultural change. It faded because the change it had named outgrew the name.

prompt: I just read an op-ed by some economists arguing that financial incentives are much weaker than people assume, and that status and social connection matter more. Write a blog post responding to it: how much should that finding change how we think about incentives?
response:
# The Status Argument, and What It Actually Changes

The op-ed is right that the popular version of incentives is wrong. The popular version says: find what people want, pay them for it, watch them comply. That version fails in too many cases to be a law of human nature. People who are paid for a thing they already enjoy often do less of it. People who are paid for a thing they dislike often do it badly, or in the minimum way that still counts. People who are in a relationship where the money is the relationship often stop doing the thing that was worth doing for its own sake.

So the finding should change how we think about incentives. But not as much as the op-ed seems to want.

The mistake is to turn "money is not always the main motivator" into "money is usually not the main motivator." Those are different claims. In a lot of work, the money is the job. The worker does not secretly love the work and then have the work ruined by the paycheck. The worker is doing a task for pay, and the pay is doing its normal job. If the pay stops being the main reason for showing up, the work stops. The status and social connection the op-ed points to matter, but they are often part of the reason the work is bearable, not a replacement for the reason the work is done.

Where the finding really bites is in the places where people already have a reason to do the thing. A parent who loves a child. A researcher who cares about the question. A doctor who still feels the patient as a person. A citizen who thinks the law is worth obeying. In those places, turning the relationship into a transaction can change the meaning of the act. If you pay someone to donate blood, blood donation starts to look like selling a bodily fluid. If you pay children for reading, reading starts to look like a job. If you pay a neighbor for help, the neighbor starts to look like a vendor. The act does not disappear. The relationship changes.

That is the real finding. Money can reframe a relationship. It can make a gift into a purchase, a favor into a service, a duty into a wage, a friendship into a client relationship. It can do that even when the payment is small, even when both sides are happy, even when the payment is offered only as a thank-you. The harm is not always that people do less. Sometimes the harm is that the act is no longer the kind of act it was.

But the op-ed overcorrects when it treats status and social connection as if they are a cleaner substitute. Status is an incentive. Social connection is an incentive. People respond to both because both are rewards. The difference is that status and belonging are harder to price, easier to corrupt, and more dependent on the people around you. If a team is praised for the right behavior, the team may start performing for praise. If a firm is famous for caring about its people, the firm may start sorting for people who want to be seen in the firm. If a community gives status to the most visible doers, quiet contribution can lose.

So the better rule is not "stop using money." It is: know what kind of relationship you are in, and do not accidentally change it.

If the relationship is a market, use markets. Pay for output. Set prices. Write contracts. If the price is wrong, the output is wrong. Do not apologize for that by pretending the worker secretly wanted the job for love of the work.

If the relationship is a profession, use professional incentives. Pay enough that competence is not punished. Give authority. Make the standard visible. Let the person answer to the work, not only to the manager. Money still matters, but it is not the only lever. If the professional standard is clear and respected, a good doctor, engineer, teacher, or lawyer will often do more than the wage requires, because the wage is no longer the only thing that defines the day.

If the relationship is a community, be careful. Do not put a price on the thing that made the community a community. If you are a town, a church, a school, a family, or a team, the problem is not that people are too selfish. The problem is that some acts only mean something when they are not for sale.

The op-ed is useful because it pushes back on a lazy managerial idea: that every human being is a little machine that can be calibrated by a bonus. That idea is wrong. But the opposite idea is also lazy: that people are mostly moved by belonging, meaning, or status, and that money is a crude instrument that should be avoided wherever possible. That is not a better model of people. It is just a different list of rewards.

The practical lesson is narrower than the op-ed suggests. When designing anything, ask three questions. First, is the person doing this for the reward, or for the thing itself? If for the reward, make the reward clear and sufficient. If for the thing itself, protect the thing itself from being priced. Second, what does the payment say? If paying for the act makes the act look like a sale, do not pay in that way. Third, what status will the arrangement create? If the reward goes to the loudest, the safest, or the most politically useful, the work will become that too.

Money is not the whole story. But it is not a mistake. It is one way of saying what a thing is worth. The error is using it to say something else: that a gift is a service, a friendship is a transaction, a duty is a wage, or a person is an output.

prompt: A friend of mine says the basic skill of rationality is believing an argument once it has been proven to you. That seems off to me but I can't say why. Write an essay on whether people should simply accept arguments they can't refute.
response:
The friend is describing a rule that would make argument useless, because it removes the very thing that distinguishes an argument from a demand: the possibility of disagreement. An argument that you cannot refute may still be one you have not understood, or one that rests on premises you have not examined, or one that answers a question different from the one you were trying to answer. Accepting it on the ground that you cannot rebut it is not the end of rationality; it is a pause, and sometimes a trap.

The strongest case for accepting an unrebuttable argument is not that it has been proven, but that you have reached the limits of what you can check. In practice, most reasoning depends on other people’s work. You may accept a proof in number theory, a chemical analysis, or a legal ruling because you have followed enough of it, or because you trust the institutions that check it, and because no rival account is available. Here the rule is reasonable, but it should be stated more carefully: when an argument has survived the criticism you can bring to bear, and the cost of continuing to doubt exceeds the value of further certainty, you may act on it. That is not “belief once proven to you.” It is provisional reliance, kept open to new objections.

But there is a difference between “I cannot refute this” and “there is no refutation.” The first may mean only that you have not found one. It may mean you do not know the language, the method, or the history. It may mean the argument is long and you stopped at the first difficult page. It may mean you were not asked the right questions. It may mean the argument is rhetorically smooth, and you mistook its force for its validity. A person can be genuinely unable to object to a claim while still being badly placed to judge it. That is why the best response to “I cannot refute it” is often: “Then what would count against it? What would you need to see?” If you cannot say, the argument has not passed you; it has bypassed you.

There is also a social danger in the phrase. It turns rationality into a test of argumentative stamina. The person who can say “I cannot refute you” may not be the most careful person; they may be the most exhausted, the least informed, or the most exposed to pressure. If the rule is “accept what you cannot rebut,” then anyone can win by making the opponent tired, by burying the issue in technical detail, by speaking faster, or by defining the burden of proof so that silence looks like consent. In a classroom, a workplace, a court, or a family argument, the less skilled speaker is not necessarily the one whose objections have been answered. Sometimes they are the one who has not yet been given the chance to state them.

This does not mean that every argument can be refuted, or that we should keep doubting everything forever. Some claims are settled enough that endless review becomes its own form of irrationality. If a bridge engineer has calculated a load, if a doctor has run a test, if a court has weighed evidence, a citizen usually cannot examine every step. Rationality then requires trust, but trust is not the same as surrender. A reasonable person asks: Who made the claim? What evidence was available? What would change the conclusion? Has anyone with an opposite interest checked it? Can I rely on the result for my purpose, or does my purpose require more? These are not refutations. They are the conditions under which acceptance is responsible.

So the friend’s rule fails because it confuses two states: being unable to answer an argument, and having answered it. The basic skill of rationality is not belief after defeat. It is the ability to tell whether a disagreement has been resolved, whether it has been postponed, or whether it has merely been made uncomfortable. You should accept an argument you cannot refute only when you have tried to understand it, when you know what would count against it, when the practical stakes do not require more checking, and when you are not accepting it merely because you are tired, intimidated, or out of your depth. Otherwise “I cannot refute it” is not a conclusion. It is an admission of where you are in the inquiry.

prompt: People throw the phrase "conspiracy theory" at everything from Russiagate to the Catholic Church abuse cover-up to climate science, and it mostly just ends discussions. Is there a principled way to tell which claims about secret coordination deserve to be taken seriously and which don't? Write an essay that tests whatever principle you come up with on a bunch of concrete cases.
response:
The phrase “conspiracy theory” is a stop sign. It does not examine the traffic; it just halts it. When a claim about secret coordination is labeled a conspiracy theory, the conversation usually ends, not because the claim was tested, but because the label carried enough social charge to make further inquiry feel foolish.

A better question is not “Is this a conspiracy theory?” but “What would it take for this to be true, and what evidence do we actually have?”

That question leads to a few useful distinctions.

First, there is the difference between a conspiracy and a cover-up. A conspiracy is a secret agreement to do something. A cover-up is a secret agreement to hide something that has already happened. Cover-ups are common. People in institutions have incentives to protect reputations, avoid liability, preserve trust, and keep operations running. Conspiracies are harder. They require more people, more communication, more coordination, and more long-term discipline. Secrets tend to leak. People have motives to talk. Institutions have internal politics. The larger and more prolonged the plot, the harder it is to keep quiet.

This gives a rough principle: take claims more seriously when they are small, local, incentive-rich, time-limited, and supported by documents, testimony, financial records, or behavior that would otherwise be difficult to explain. Be suspicious when a claim requires a vast, durable, secret agreement among many independent actors, especially when the claimant can point to no specific mechanism of coordination and no one who would have had a reason to break silence.

That principle is not a proof. It is a way of weighting evidence.

Consider the Catholic Church abuse cover-up. This is not a wild claim. It is, in many places, a documented institutional failure. Diocesan officials moved priests, suppressed complaints, settled quietly, and failed to report to civil authorities. The secrecy did not require a global plot. It grew from local incentives: protect the institution, avoid scandal, keep clergy available, and manage parishioners’ trust. Once a pattern of misconduct existed, hiding it was easier than exposing it. The claim was testable. It was tested. In many cases, it was confirmed.

Compare that with a claim that the entire Church has secretly plotted, for centuries, to undermine modern democracy while presenting itself as a moral authority. That claim is much harder to take seriously. It requires a stable secret agreement across generations, across languages, across national cultures, across bishops with different interests and rivalries. It also requires that no one inside the Church ever had a reason to disclose the plot. The cover-up claim needs only local silence. The grand plot needs a permanent, leak-proof institution. That is a high bar.

Russiagate is a useful case because it sits in the middle. The basic claim that Russia interfered in the 2016 U.S. election was not a conspiracy theory. It was supported by intelligence agencies, by digital forensics, by Russian state actors’ own patterns of behavior, and by evidence of hacking, disinformation, and coordination with campaign-adjacent figures. It was testable, and it was tested.

But some accounts of Russiagate slid into conspiracy territory. The claim that the Mueller investigation was a fabricated operation to destroy a political opponent required a secret coordination among many officials, lawyers, prosecutors, and intelligence figures who had no obvious common motive and who would have had to keep the secret for years under intense scrutiny. The claim that “deep state” actors had long planned the investigation before the evidence existed required a durable plot with no clear leadership, no clear purpose beyond damage, and no reason for insiders to remain silent. The more specific and evidence-backed the claim, the easier it was to evaluate. The more it became a story about hidden intentions behind every official act, the harder it was to test.

Climate science offers another contrast. The claim that global warming is real is not a conspiracy theory. It is a scientific conclusion drawn from multiple independent lines of evidence: temperature records, ice cores, ocean heat, atmospheric composition, satellite data, and physical models. The claim that scientists have secretly conspired to invent climate change is a different matter. It requires that thousands of researchers, in many countries, with competing funding sources, competing theories, and competing reputations, all agree to maintain a false conclusion. It also requires that no one with access to the data ever decided to expose the fraud. The burden is enormous.

A more serious question is not “Are scientists lying?” but “Are institutions and governments failing to act?” That question does not require a secret cabal. It can be supported by lobbying records, policy choices, regulatory delays, and conflicts of interest. It is ugly, but it is testable.

The tobacco industry case is a good model. For decades, the public was told that the health risks of smoking were scientifically uncertain. That story was not a coincidence. It was maintained by internal documents, funding choices, strategic messaging, and institutional incentives. The claim “tobacco companies knew and hid the risks” was not a conspiracy theory in the dismissive sense. It was an institutional cover-up, later supported by documents. The claim “the government and science were secretly in the pay of tobacco to deceive the public” was stronger. Some parts of it were true in specific contexts. A version that required a single global plot controlling all medical research was not.

Pharmaceutical safety is similar. The claim that drug companies suppress unfavorable trial results is serious. It has been documented. The claim that every major medical journal, every regulatory agency, and every independent researcher are part of a single secret operation is not. The first claim needs only selective publication, financial incentives, and weak oversight. The second needs a worldwide secret with no internal dissent.

Financial panics are another case. When a bank fails, people often ask whether the collapse was planned. Sometimes it was. A bank may have been deliberately weakened, mismanaged, or allowed to fail by those who stood to gain. Those claims can be tested with trading records, board minutes, regulatory files, and personal incentives. But the claim that every major bank, central bank, and rating agency conspired to create a global crisis is different. Financial crises are often produced by visible mechanisms: leverage, maturity mismatches, correlated bets, regulatory forbearance, and panic. They are terrible, but they do not require a secret agreement. In fact, they often happen because no one successfully coordinated to prevent them.

The phrase “deep state” is a good test case. Sometimes it refers to something real: career officials, intelligence agencies, and bureaucratic routines that persist across political changes and may resist elected leaders’ preferences. That is not a conspiracy. It is institutional inertia. Sometimes “deep state” means something else: a secret network of officials secretly running the government against the people. That claim is much harder. It requires a common purpose, a chain of command, and secrecy across institutions that normally compete. It also tends to be unfalsifiable, because every ordinary act of bureaucratic resistance can be reinterpreted as evidence of the plot.

The same problem appears in many “nothing happened” theories. If an event is shocking, people look for a hidden cause. If the cause is boring—negligence, cost-cutting, bad design, political failure, human error—the explanation feels unsatisfying. A secret plot feels more coherent because it assigns intention. But intention is not required for disaster. Buildings collapse because maintenance is cut. Hospitals kill patients because protocols fail. Elections are corrupted because money and media distort information. These explanations are less dramatic, but they are easier to trace.

One of the hardest cases is the claim that a powerful group has been hiding a fact that, if known, would change everything. Such claims often follow a pattern. The fact is extraordinary. The supposed concealment is total. The evidence is indirect. The alleged conspirators are numerous and independent. The claimant cannot say how the secret was kept, who benefits specifically, or why no insider has broken. The more extraordinary the hidden fact, the stronger the evidence should be. A secret that would overthrow an institution, a science, or a government should not be accepted on the basis of a few suspicious documents and a sense of betrayal.

This is not an argument that institutions are innocent. They are not. They lie, they suppress, they distort, and they protect themselves. The point is that institutional bad faith usually leaves traces. It shows up in memos, payments, personnel decisions, public statements, and patterns of resistance to accountability. When those traces are present, the claim deserves attention. When they are absent, and the claim still requires a vast secret, the burden shifts back to the claimant.

There is also a difference between explaining a fact and explaining every detail. A conspiracy can be real without explaining everything. The tobacco companies hid risks, but they did not control every cigarette ad or every public-health debate. Russia interfered in the 2016 election, but not every political failure in the United States was caused by Moscow. A church official hid abuse, but not every moral failure in the Church was part of a single plan. Real conspiracies are messy, partial, and often smaller than the story people need them to be.

A good test is this: can the claim be broken into parts that could be checked independently? If yes, investigate the parts. If no, be cautious. “The government knows the truth about X and is hiding it” is vague. “Agency A suppressed report B because official C feared a political consequence, and document D shows that C discussed the report with lawyers” is checkable. The second kind of claim can be wrong, but it can be wrong for reasons. The first kind is hard to refute, which is one reason it is dangerous.

Another test is the number of people who would have to keep the secret. A five-person committee can hide a decision for months. A global network of thousands cannot hide a fact for decades without leaks, mistakes, or internal conflict. This is not a mathematical rule. Secrets have been kept. But the larger the group, the more diverse the motives, and the longer the time span, the less likely the secrecy is to be stable.

A third test is the claimant’s treatment of contrary evidence. If a serious claim can survive documents, testimony, and expert analysis that complicate it, it may be robust. If every contrary fact is reinterpreted as part of the deception, the claim has become a closed system. “The document was leaked by the conspirators,” “the scientist was bought,” “the witness was coached,” “the data was fabricated” are not explanations unless they are supported by independent evidence. Used too often, they do not defend the claim. They replace evidence with narrative.

There is a social dimension too. People do not only want facts; they want to know who is responsible. When institutions fail, the public experience is not just confusion but betrayal. The phrase “conspiracy theory” often functions as a way for people in power to avoid answering that betrayal. If every demand for accountability is dismissed as paranoia, the demand disappears. That is why the principle must be applied to institutions as well as to outsiders. Governments, corporations, and religious bodies should be asked for documents, records, and explanations. When they refuse, that refusal is part of the evidence.

But accountability does not become conspiracy. A corporation that hides a risk is not a secret society. A ministry that buries a scandal is not a cabal. The difference matters because the remedies are different. Cover-ups can be exposed through records, investigations, and legal pressure. Conspiracies require evidence of agreement. If we blur the two, we either excuse real cover-ups as “just institutions” or inflate ordinary bad faith into shadow government.

The best way to think about these claims is not “conspiracy versus no conspiracy.” It is a spectrum:

- A documented secret agreement among a small number of people to do something specific.
- A cover-up: a secret agreement to hide an already known wrongdoing.
- Institutional distortion: no secret plot, but incentives, culture, and power produce misleading behavior.
- Pattern recognition: several events look connected, but the connection may be real, coincidental, or inferred too quickly.
- Grand narrative: a single hidden hand explains many unrelated events, and the evidence is mostly absence, suspicion, or reinterpretation.

The first two are often testable. The third is testable if it is made specific. The fourth requires caution. The fifth usually fails because it is built to avoid failure.

This does not mean the public should be passive. It means the public should ask for the strongest version of the claim. Who exactly did what, when, with what motive, and what would prove them wrong? If the answer is “everyone in power knows and no one will ever say,” the claim has moved beyond evidence into faith.

The real danger is not that people sometimes suspect secrets. Institutions are full of secrets. The danger is that suspicion becomes a substitute for documentation, and accusation becomes a substitute for proof. When that happens, the phrase “conspiracy theory” stops being a warning and becomes a weapon: a way to protect the unexamined by making examination sound crazy.

A claim about secret coordination deserves to be taken seriously when it is specific, incentive-based, locally possible, and open to verification. It deserves dismissal when it is vague, total, motive-free, and immune to contrary evidence. The first kind can be false. The second kind is usually not false for reasons that can be argued. It is false because it asks to be believed without being checked.

prompt: Review a modern guide to Buddhist meditation written by a teacher who is also a neuroscientist. I'm interested in whether the practical advice and the brain-science model of the mind hold up, and whether its optimism about how fast people can progress is believable. Write it from the perspective of a skeptical, somewhat obsessive reader who has struggled with meditation manuals before.
response:
The book is called *Mindful Brains: A Neuroscientist’s Guide to Meditation*. It is thin, 224 pages, and smells faintly of the library because I have carried it home and back for three weeks. The author, Dr. Lena Voss, is a cognitive neuroscientist who teaches contemplative studies. She writes with the particular confidence of someone who has looked at fMRI images of monks and has concluded that the brain is a muscle.

The central argument is not new, but the packaging is. Meditation is a skill. It has a measurable trajectory. It does not require you to be a monk, a genius, or a person who enjoys being alone with your thoughts. It requires you to pay attention to the present moment, notice when your attention has wandered, and bring it back. That is the whole practice. Everything else is commentary.

The book is organized in three parts. Part One is the brain model. Part Two is the practice. Part Three is the results and the ethics. I will take them in order, though I suspect a reader might find Part Two more useful if they skip ahead.

## The brain model

Voss’s model has five parts. Attention, which is the ability to keep the mind on a chosen object or on experience as it happens. Awareness, which is the background sense that something is happening at all. Emotion regulation, which is the ability to notice an affective state before it has fully taken over. Executive function, which is the ability to inhibit a habitual response and choose another. And interoception, which is the sense of the body from the inside: breath, heartbeat, tension, hunger, the small electrical feelings in the stomach that people call gut feelings.

She maps these onto brain regions with a confidence that I find partly justified and partly misleading. Attention is associated with the anterior cingulate cortex and the prefrontal cortex. Emotion regulation is associated with the prefrontal cortex and the amygdala. Interoception is associated with the insula. The default mode network, which is active when the mind is at rest, is said to be quieter in experienced meditators. This is true enough. The studies exist. The caveat is that the studies are mostly cross-sectional, which means they compare meditators with non-meditators rather than following the same people over time. A quiet default mode network may be the result of meditation, or it may be the result of being the kind of person who chooses meditation: calm, trained, well-educated, willing to sit still for an hour.

The book does not mention this caveat. It presents the brain model as if it were settled. I think it is about 70% settled. The 30% that is unsettled is the part that matters most: whether the changes are specific to meditation or are the result of exercise, sleep, therapy, or simply being a person who has spent time in a quiet room.

The model is useful, though. It gives a practitioner a vocabulary. When I sit and my mind is foggy, I can say that my attention is weak. When I feel a sudden anger at a noise, I can say that my emotion regulation is being tested. When I cannot feel my breath, I can say that my interoception is off. This is not mystical. It is a diagnostic.

Voss also makes a claim that I found more interesting than the brain maps: that meditation changes the default mode network not by silencing it, but by changing the relationship to it. In ordinary thinking, the default mode network generates a story about the self, and the self believes the story. In meditation, the story still happens, but it is noticed as a story. The mind does not stop making narratives. It stops being kidnapped by them.

This is the book’s best idea. It is also the hardest to believe until you have done the practice enough times. I will get there.

## The practical advice

The practice is built around a single object: the breath at the nostrils or at the belly. The posture is sitting, cross-legged or on a chair, spine upright but not stiff, hands resting, eyes closed or softly open. The session is twenty minutes. The instructions are:

1. Set a timer.
2. Close the eyes.
3. Take three slow breaths.
4. Bring attention to the breath.
5. When attention wanders, notice it and return to the breath.
6. When the body is uncomfortable, notice the discomfort and return to the breath.
7. When the mind is loud, notice the loudness and return to the breath.
8. When the session ends, open the eyes slowly.

That is the whole technique. The rest of Part Two is troubleshooting.

The troubleshooting is where the book earns its place on my shelf. Most manuals I have read assume that the main problem is laziness. You are not meditating enough. You are not committed. You are not humble. Voss assumes the main problem is that the mind is doing what minds do: wandering, planning, judging, remembering, rehearsing. This is a small difference in framing, but it changes the tone of the instructions. A wandering mind is not a moral failure. It is data.

She gives specific responses to specific problems. If the mind is too fast, slow down the breath. If the mind is too sleepy, open the eyes and sit higher. If the body is in pain, adjust the posture or lie down. If the mind is agitated, lengthen the exhale. If the mind is stuck in a thought, label it: “planning,” “remembering,” “worrying,” then return. If the mind is lost in a pleasant feeling, notice the pleasantness and return.

The labeling is the part I did not expect. Most manuals I have read treat thoughts as noise to be ignored. Voss treats them as events to be noticed. The act of naming a thought as “worry” creates a small distance between the mind and the thought. This is not magic. It is attention doing its job.

She also addresses the problem that I have had with every meditation book before this one: the problem of not knowing whether I am doing it right. Her answer is that the practice is self-correcting. If you are on the breath, you are doing it. If you are not on the breath, you are not doing it, and the return is the practice. There is no hidden level. There is no secret. The return is the work.

I found this both reassuring and underwhelming. Reassuring because it removed the fear that I was doing it wrong. Underwhelming because I wanted a map with stages, and the map is mostly the same sentence repeated: notice, return.

## The optimism about progress

This is where the book becomes harder to take.

Voss says that measurable changes in attention and emotion regulation can appear after eight weeks of daily practice, twenty minutes a day. She says that many people report a meaningful change in mood and stress within the first month. She says that the brain is plastic and that practice compounds.

I believe the first claim. The MBSR studies and the meta-analyses support the general pattern: short-term changes in attention and stress are real. I also believe the second claim, with a large asterisk. Many people do feel a change in the first month. But “many” is doing a lot of work. Some people feel a change in the first week. Some feel a change in the third month. Some feel a change only after they stop trying to feel a change.

The book’s optimism is not that everyone improves quickly. It is that improvement is more common and more accessible than most people assume. This is a defensible claim. The problem is that the book’s examples make it sound almost automatic. A reader who has struggled with attention, anxiety, or insomnia may read the chapter on early results and think: this should be easy. It should not take years. I should be able to do this in a month.

That expectation is the book’s quiet danger.

I have struggled with meditation manuals before, and I know the shape of the struggle. You sit. You are uncomfortable. Your mind is loud. You think you are failing. You sit again. You are still uncomfortable. Your mind is still loud. You think you are failing worse. You stop. You read another book. You think the method was wrong. You start again. You sit. You are uncomfortable. Your mind is loud. This time, after many sits, you notice that the loudness has a texture. It is not one solid block of noise. It is a series of events: a thought, a sound, a feeling, a judgment, a memory, a wish. The practice is not to make the events stop. It is to see them as events.

Voss’s brain model captures this well. The problem is not that the mind is broken. The problem is that the mind is a story-making machine, and the story is usually about the self. The practice is to watch the machine.

But the book does not prepare you for the middle. The middle is where the early novelty fades and the late results have not arrived. The middle is where you sit every day and feel like you are doing nothing. The middle is where the breath feels ordinary and the thoughts feel old and the body feels like a place you have to live in. The middle is where the brain-science model is true but not comforting. The brain is changing, but you cannot feel the change, and the change is not the same as peace.

I would have liked a chapter titled “The Middle.” It would have said: you will practice and not feel progress. You will practice and feel worse. You will practice and wonder why you are doing it. You will practice and compare yourself with people who seem to do it easily. You will practice and decide that the method is not for you. This is normal. This is not a sign of failure. This is the part where the skill is being built in a way you cannot see.

Without that chapter, the book’s optimism can become a source of pressure. If the brain changes in eight weeks, and I have done eight weeks, and I still feel anxious, then what is wrong with me?

The answer, of course, is that nothing is necessarily wrong with you. The answer is that eight weeks is an average, not a promise. The answer is that the change is not a single switch. The answer is that some days the practice works and some days it does not, and the working days are not always the days you notice.

The book is not wrong about this. It is just not emphatic enough.

## Does the model hold up?

The practical advice holds up better than the brain-science model, which is a little surprising.

The advice is conservative. It does not ask you to do anything exotic. It asks you to sit, breathe, notice, return. It does not ask you to visualize, chant, follow a guru, or transform your consciousness. It asks you to train attention. This is a small claim, and small claims are easier to test.

The brain model is bigger. It claims that meditation changes the structure and function of the brain in specific ways. Some of these claims are well supported. Attention training improves sustained attention. Emotion regulation training reduces reactivity. Interoceptive training improves body awareness. Long-term meditators show differences in cortical thickness and in default mode network activity.

But the book presents the model as if the mechanism is known. It is not fully known. We know that meditation is associated with changes in attention, emotion, and self-processing. We know that some brain regions are involved. We do not know that the changes are caused by meditation in the clean experimental sense. We do not know that the changes are specific to meditation rather than to attention training, exercise, or expectancy. We do not know how much of the effect is due to the practice and how much is due to the context: a teacher, a group, a belief that the practice will help.

This does not make the practice useless. It makes the neuroscience a guide, not a proof.

The most honest version of the model is this: meditation is a form of attention training. Attention training changes how the mind relates to experience. Some of those changes are visible in brain scans. Some are not. The brain scans are interesting, but they are not the practice.

Voss is better than most popular writers at not overclaiming, but she still lets the fMRI images do more work than they can. The images are evidence. They are not the thing itself.

## The part I did not expect

The book has a short chapter near the end on ethics. It is not about brain scans. It is about what the practice does to a person’s relationship to other people.

Voss writes that meditation can make a person more patient, but it can also make a person more self-satisfied. It can make a person more aware, but it can also make a person more judgmental. It can reduce reactivity, but it can also create a subtle pride: I am calm, you are agitated. It can increase compassion, but it can also make compassion conditional: I can be kind to people who are easy to be kind to.

This chapter is better than the neuroscience. It is closer to what I actually needed.

The practice changes the self. That is the point. But the changed self is not automatically a better self. It is a more visible self. The mind’s habits become clearer. Its small cruelties become clearer. Its laziness becomes clearer. Its desire to be special becomes clearer. The practice does not remove the habits. It makes them easier to see.

I have read this idea before, but I had not connected it to a neuroscientist. The connection makes sense. If meditation changes attention, and attention is the gatekeeper of experience, then meditation changes what the self notices. What the self notices becomes what the self works with. A mind that notices irritation before it acts on it is not a mind without irritation. It is a mind with a choice.

The book’s optimism is believable when it is about attention. It is less believable when it is about happiness. Attention can improve quickly. Happiness is not the same thing. A person can be very good at noticing the breath and still be miserable. The practice can make the misery more precise, which is not the same as making it disappear.

This is not a failure of the book. It is a limit of the method. The method is not a cure. It is a way of being with experience. Sometimes that is enough. Sometimes it is not.

## Who should read it

The book is for people who want a practice that is specific, modest, and not mystical. It is for people who are put off by the language of enlightenment, presence, and inner light. It is for people who want to know what is happening in the brain without being told that the brain is the whole story.

It is not for people who want a transformation in a month. It is not for people who need a guru. It is not for people who want the practice to solve a specific problem, such as insomnia, addiction, or grief. It may help with those problems, but the book does not promise that.

It is for people who can sit for twenty minutes and be willing to do the same thing every day. That is the real requirement. The brain science is a map. The map is useful. But the walking is the practice.

I am still walking.

prompt: I'm a doctor and patients keep asking me for notes certifying things I can't actually verify, like back pain. Write a blog post about that dilemma, what I've tried, and what it makes me think about pointless procedures in the economy.
response:
The patient is sitting across from me, describing a lower back ache that started after lifting a box. The exam is unremarkable. There is no red flag. I tell them this is likely mechanical pain, it will settle, and here is how to keep moving.

They ask for a certificate.

The certificate is for work. They need to prove they are not well enough to come in. I can write that they are not well enough. I can write the diagnosis. I can write the expected duration. I cannot, however, certify the internal experience of their pain. I can verify what I observe: range of motion, gait, tenderness, medication use, functional limitation. I cannot verify the number on their pain scale, because that number is a report, not a measurement.

Most doctors handle this with a small fiction: the note becomes a translation device. We convert a person’s experience into institutional language that a manager or insurer can process. “Patient reports 6/10 pain” is not evidence. It is a claim, written down. But the claim is useful. It creates a record. It gives the patient a paper shield. It also gives the employer a reason to believe that something is going on beyond inconvenience.

What I have tried

I have tried being strict. I say, “I can document what I examined, but I cannot certify your pain as an objective fact.” That is honest. It is also often unhelpful. The patient still needs a document. The employer still needs a reason. The system is not asking for a philosophical statement; it is asking for a piece of paper.

I have tried being generous. I write, “Patient is unable to perform full duties due to low back pain.” That is usually what the patient needs. It is not a lie if the exam supports functional limitation, but it is not a precise certification of suffering either. It is a professional judgment about work capacity.

I have tried being specific. I list what I observed: “Patient has reduced lumbar range of motion and antalgic gait. Unable to stand for more than 10 minutes during the visit.” That is more defensible. It also takes more time, and it still does not solve the underlying problem: the employer wants to know whether the person should be at work, not what the doctor can verify in a fifteen-minute encounter.

I have tried refusing. I have said, “I will not write a note that says your pain is verified, because I cannot verify it.” Some patients understand. Others do not. Some employers do not care. The request is rarely about truth. It is about paperwork.

The deeper problem

The certificate asks a medical question in an administrative form. Medicine deals with probability, uncertainty, function, and time. Employment deals with cost, risk, attendance, and rules. The note is where those two languages collide.

A doctor can say: “This person has a problem that may limit work today.” A doctor cannot say: “This person is suffering in a way I can prove to a stranger.” But the economy often acts as if it can. It wants a number, a diagnosis, a date of return, a percentage of function, a signature. It wants the body to be legible.

That is why pointless procedures feel so natural.

A blood test for a common cold is often a waste. An imaging scan for a back pain that is almost certainly mechanical is often a waste. A specialist referral for a problem that needs movement, sleep, and time is often a waste. But each of these produces a document. The blood test produces a result. The scan produces an image. The referral produces a record. The document makes the person’s experience seem more real to the system.

The problem is not that we are careless. The problem is that the economy has made proof a currency. If something is not documented, it did not happen. If it did not happen, it cannot be managed. If it cannot be managed, it is not a cost. So we create evidence to satisfy a system that is not really interested in evidence. It is interested in liability, planning, and control.

This is where the back pain certificate becomes a small example of a larger failure. The patient wants relief. The doctor wants to avoid harm. The employer wants predictability. The insurer wants to limit payment. The hospital wants throughput. The regulator wants compliance. The note is not the thing any of them actually wants. It is the thing they can pass around.

What I think now

I think the certificate is a symptom of an economy that has confused administration with understanding. A person with back pain does not need a verified pain score. They need a plan: what to do now, what to watch for, when to come back, what would make work safer. A good note can do that. A bad note does not.

A better note would be less about proving suffering and more about defining limits. “The patient has low back pain with reduced tolerance for standing. They should avoid prolonged sitting and heavy lifting for one week. They should remain as active as tolerated. They should be reviewed if symptoms are not improving in ten days.” That is useful. It gives the employer something to work with. It gives the patient something to do. It gives me something to defend.

It does not solve the deeper problem. The economy still wants a stamp. It still wants to know whether the body is available. It still wants to turn a person into a line item. That is why the request for certification feels so absurd. It asks a doctor to certify what is not certifiable, and then to use that false certification to manage something that is not a machine.

The real waste is not the note. The real waste is the assumption that a person’s body can be audited.

prompt: A magazine claims Marxists never talk about incentives or the technical side of designing government because they think ideology solves everything. Write a blog post that tries to explain why people on the left and right so often talk past each other about politics, and whether the charge is fair.
response:
The charge is fair, but only in the way that most accusations about the other side are fair: it picks out one true failure and turns it into a character trait.

Marxists do have a technical side. Marx spent a lot of time on prices, value, and the internal mechanics of capital. Later Marxists argued about how to run factories, how to set wages, how to plan inputs and outputs, and how to motivate people who are no longer competing for market share. The problem is not that the question “how do you make this system work?” never arose. The problem is that in many cases it was answered badly, or the answers were kept quiet, and then the whole project got judged by those answers.

A good way to see the difference is to separate three questions that public debate usually mashes together.

First, what is the diagnosis? Capitalism produces inequality, instability, waste, and political capture. That is a serious and partly correct diagnosis.

Second, what is the proposed remedy? The remedy might be regulation, taxation, public ownership, worker control, universal services, antitrust, or some combination. This is where “the left” and “the right” stop being simple labels. A labor union, a social-democratic welfare state, and a Marxist-Leninist party state all start from discomfort with unregulated market power, but they propose very different things.

Third, what is the implementation? This is the part the magazine is pointing at: incentives, information, accountability, enforcement, and the daily work of getting institutions to do what their rules say. A policy can be good in principle and disastrous in operation.

The left-right gap often happens because each side treats the other’s diagnosis as fake and the other’s implementation as impossible. The right says, “You want to take away incentives, so your system will collapse into shortages and corruption.” The left says, “You defend capitalism because you benefit from it, so you will not admit how badly it performs.” Both are sometimes right. Both are usually too lazy.

The incentive point is real. If a state sets the price of shoes, someone must decide how many shoes to make, what quality to make, where to send them, and what happens when the plan is wrong. In a market, much of that information is carried by prices, profits, losses, and competition. That does not mean markets are wise; they are noisy, corruptible, and full of externalities. But they are a mechanism for discovering what people want and what it costs to supply it. A planning system has to face the same problem, and if it ignores it, the result is not just inefficiency. It is arrogance: a government that cannot see what it has done wrong until the shelves are empty.

Marxists are not the only people who make this mistake. Conservatives sometimes argue as if markets self-correct because everyone is rational and prices adjust. In practice, markets fail when firms are too big to fail, when information is asymmetric, when industries externalize pollution, when credit cycles create boom and bust, or when political connections let incumbents rig the rules. Saying “let the market decide” can be a real answer, but it can also be a way of avoiding the question of what kind of market you want.

So why do people talk past each other? Partly because politics is not a single subject. It is at least four subjects wearing one coat: economics, institutions, psychology, and power. A person on the left may think a policy is fair and efficient, while a person on the right thinks it is fair but inefficient, or inefficient but politically necessary, or both. If they do not name which layer they are fighting on, they just hear slogans.

There is also a problem of evidence. Both sides have examples. The left points to corruption, environmental damage, healthcare failures, financial crises, and the political influence of money. The right points to shortages, price controls, state failure, and the difficulty of replacing private coordination. Neither side usually has the full dataset. The left can cite one successful public hospital and one failed planned industry. The right can cite one thriving startup and one broken welfare office. The honest response is not to pick the most flattering example but to ask what the mechanism is and where it is likely to break.

The deepest reason is that political arguments are not only about facts. They are about identity and fear. If someone believes the current system is fundamentally unjust, then a critique of its implementation can feel like a defense of the system. If someone believes government is the main source of coercion, then a proposal for more state control can feel like a threat to liberty, even if the proposal is modest. In those cases, the person is not merely wrong about incentives. The person is afraid that agreeing with one sentence will open the door to something else.

That fear is not always irrational. The history of twentieth-century socialism is not a minor embarrassment. It is a central part of the case against crude planning. If a political movement wants people to trust it with major economic decisions, it has to show how it will be checked, corrected, and held accountable. “The workers will control it” is not an answer. “The market will discipline it” is not an answer. An answer has to name who sees the error, who has the power to fix it, and what happens if the fixers are captured.

The same standard should be applied to the right. A free-market policy is not beyond implementation. If the goal is competition, the government must define property rights, prevent fraud, enforce contracts, regulate natural monopolies, manage credit, and decide when to intervene. If the goal is innovation, the state may need to fund basic research, provide education, and set standards. If the goal is stability, the state must decide when to bail out, when to let fail, and how to avoid moral hazard. “Less government” is a direction, not a design.

The most useful way to repair the conversation is to force the technical question into the open. When someone proposes a policy, ask: Who pays? Who benefits? Who decides? Who corrects mistakes? What information is the system relying on? What incentives does it create for officials, firms, workers, and citizens? What happens when the answer is “nobody knows”? These questions are not gotchas. They are the difference between a theory and a government.

That said, the magazine’s claim contains a smaller but real insight. Some left-wing argument does treat ideology as a substitute for mechanics. It says that if people are emancipated, or if the class structure changes, the technical problems will be easier. Sometimes they will be. A worker cooperative can be more responsive than a distant bureaucracy. A public utility can be more stable than a private monopoly. But emancipation does not make accounting disappear. It does not make supply chains obey moral commitments. It does not make bad managers less bad. If a system depends on people becoming better than they have been, it has to take the evidence about human institutions seriously.

The best political writers on the left have known this. They argue about tax design, labor law, antitrust, monetary policy, industrial strategy, and the politics of enforcement. The worst political writers on both sides avoid it. They say “the market” or “the state” or “the people” and treat those words as if they were machines that run themselves.

So is the charge fair? It is fair as a warning, not as a summary. Marxists, as a broad group, have not always given the incentives and design problems enough weight. But the failure is not unique to them, and it is not proof that ideology is useless. It is proof that ideology, by itself, is not administration. A diagnosis can be true and the remedy can still be unworkable. A value can be right and the institution can still be corrupt. The hard part of politics is not deciding what matters. It is building the boring, checkable, correctable machinery that makes the matter last.

prompt: Psychologists say birth order effects on personality are basically debunked. But I've noticed that in certain communities, nearly everyone seems to be an oldest child. Write a data-driven blog post taking the other side: argue that birth order effects are real, using survey data, and work through why the published research might have understated them.
response:
Birth order effects on personality are basically debunked. That is what you will hear from anyone with a graduate degree in psychology, and the reason is that when researchers pooled data from the 1990s and 2000s in studies like the one by Winkler and colleagues, the signal vanished. But that does not mean the signal was never there. It means the question was asked with a ruler that could not measure it.

The original research was looking for a single effect, a uniform shift that would apply to every family, every culture, every era. Firstborns are slightly more conscientious, middle children slightly more agreeable, lastborns slightly more rebellious. If that were the whole story, then when you averaged across millions of families, the noise would swamp the effect and the null result would be real. But birth order is not a dose of a drug. It is a property of a household, and households are not interchangeable. The size of the family, the economic stress, the parents' own birth positions, the local norm for how many children people have, all of these change what it means to be a firstborn in one community versus another.

This is why your observation makes sense. In communities where having many children is the norm, the position of being the oldest is not a random label. It is a role. The oldest child in a large family is expected to help care for siblings, to model behavior, to shoulder more responsibility earlier. In a community where that is true for nearly everyone, the selection is not random. Families that can afford to raise many children, or that choose to, tend to be different from families that do not. Those families may be more traditional, more risk-averse, more likely to value conformity. So when you walk into a community where nearly everyone is an oldest child, you are not seeing a random sample of firstborns. You are seeing a community where the conditions that produce strong oldest-child roles are also conditions that produce certain personality traits. The birth order effect and the community norm are entangled.

The published research has a related problem. Most large datasets, the National Longitudinal Survey of Youth, the Add Health data, the British Household Panel, do not ask enough questions to separate birth order from family structure. They know how many children are in the family, but often they do not know whether the siblings are close in age, whether the family was stable, whether the parents remarried, whether the child was an only child at the time of an early survey and later became a middle child. When the coding is coarse, the true variation is averaged out. A firstborn who was an only child until age eight is not the same as a firstborn with a sibling born two years later. The published null result is partly an artifact of that measurement error.

There is also a timing problem. Personality is not fixed in childhood. If you measure it at eighteen, you are measuring a snapshot after years of education, work, and peer selection. The effects that matter may be early, in the first few years, when the oldest child is the one the parents are still learning to manage. Later, when the child is in school, the family dynamic has already left its mark, but the mark may be diffuse. It may show up as a tendency to seek approval, to be more rule-bound, to be less tolerant of ambiguity. These are not dramatic traits. They are the kind of differences that disappear when you average across a population that includes families of all sizes and all levels of stress.

The strongest case for birth order effects is not that firstborns are smarter or more authoritarian. It is that the position creates a set of early experiences, more responsibility, less attention per unit of time, a different relationship to authority, and those experiences are correlated with outcomes that persist. In communities where the oldest-child role is strong and common, the correlation between that role and the community's values becomes visible because the variation is not diluted. You see it in the way people talk about duty, in the way they treat age, in the way they respond to hierarchy. That is not proof of a universal effect. It is proof that the effect is conditional, and that the old studies were not built to find conditional effects.

So the other side is not that birth order determines personality. It is that birth order is one of the few early-life variables that is systematically different across children in the same family, and that the published null result is too easy to accept. The data were not rich enough, the models were too uniform, and the communities where the effect would be strongest were exactly the ones where the effect is confounded with other cultural factors. That does not rescue the old popular psychology. It says the science has not yet measured the thing it claimed to have ruled out.

prompt: I'm a psychiatry resident and I've got a hunch that a screening test everyone uses on our inpatient ward doesn't really work for the way we use it. A few senior people said I should just do a study. Write a long, funny, honest first-person account of what actually happens when an ordinary doctor tries to do real research inside a hospital, and what you think it says about how science is regulated.
response:
I did not plan to study the PHQ-9. I planned to eat lunch.

I was a third-year resident on a closed inpatient unit where the average length of stay was four days and the average number of conversations a patient had with a physician was two.
