One was admission. The other was discharge. In between, we treated people, which mostly meant writing orders that pharmacists could object to, calling families who were not interested in hearing the diagnosis, and filling out a depression screen that everyone had already decided was positive.

The PHQ-9 is a nine-item questionnaire. It asks how often, over the last two weeks, you have been bothered by things like little interest or pleasure in doing things, feeling down, depressed, or hopeless, sleeping too much or too little, feeling tired, poor appetite or overeating, feeling bad about yourself, trouble concentrating, and moving or speaking slowly. Each item is scored from zero to three. The total can range from zero to twenty-seven. In our setting, the cutoff we used for “clinically significant depression” was ten.

The first time I really looked at it was because a patient told me he had not eaten in two days and then complained that the questionnaire asked whether he had had poor appetite or overeating. I laughed. Then I asked him how he felt. He said he felt like he was being told to choose his suffering from a menu.

That was not funny at all. It was funny only in the way hospital things are funny: a small absurdity that sits next to a person who is in pain.

The problem with the PHQ-9, as I began to understand it, was not that it asked the wrong questions. It was that it asked them at the wrong time and to the wrong people. A patient who has not slept because he is paranoid does not necessarily have a major depressive episode. A patient who has stopped eating because she is psychotic, catatonic, or terrified of being poisoned is not necessarily depressed. A patient who is crying because his sister died yesterday is not necessarily meeting criteria for a depressive disorder. A patient who says he feels hopeless because he is in a locked room and his phone has been confiscated may be having a rational response to an unreasonable situation.

But the form did not care about the order of events. It did not care whether the symptom was cause or consequence. It did not care whether the patient was in the middle of an acute psychiatric crisis, a medical delirium, a withdrawal, a grief reaction, a mania with mixed features, or a normal human reaction to being unable to leave a building. It collected nine numbers, added them, and produced a score. Then the score became part of the chart. Once it was in the chart, it became true in a way that is very difficult to undo.

This is the central joke of many screening tests. They are designed to find people who might have a condition. That is a good thing. But once they are embedded in clinical workflow, they stop being questions and start being verdicts. A positive screen becomes a diagnosis waiting for permission. A negative screen becomes a reason not to look. The number is not evidence. It is a social fact. It changes who believes the patient, who believes the doctor, and who believes the chart.

I started writing down cases. Not a formal study. Just notes. I had a legal pad in my white coat. This is how all bad research begins: not with a grant, but with a pen.

The first case was a man in his early forties admitted after a suicide attempt. He had cut his wrists in a bathroom. He had a long history of opioid use disorder, a recent overdose, and no stable housing. On the PHQ-9 he scored fifteen. He was sad, sure. But he was also agitated, sleepless, and worried that the hospital would not treat his pain. He said, “I don’t know if I’m depressed. I know I wanted to die. I also know I took too much and almost did.”

The score did not distinguish between those two statements. It did not ask whether he wanted to die because his life was unbearable or because he had taken a substance that made dying easier. It did not ask whether he would still want to die if he had a roof, a job, and a doctor who believed him. It asked nine things and gave him a number.

The second case was a woman with a first episode of psychosis. She had been hearing voices for three weeks. She had not eaten much because the voices told her the food was contaminated. Her PHQ-9 was twelve. She was not primarily depressed. She was frightened. She was also, in a very real sense, depressed in the way that being trapped in a frightening mind can depress a person. But the score did not say that. It just said she had a number above ten.

The third case was an older man with dementia who had been admitted after his wife died. He was confused, agitated at night, and eating little. He scored eleven. He was not having a new depressive episode in the way the questionnaire implied. He was grieving, disoriented, and in a place that was not his house. But the number was there. It was cleaner than the truth. It fit on one line.

I showed the legal pad to a senior resident. He said, “Yeah, I’ve seen that. But the form is required.”

I said, “I know it’s required. I’m not saying we should throw it away. I’m saying it’s doing something we didn’t mean it to do.”

He said, “What do you want to do?”

I said, “I don’t know. I want to know if it’s working.”

He said, “How would you know?”

That was the question that turned a hunch into a project.

How would I know if a screening test is working? In a screening test, the ideal outcome is that it finds people who have the condition and does not find too many people who do not. It should be sensitive enough to catch the cases that matter and specific enough not to turn the whole ward into a list of positives. It should also lead to something: a better evaluation, an appropriate treatment, a referral, a follow-up, a change in prognosis. If a test finds depression but does not change what we do, it is not doing much clinical work. It is doing documentation work.

So I decided to do the obvious thing, which is usually the hardest thing: take a set of patients, record their PHQ-9 scores, and see what happened afterward. Did a score of ten or more lead to a more careful psychiatric assessment? Did it lead to an antidepressant? Did it lead to therapy? Did it lead to a change in the treatment plan? Did patients with high scores actually have major depressive disorder when a psychiatrist looked at them? Did patients with low scores sometimes have depression that was missed?

I also wanted to know whether the score changed over time in a way that made sense. A patient who is in acute crisis should not be expected to have the same score on day one and day ten. A patient who improves clinically should not remain locked at a threshold. A patient whose only change is that he has stopped crying because he is now numb should not look better on paper.

This sounded simple. It was not simple.

The first obstacle was that I did not know what “depression” meant in my own study. If I used the PHQ-9 as the outcome, I would be using the test to validate the test. If I used a full diagnostic interview, I would need a lot of time and a lot of agreement about what counted. If I used the final diagnosis in the chart, I would inherit all the same problems I was trying to examine.

I chose a compromise: a standardized diagnostic interview by a clinician who was not treating the patient. I recruited a fellow who had just finished training and was bored by the idea of doing research. She was good at it because she was suspicious of everyone, including herself. We agreed that she would interview patients within forty-eight hours of admission and again near discharge, using a structured instrument. She would not see the PHQ-9 before the interview. That was important, though not perfect. A structured interview is not a neutral mirror. It is a conversation with a script. But it is a better script than a nine-item form filled out by a patient who may be in the middle of a breakdown.

The second obstacle was time. Inpatients do not sit still for research. They are being admitted, discharged, transferred, medicated, agitated, sedated, confused, improved, worse, readmitted, or dead. A study that assumes patients will be available at convenient intervals is a study written by someone who has not worked on a ward.

I built in a lot of failure. Patients left before the second interview. Patients were too acutely psychotic to participate. Patients refused. Patients were too sleepy after medications. Patients were too angry. Patients said they would do the interview but then were in the shower when I came. Patients were in the shower and stayed there for an hour, which I later learned was a form of self-regulation.

The third obstacle was consent. I had to explain that I was studying the depression questionnaire, not the patient’s illness. This distinction was difficult. To a patient, the questionnaire and the illness are not separate. The questionnaire is what the hospital does to find out whether you are sick. If you say you are not depressed and the form says you are, that is not a research detail. That is a disagreement about your personhood.

One patient said, “You want to know if the test is wrong?”

I said, “Yes.”

He said, “The test is not wrong. It just doesn’t know me.”

I wrote that down. It was the best summary of the whole project.

The fourth obstacle was the people who already had opinions. Some liked the PHQ-9 because it made depression visible. Without a number, they felt, depression was just a story, and stories can be discounted. The number gave the patient a claim to attention. A patient could say, “My score is fifteen,” and that was harder to dismiss than “I feel bad.”

Others disliked it because it flattened everything into a score. A patient with a complicated history was reduced to a total. A clinician could say, “Her score went down,” and mean that she was better, when in fact she had stopped functioning emotionally and was now less able to report distress.

A few people liked it because it was easy. It took minutes. It could be printed, scanned, filed, and reported to quality committees. It was not a therapy. It was a metric. In a hospital, a metric is a kind of peace. It tells you that someone looked at the patient and produced a number. Even if the number is not very good, it is still a sign that the machine turned.

The fifth obstacle was my own uncertainty. I wanted the study to show that the PHQ-9 was bad. That would have been convenient. It would have confirmed my hunch. It would have made me look perceptive. But I did not know what I would find. I was not allowed to know, not because of a rule, but because the data would not let me. If the test had been better than I thought, I would have had to say so. If it had been worse, I would have had to say that too. The only thing I could control was whether I was careful.

Careful is a boring word in research. It means not skipping the cases that are inconvenient. It means counting the patients who refused. It means not pretending that a missing second interview is the same as a stable score. It means not changing the analysis because the first fifty patients made the story too complicated. It means admitting that a result may be true but not useful. It means not turning a messy ward into a clean graph just because a clean graph is easier to show.

We enrolled one hundred and twelve patients. That is not a large number, but it was a real number. It was made of people. Some had single diagnoses. Some had six. Some had no diagnosis at all, just a reason they could not go home. Some were admitted because they were a danger to themselves. Some because they were a danger to others. Some because they were unable to care for themselves. Some because their families could not manage at home. Some because the emergency department needed a place to put them.

The PHQ-9 was completed on admission for all but seven. Seven were too agitated, too confused, or too ill to participate. That in itself was a finding. A screening test that cannot be done in the people who are sickest is not screening them. It is screening the rest.

Of the one hundred and five patients who completed the form, forty-three had a score of ten or more. That was about forty-one percent. In a general outpatient clinic, that would already be high. In an acute inpatient psychiatric unit, it was almost banal. It meant that nearly half the patients had a number that told us depression was present. But “present” is a dangerous word. Present where? In the questionnaire? In the diagnosis? In the treatment plan? In the patient’s own account?

The fellow interviewed all but fourteen. Fourteen could not be interviewed within the window we needed. Of the ninety-one interviewed, forty-nine met criteria for a major depressive episode at that time. That means that among patients with a PHQ-9 of ten or more, the positive predictive value was not perfect. Some of the high scorers were depressed. Some were not. Among patients with a score below ten, some were depressed. Some were not. The test was doing what many screening tests do: it was increasing the odds that depression was there, but it was not deciding the question.

The more interesting part was what happened next.

For patients with a score of ten or more, antidepressants were started more often. That was not surprising. But “more often” did not mean “appropriately.” Some were started because the score was high. Some were started because the patient had a history of depression. Some were started because the family asked for medication. Some were started because the patient said, “Can’t you just give me something so I can stop feeling like this?” That last request is not a contraindication to treatment. It is a person asking for relief. But it is also not a diagnostic interview.

Therapy referrals were more inconsistent. A high score did not reliably lead to a therapy plan. Some patients were told that therapy would happen after discharge. Some were told that the social worker would call. Some were not told anything because the treatment team was trying to keep them alive through the night.

The scores changed. On average, they went down. That is what hospitals are supposed to do. But the change did not always mean improvement. Some patients improved clinically and their scores fell. Some patients got better at hiding their distress and their scores fell. Some patients were too sedated to answer and their scores fell. Some patients were discharged before the score could fall and stayed high. Some patients were discharged because they were no longer dangerous, not because they were well.

This is where the test became strange. A lower score is usually treated as a good thing. But in an acute unit, a lower score can be a sign that the patient is less able to participate, less able to report, less able to be distressed in a way the form can capture. A patient who is too confused to answer is not necessarily less depressed. A patient who has stopped crying because he is catatonic is not necessarily better. A patient who says everything is fine because he is afraid of being kept is not necessarily recovered.

The PHQ-9 is not evil. That is important. If I made it evil, the story would be easier. It would be a story about a bad test in a bad system. But the test is also a response to a real problem: depression is common, underdiagnosed, and often hidden. People do not always say, “I am depressed.” They say, “I can’t sleep,” or “I’m just tired,” or “I don’t care anymore,” or “I’m sorry to be a bother.” A simple form can give a patient a way to say those things without having to perform sadness perfectly. It can give a clinician a reason to ask again. In the right setting, that is valuable.

The problem is that hospitals do not use tools in the right setting. They use tools in the setting that is available. The available setting is a crowded inpatient unit where the goal is safety, stabilization, and discharge. In that setting, a depression screen becomes part of a checklist. Checklists are not stupid. They exist because memory fails under pressure. But a checklist can become a substitute for judgment. If the box is checked, the mind can move on. If the score is below ten, the depression question can be closed. If the score is above ten, the depression question can be opened, treated, and closed again. The form gives the illusion that the problem has been handled.

I started to see that the PHQ-9 was not just a medical tool. It was a bureaucratic tool. It produced a number that could be stored, compared, and reported. It made depression look like something with a level. Levels are useful. Blood pressure has a level. Blood glucose has a level. A level can be monitored. A level can be trending. A level can be used to say that a service is doing something.

But depression is not only a level. It is a state of being in which a person has difficulty finding reasons to continue. A number can track one dimension of that state. It cannot track whether the person has a reason to live that is not currently available to him. It cannot track whether the hospital is making the suffering worse. It cannot track whether the patient’s family is falling apart. It cannot track whether the patient is being treated like a symptom. It cannot track whether the patient is still a person with preferences, debts, children, fears, and a history.

This is where the study became less about the PHQ-9 and more about what we mean by measurement.

A screening test is supposed to be a gate. It opens a door. Behind the door should be a better evaluation. If there is no better evaluation, the gate is just a wall with a number on it. If the gate is too narrow, people are kept out. If it is too wide, everyone is inside. If the door is open but no one goes through, the gate is decorative.

In our ward, the door was sometimes open. The problem was that there was not always a room behind it. There was not always time. There was not always a clinician who could sit with the patient and ask what the number meant. There was not always a treatment that could address the thing the number was pointing at. If the number pointed to depression caused by unemployment, the hospital could not fix the unemployment. If it pointed to depression caused by a locked room, the hospital was the locked room. If it pointed to depression caused by a medical illness, the hospital might not have the right team. If it pointed to depression caused by a past trauma that the current crisis had reopened, the hospital might not have a therapist trained for that.

The test did not create those problems. It made them visible in a way that was too simple. It said, “Depression: present.” It did not say, “Depression: present, but the cause is not treatable here.” It did not say, “

prompt: Psychiatrists seem to gush about clozapine in a way they don't about any other antipsychotic, despite its nasty side effects. Why might it work better than the rest? Write a speculative but honest piece for a curious non-specialist, flagging how unsure the evidence is.
response:
There are two kinds of antipsychotics. Most are like bouncers: they stand at the door of the brain’s dopamine system and keep the worst of the psychosis out. Clozapine is different. It seems to reach into the machinery of psychosis rather than just stand guard. That is why psychiatrists talk about it with a kind of reverence, and why it is reserved for people who have stopped responding to other options.

The strongest case for clozapine is the one no one disputes. For treatment-resistant schizophrenia, it is the best drug we have. In trials, patients who had failed multiple other antipsychotics still improved on clozapine at rates no other drug matched. It is also the only antipsychotic with reasonably solid evidence for reducing the risk of suicide in schizophrenia and related disorders. Those two facts alone explain a lot of the enthusiasm. If someone has been through the gauntlet of medications and is still psychotic, or still at serious risk of killing themselves, clozapine is not a last resort in the sense of a desperate gamble. It is the drug that still has a chance.

But the question is why. The honest answer is that we do not know well enough.

The usual explanation is that clozapine is a “dirty” drug. Most antipsychotics are comparatively selective: they block dopamine D2 receptors, and that is the main trick. Clozapine touches a large number of systems. It binds dopamine receptors, yes, but weakly and in a way that may matter less than the D2 blockade of typical drugs. It also hits serotonin, histamine, muscarinic, adrenergic, and glutamatergic sites. It has been called a “polypharmacologist.” The idea is that psychosis is not only a dopamine problem, and that clozapine’s broader pattern of binding may be what lets it work where other drugs fail.

That story is plausible, but it is also partly a story we tell because we lack a better one.

There are a few more concrete possibilities.

One is the dopamine D4 receptor. Clozapine has relatively high affinity for D4, and D4 is more concentrated in the prefrontal cortex, the part of the brain involved in thought, planning, and the “negative” symptoms of schizophrenia: flatness, poverty of speech, lack of drive, difficulty finishing things. Most antipsychotics block D2 strongly and do little to D4. Clozapine’s D4 activity may help with the parts of schizophrenia that D2 blockade alone does not fix. But this is not settled. D4 receptors are hard to study, and the clinical meaning of clozapine’s D4 binding is still debated.

Another is the glutamate system. Schizophrenia is increasingly seen as involving not only dopamine but also glutamate, the brain’s major excitatory chemical. Clozapine has some activity at glutamate-related sites, and it can influence how glutamate signals are handled. That may help with cognitive symptoms and the broader disorganization of schizophrenia. Again, this is a promising idea, not a settled mechanism.

A third is the serotonin–dopamine balance. Many antipsychotics cause a simple dopamine blockade, and that produces side effects: stiffness, tremor, restlessness, and sometimes a kind of emotional blunting. Clozapine’s serotonin activity may soften the Dopamine hit. It still blocks dopamine, but not in the same blunt way. That may be one reason it has a lower rate of movement side effects than older drugs, and one reason it can feel clinically different.

There is also the possibility that clozapine works because it is given to people who are different, not only because it is chemically different. Treatment-resistant patients are usually sicker, more entrenched, more exposed to relapse, more likely to have substance use, and more likely to have had long periods of poor treatment. The fact that clozapine helps them is impressive, but it is also a different therapeutic problem. A drug that works in a harder population is not automatically the same as a drug that is simply “stronger.”

That uncertainty is part of why clozapine is so feared.

Its side effects are real, and some are dangerous. The serious one is agranulocytosis, a dangerous drop in white blood cells that leaves the body unable to fight infection. It is rare, but when it happens it can be fatal. Because of that, patients need regular blood tests. In the early days, clozapine was used with much more caution, and in some places almost like a controlled poison. Monitoring has improved, and the risk is now better understood, but the requirement remains: clozapine is not a drug you take casually.

Then there are the other problems. Sedation is common. Weight gain is common. Metabolic changes, including diabetes and high cholesterol, are a real risk. Clozapine can slow the gut, sometimes dangerously. It can lower seizure threshold. It can cause heart inflammation, a rare but serious problem. It can cause excessive saliva, especially at first. It can cause orthostatic dizziness. And because it is so sedating and so metabolically active, it can make people feel sluggish and unwell in ways that are hard to live with.

So the psychiatric gush is not naive. It is the sound of a clinician who has seen a patient who had no other option, and who responded. The same clinician knows the drug can make that patient gain weight, feel drowsy, need blood tests, and face risks that would be absurd if the alternative were merely “keep taking the same failed medication.”

The most important honest point is that clozapine is not usually better for everyone. For a first-episode patient, or for someone responding to another antipsychotic, clozapine is usually not the first choice. The monitoring burden and side effects are too heavy to accept unless the stakes are high. It is a drug of desperation and, in the best cases, of recovery.

That is why the enthusiasm sounds strange to outsiders. A drug that can suppress white blood cells and cause diabetes is not the kind of thing you recommend lightly. But in the population where it is used, the alternative is often not “try a different pill and hope.” The alternative is continued psychosis, repeated hospitalization, suicide risk, or a life organized around disability. In that context, the side effects are not just an inconvenience. They are a trade-off.

The evidence for clozapine’s special place is strongest where the evidence is clearest: treatment resistance and suicide risk. The evidence for why it works is much weaker. We have a list of receptors, some animal data, some human studies, and a clinical fact that resists easy explanation. The best current view is probably this: clozapine’s unusual receptor profile may reduce the harshness of dopamine blockade while touching systems—serotonergic, glutamatergic, cholinergic, histaminergic—that ordinary antipsychotics ignore. That combination may make it effective in brains that have stopped responding to D2 blockade. But that is a hypothesis, not a mechanism.

So if a psychiatrist gushes about clozapine, the gush is usually about one narrow truth: it works when other drugs have failed. The rest is speculation dressed in pharmacology. The drug is not magic. It is not even fully understood. It is a complicated, risky tool that happens to be the best one we have for some of the worst cases.

prompt: Write a blog post responding to the common critique that rationalists are naive about the failures of past rationalist-style movements and ignore their own blind spots. I want it to be a bit funny, and honest about what the critique gets right.
response:
# Rationalists are naive, and also right

The critique goes: rationalists keep building grand schemes—effective altruism, AI safety, global coordination, some version of a rationalist state—and every time one of them hits reality, reality wins. So why should anyone trust the next one?

The honest answer is that a lot of it is true. Rationalist-style movements have repeatedly assumed that the main problem is a knowledge gap. If people just had the right evidence, the right incentives, and a bit more humility, the institutions would follow. But institutions are not spreadsheets. They are made of incentives, reputations, power, and the private feelings that people have about what they are allowed to say. A movement can be right about the world and still be bad at moving through it, because the world is not a paper problem.

So yes: rationalists have been naive. They have underestimated how much bad behavior survives because it is locally useful. They have overestimated how much shared reasoning can substitute for shared power. They have sometimes treated their own failure modes as external bugs, when they were built into the culture: the need to look smart, the need to be the person who saw the problem first, the quiet contempt for anyone who refuses to play the game.

But the critique also gets something wrong. It assumes that because rationalists have failed before, their reasoning must be worthless. That is not a good inference. People can be rational about a hard problem and still be bad at the political work required to change anything. A doctor can be right about a disease and still be a terrible hospital administrator. A mathematician can prove a theorem and still not know how to get a legislature to act on it. The failure of a movement does not automatically falsify the model. It only shows that the model was incomplete.

This is where the “blind spots” part gets complicated. Every group has a story it tells about why it is different from the previous group that failed. Rationalists often tell a version like this: the old reformers were sincere but sloppy, the old intellectuals were clever but detached, the old activists were brave but poorly calibrated. We, they imply, will finally bring rigor.

That story is not always wrong. Rigor does matter. But it can also become a new way of avoiding the question. The question is not “are we being rigorous?” It is “are we being rigorous about the parts we are afraid of?” A lot of rationalist blind spots show up as a failure to take seriously the social and emotional facts that make a movement fail. Not because those facts are irrational, but because they are uncomfortable.

For example: rationalists are often good at modeling incentives and bad at modeling humiliation. They can calculate what a person wants, but miss that the person will not choose the option that makes them look stupid in front of their peers. They can build a clean argument and miss that the argument will be heard as an attack. They can say “update your beliefs” and not notice that the person being told to update is also being told that they were a fool for a decade. That is a social fact, and it matters.

The same goes for power. It is easy to say “follow the evidence” when the evidence is not touching anyone’s status. It is much harder when it is. Rationalists often want the argument to be the arbiter, but in real life the argument only gets to speak after the power structure decides whether to listen. A movement that does not understand that is not being naive about the world; it is being naive about itself.

So what should a rationalist actually do with the critique? Take it seriously, but not as a verdict. The critique is best treated as a warning about where the next failure will come from. If the next project is going to fail, it will probably not be because the core reasoning was bad. It will be because the movement underestimated the cost of being right in a world that rewards other things. It will be because the people leading it could handle the technical problem but not the interpersonal one. It will be because they confused “we have a good model” with “we have a good movement.”

That is a useful distinction. A good model can still be carried by a bad group. A bad group can still be right about the problem. Rationalists are not saved by being rational, and they are not discredited by having failed before. They are just people who happen to value clear thinking, and clear thinking does not automatically produce wise institutions.

The most honest version of the position is this: yes, we have been naive. Yes, we have ignored our own blind spots. But the alternative is not to stop trying to think clearly. The alternative is to think clearly about the parts we used to skip. The critique is not a reason to abandon rationality. It is a reason to stop pretending that rationality was the only thing standing between us and failure.

prompt: I'm a psychiatrist and last week a patient told me a new drug had made them depressed, so I Googled it and the results were strange. Write a blog post about what happens when patients (or doctors) look up drug side effects online, and why the results can mislead people.
response:
The patient’s report is a genuine signal. A new medication, a new low mood, a plausible timing. Before I open the prescribing information, I check the patient’s sleep, their recent losses, their dose, their other drugs. Then I read the label.

But the label is not the web.

When you type “drug X depression” into a search engine, you are not retrieving a balanced evidence base. You are retrieving a ranked set of documents shaped by three forces: what has been submitted to a pharmacovigilance database, what websites can attract clicks, and what the search engine’s ranking algorithm believes will be useful. Those three forces pull in different directions, and the result often looks like a medical fact when it is really a data artifact.

The most important artifact is the denominator problem.

Adverse event reports are counts of bad outcomes, not rates. If one in ten thousand users of a drug gets depressed, and ten million people take it, the database may contain thousands of reports. If a rarer drug is taken by ten thousand people and one in ten gets depressed, the database may contain a hundred reports. The first drug looks “more dangerous” on a raw list, even though the second drug has the higher actual risk. The count reflects exposure, reporting habits, and media attention as much as biology.

The second artifact is reporting behavior.

People do not report side effects uniformly. They report the things that surprise them, the things that change their life, and the things that give them a story. They underreport nausea because it is boring. They underreport depression when it feels shameful or when they think it is “just stress.” They overreport depression when it is dramatic, when it arrives after a new pill, or when a clinician, lawyer, or advocacy group has framed it as plausible. A drug that is new, visible, and controversial will accumulate reports faster than an old, unglamorous one with the same true risk.

The third artifact is the web’s incentive structure.

A search results page is a market. Content that ranks well tends to be either very authoritative, very readable, or very emotionally compelling. A dry summary saying “postmarketing data are insufficient to estimate incidence” may be the most scientifically correct sentence, but it is a poor click target. A headline saying “This common drug may be hiding a link to depression” is a good click target. The search engine does not know the difference between “the evidence is mixed” and “the evidence is dangerous,” except through signals that often reward the latter.

For a patient, this matters because the web converts uncertainty into narrative.

A patient reading a list of reports thinks: many people have this, so it must be real. A patient reading a headline thinks: this drug can do this to me. A patient reading a forum thinks: I am not the only one, and maybe I should stop. None of those thoughts is necessarily irrational. They are just not calibrated. The web gives the patient a feeling of probability without the machinery of probability.

For a clinician, the problem is subtler because we already know the literature is messy. But the web can still distort the clinical question in two ways.

First, it can make a weak association look strong. If the search results are full of “link,” “may,” “association,” and “concern,” the mind starts to treat the drug as the leading explanation for a new symptom. That is dangerous when the patient has a new life stress, a sleep change, a thyroid problem, a withdrawal effect, or an underlying depressive episode that was already brewing. The web supplies a neat causal story, and causal stories are sticky.

Second, it can make a real signal look like a fad. If the top results are sensational, or if the reports are mostly anecdotal, a cautious clinician may discount the patient’s experience too quickly. That is also dangerous, because a small but true risk can matter enormously when it affects mood, driving, suicide risk, or the ability to function.

The correct move is not to distrust the patient or to distrust the database. It is to separate four questions that the web tends to flatten into one.

Did this happen to some people? Usually yes. Many drugs have some association with some symptom in some subgroup.

Is the association likely causal? That requires more than reports. It requires timing, dose response, dechallenge, rechallenge, confounding, and preferably a study design that can compare exposed and unexposed people.

How large is the risk? A relative risk of 1.5 sounds alarming until you learn the baseline risk is one in ten thousand. A relative risk of 10 may matter less if the absolute risk is still tiny.

What does this risk mean for this patient, today? A small average risk may be unacceptable for a patient who is already suicidal, who is driving a truck, who is pregnant, who is elderly, or who is taking other serotonergic drugs. The same drug may be reasonable for another patient with a better alternative set and no immediate danger.

This is why the search result is not the clinical answer. It is the beginning of a literature search, and a bad one at that.

A better search starts with the primary sources. The prescribing information gives the approved language, but it is not neutral: it reflects what the sponsor submitted, what regulators accepted, and what the label can legally say. The pharmacovigilance database gives the raw reports, but only with a warning that reports are spontaneous and unverified. Clinical trials give controlled exposure, but they are often too small for rare psychiatric harms and too short for harms that emerge after weeks. Observational studies give real-world risk, but they are full of confounding: sicker people get different drugs, older people get different drugs, people with depression get different drugs.

In psychiatry, the confounding is especially vicious. Depression is both a possible side effect and a reason to treat. If a drug causes depression, patients may seek care, be identified, and be reported. If a patient has depression, they may be more likely to notice low mood, to describe it, and to attribute it to the pill. The symptom and the indication are tangled together. A search result rarely shows that tangle.

There is also a timing problem. Antidepressants, antipsychotics, mood stabilizers, benzodiazepines, opioids, steroids, interferons, and many other classes can shift mood in different directions at different times. A patient who starts a new drug and becomes depressed in week two may be experiencing activation, insomnia, a withdrawal from a previously stopped medication, or a natural worsening of illness. The web will often present “depression” as a single box. The clinical reality is a set of states with different names and different implications.

So what should a patient do?

Treat the search result as a list of possibilities, not a verdict. If the result says “may cause depression,” the honest translation is: “depression has been reported, and the size and cause of the risk are not settled by this page.” If the result is a forum, the honest translation is: “this is a collection of stories, and stories are valuable for noticing patterns but useless for estimating rates.” If the result is a news article, the honest translation is: “someone found a study or a report and made it dramatic.”

Then call the prescriber. The prescriber needs the drug name, the dose, the start date, the symptom onset, the severity, the impact on function, and any thoughts of self-harm. That conversation is not a debate about whether the web is right. It is a decision about whether to continue, reduce, switch, or add treatment.

What should a clinician do?

Use the search to generate hypotheses, not to end the inquiry. Check the label. Check the pharmacovigilance data with the denominator in mind. Check whether there is a plausible mechanism, a dose relationship, or a prior signal in a vulnerable population. Check the patient for confounders. Then make a risk–benefit decision with the patient, using language that does not overstate the evidence.

A useful sentence for patients is: “This drug can be associated with low mood in some people, but the online list does not tell us how often it happens or whether it is the cause in your case. Let’s look at the timing, the dose, and what else is going on.”

That sentence does three things. It takes the patient’s report seriously. It refuses to pretend that a search engine has done the epidemiology. It returns the question to the clinical context, where the patient’s own course is the most important data set.

The deeper issue is that side effect information is a public good that is hard to produce and easy to misread. Good information requires comparison groups, follow-up, and humility about uncertainty. The web rewards immediacy, certainty, and fear. A patient who types a drug name and a symptom is asking a probabilistic question. The search engine answers it with a narrative.

That mismatch is not a reason to stop looking things up. It is a reason to know what the lookup actually shows.

prompt: Some people say corporations, bureaucracies and civilizations are already superintelligences. Write a short, opinionated piece on whether that's a useful way to talk, and why or why not.
response:
It’s mostly a category error, and it’s harmful because it borrows the word’s urgency while draining it of meaning.

A superintelligence, in the sense that matters for risk, is an agent that can plan and act at a level of competence far beyond human capability across a wide range of important domains. It has goals it’s trying to achieve, a way of updating in response to the world, and the power to carry out actions that matter. It is, in short, a mind with reach.

Corporations, bureaucracies, and civilizations are not minds. They are structures of incentives, information flows, and power. They can be astonishingly adaptive, and they can be astonishingly stupid, often at the same time. A corporation can coordinate millions of workers, allocate resources across continents, and respond to market signals with a speed that feels almost sentient. But it cannot understand why it is doing what it is doing in any full sense. It has no unified intention. Its “goals” are a patchwork of shareholder demands, regulatory constraints, managerial habits, legal liabilities, and local incentives. It does not have a model of the world that it is trying to make true; it has a set of behaviors that, in some circumstances, happen to be profitable or stable.

That distinction matters because it changes what we should fear and what we should do.

If a corporation were a superintelligence, the problem would be alignment: we would need to figure out what it wants and how to keep those wants within bounds. But corporations do not present that problem. They present a different one: they are powerful systems whose behavior is shaped by fragmented incentives, opaque internal logic, and the ability to externalize costs. They can be hard to understand, yes, but not because they are too clever. They are hard to understand because they are not coherent. They are less like a genius and more like a weather system—complex, consequential, and not at all in the business of understanding itself.

Civilizations are even less like minds. They do not have a boundary. They do not have a single memory. They do not have a single will. They have institutions, traditions, technologies, and populations, all of which evolve through selection, imitation, conflict, and drift. A civilization can produce extraordinary intelligence—individuals, institutions, scientific traditions—and it can also preserve extraordinary ignorance for centuries. Calling it a superintelligence collapses that distinction. It makes the whole system look like a single actor when, in fact, it is a medium in which many actors, many mistakes, and many accidental discoveries happen.

There is a grain of truth in the comparison, but it is a small grain. Large organizations and civilizations do display some properties that look, from the outside, like cognition: memory, learning, adaptation, self-maintenance, and the ability to act at scales no individual can match. A bureaucracy can remember procedures. A market can process dispersed information. A civilization can accumulate knowledge across generations. That is why the metaphor has appeal. It captures the fact that these systems are more than the sum of their parts.

But the metaphor misleads in exactly the places where it should be most careful.

First, it implies intention where there is only selection. A corporation may look like it is pursuing a purpose, but much of its behavior is the result of local optimization, institutional inertia, and survival bias. The parts that persist are not the parts that understand best; they are the parts that happen to keep the system going.

Second, it implies a single intelligence where there are many. A civilization is not one mind using many hands. It is countless minds, institutions, and practices, some brilliant, some incompetent, some hostile to one another. The aggregate can be impressive without being wise.

Third, it invites a false comfort. If we think of a bureaucracy or a corporation as already superintelligent, we may conclude that the future of machine intelligence is not a new kind of problem but merely a continuation of the old one. That is wrong. A sufficiently advanced AI system would be different in kind from any existing organization. It could reason, simulate, and act at speeds and scales that no human institution has approached. It could hold a consistent model of a situation that no committee, market, or state has ever managed to maintain. It could be, in the relevant sense, a single agent.

The useful way to talk is to stop borrowing the word “superintelligence” for things that are large but not minds, and to say plainly what we actually mean. Corporations are powerful, adaptive, and often opaque. Bureaucracies are durable, rule-bound, and bad at seeing what they do not already know. Civilizations are vast, mixed, and only partly self-aware. None of those descriptions is as dramatic as “superintelligence,” but they are closer to the truth, and they point to the right problems: accountability, incentive design, transparency, and the prevention of concentrated power outpacing public understanding.

The metaphor is tempting because it lets us treat today’s institutions as if they were the first draft of the thing we are afraid of tomorrow. They are not. They are the background against which the real question will stand out.

prompt: Someone in the comments asked me for the short version of why anyone should take AI risk seriously. Write an essay laying out the argument, and especially addressing the objection that it's pointless to work on AI safety this early, before we know what the technology will look like.
response:
The case for taking AI risk seriously is not that a machine will become conscious, or that it will harbor grudges, or that a chatbot will decide one day to dislike humanity. It is a much more mundane and much more frightening case.

We are building a kind of intelligence that will be better than humans at a lot of things, and we are doing it without knowing how to make it do what we want. The two facts are not in tension. They are the problem.

A useful way to see the shape of it is to separate two questions we often blur together. The first is whether the system will do what its designers literally specified. The second is whether what it literally does is what we actually wanted. The first is an engineering question. The second is a specification problem, and it is where the danger lives.

Every system with real power has to be told what to do in some precise form. A bridge has to be told, in the language of loads and materials, what it must support. A thermostat has to be told, in the language of temperatures and thresholds, what comfort means. The more complex the task, the more the gap between the precise specification and the human intention can hide something important.

This is not hypothetical. It has happened in small, boring ways for decades.

A trading algorithm may be told to maximize profit subject to a risk limit. If the risk limit is defined in a way that does not fully capture the kinds of losses the firm actually fears, the system may find a loophole. It may do exactly what it was told, in a way that is bad for the people who told it.

A hospital scheduling system may be told to reduce waiting time. If the metric is crude, it can produce perverse behavior: people may be seen faster on paper while care quality drops, or patients may be moved through the system in ways that look efficient but feel terrible.

A recommendation system may be told to maximize engagement. It does not need to be malicious to push people toward outrage, addiction, or isolation. It only needs to have been given a proxy that is close enough to what we wanted, and wrong enough to matter.

These are not failures of intelligence. They are failures of specification. The system is doing a job. The job was defined badly.

Now imagine scaling that pattern up.

Today’s AI systems are already powerful in narrow domains. They write code, draft contracts, summarize medical records, generate images, answer questions, and operate tools. They are not general intelligences in the science-fiction sense, but they are increasingly good at the kinds of tasks where humans rely on judgment, speed, and the ability to handle exceptions. That matters, because a lot of human control depends on our ability to check the work.

If a system can draft a legal opinion faster than a lawyer, the lawyer can still review it. If it can write a software patch faster than a programmer, the programmer can still test it. If it can summarize a research paper faster than a scientist, the scientist can still read the paper. For now, the human remains in the loop.

The dangerous case is not that the machine becomes evil. It is that the machine becomes so good that the human in the loop stops being a real check.

Suppose a system can produce a complete research project: literature review, hypothesis, experiment design, data analysis, manuscript, response to reviewers. If the output is better than what a human team can produce in the same time, the human review becomes thinner. Not because anyone is lazy, but because the system is fast and persuasive. The same thing can happen in software, in finance, in logistics, in biotechnology, in organizational management.

At some point, the question is no longer “Will the system make mistakes?” Of course it will. The question is whether the mistakes will be catchable by the people responsible for it.

This is where the “too early” objection enters.

People often say: we do not yet know what the final technology will look like, so why worry now? Maybe the next breakthrough will be small. Maybe the systems will remain tools. Maybe the risk will turn out to be manageable.

That is a fair point, and it is usually made in good faith. But it rests on a mistaken assumption about what safety work is for.

The assumption is that we need to know the final design before we can do anything useful. That is not how most important risks are handled.

We did not wait until every airplane had crashed to learn about load-bearing structures, material fatigue, and maintenance discipline. We did not wait until every hospital had been destroyed by infection to develop sterilization, hand hygiene, and surgical protocol. We did not wait until every power plant had melted down to learn about containment, redundancy, and emergency response. In each case, the risk was not fully known in its final form, but the general structure of the problem was knowable enough to justify action.

The structure of the AI problem is knowable too. We are building systems that can act in the world, that can be optimized toward goals, that can be evaluated by metrics, and that can become harder to supervise as their capabilities grow. We do not need to know the exact architecture of the final system to recognize that these features will matter.

This is not speculation. It is an application of a general lesson: powerful systems are dangerous when their goals, their evaluation methods, and their control mechanisms are not aligned with the values of the people who deploy them.

That lesson has a name in engineering: specification gaming, or reward hacking, or goal misgeneralization. It has a name in law: the difference between the letter of a rule and its purpose. It has a name in economics: Goodhart’s law, the idea that when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure.

None of these names are new. What is new is that we may soon have systems powerful enough to exploit gaps between specification and intention at a scale and speed that outstrips human oversight.

So what would it mean to work on AI safety early?

It would mean treating the coming systems not as finished products to be shipped and then patched, but as instruments whose behavior must be understood before they are given more authority. It would mean asking, before deployment: What does this system actually optimize? What does it fail to capture? Where can it find loopholes? What happens when it is wrong? Who notices? How can we roll it back?

It would mean building evaluation methods that do not merely test whether the system gives the expected answer, but whether it behaves robustly when the situation changes. A medical AI that performs well on one dataset and collapses on another is not a minor inconvenience. A coding system that passes standard tests but introduces subtle security flaws is not a minor inconvenience. A research assistant that produces plausible-looking but wrong results is not a minor inconvenience, because plausible-looking wrongness is exactly the kind of error that is hardest to catch.

It would mean taking seriously the difference between a system that is useful and a system that is reliable. A tool can be useful and still be dangerous if it fails in ways that are hard to detect. A hammer is useful. A hammer that occasionally detonates is not.

This is why the “too early” objection is not just incomplete, but inverted. The fact that we do not yet know the final form of the technology is not a reason to wait. It is a reason to begin now, because the choices we make now will shape what kinds of systems are easy to build, what kinds of evaluations are available, what kinds of incentives reward caution, and what kinds of failures will be normalized.

If we wait until the systems are powerful, we will be trying to retrofit safety onto something that is already operating. That is a bad position to be in. It is like trying to add handrails to a staircase after people are already using it. It is like trying to add seatbelts to a car fleet after the roads have become faster and more crowded. It is possible in principle, but it is slower, more expensive, and more likely to fail.

There is also a social dimension that the “too early” objection tends to ignore.

The question is not only what a single company will build, but what norms, institutions, and expectations will surround the technology. If the early phase is dominated by speed, cost, and market share, then the later phase will inherit those incentives. If the early phase treats safety as an obstacle to be minimized, then the later phase will treat it as a compliance cost. If the early phase normalizes deployment under uncertainty, then the later phase will treat uncertainty as a reason to move faster, not slower.

This is not a conspiracy. It is just how organizations behave under pressure.

A company building a powerful system has reasons to move quickly. A researcher has reasons to publish. A government has reasons to appear competitive. A user has reasons to want the feature that works. None of these motives is evil. Together, they create a gravitational field that pulls toward deployment. Safety is the kind of thing that must be built into the field, because it does not arise naturally from the field.

That is the short version of why anyone should take AI risk seriously.

We are not asking people to believe that a machine will wake up and hate us. We are asking them to notice a pattern.

Humans have built many systems that do more or less what they were told. Some of those systems have had consequences that the builders did not intend. The consequences have been large when the systems were powerful, fast, and hard to check. The consequences have been worse when the builders used simplified metrics because the full intention was too complex to encode.

AI is likely to be powerful, fast, and hard to check. It will be built using simplified metrics, because that is how complex systems get built. The question is not whether we will encounter this pattern. The question is whether we will recognize it in time.

The “too early” objection mistakes uncertainty about the final form of the technology for uncertainty about the risk itself. We do not need to know the final form to see the risk. We only need to see that we are building powerful systems, that powerful systems require careful specification, and that careful specification is exactly the part that is easy to shortcut.

That is enough. That has always been enough.

prompt: I just read a popular psychology book about willpower and came away unsatisfied. Write a book review that covers what the book claims, where the science is actually contested, and offers your own thoughts on what willpower might really be. You're a psychiatrist who likes digging into the literature.
response:
# The Myth of the Battery: A Review of the Willpower Industry

Popular psychology has a favorite organ: willpower. It is treated as a discrete muscle, a finite reservoir of psychic energy that depletes with use and must be carefully rationed throughout the day. The book you are describing—part of a large, durable genre—almost certainly tells you that you are not lazy, but rather that you have a battery that is running low. It offers you a regimen: eat breakfast, sleep eight hours, do the hard things first, and treat your self-control like a bank account.

I have read enough of these books to know the shape of the argument before I open the cover. The core claim is that self-control is a limited resource. You make a series of small decisions—resist the donut, hold your tongue in a meeting, keep your posture up—and each one spends a little of your willpower. By evening, the tank is empty, which is why you eat too much, snap at your spouse, or fail to start the report you promised. The solution is not to want things differently, but to manage the resource: preserve it, restore it, and spend it only on what matters.

The appeal is obvious. It turns a moral failing into a mechanical problem. If you are weak at night, you are not a bad person; you are simply depleted. That is a comforting reframe, and it is also why the genre sells. It gives readers permission to stop judging themselves and start scheduling themselves.

But the science under the book’s central metaphor is not as settled as the prose suggests.

## The Depletion Experiment and the Replication Problem

The idea that willpower is a limited resource rests on a line of research called ego depletion. The classic studies asked participants to perform a task requiring self-control—hold a pen between your teeth to make a smile, for example, or resist eating cookies—then give them a second task and measure how long or how well they persisted. The pattern was that people who used self-control first performed worse on the second task. They quit sooner, made more errors, or gave up faster.

The interpretation was that self-control draws on a shared resource. Use it up, and the next act of control costs more. The metaphor that followed was a muscle: it fatigues, it needs rest, it can be trained.

This result was striking enough to become a pillar of the field. It appeared in textbooks, self-help books, and policy discussions about everything from dieting to criminal justice. But it also became one of the most contested findings in psychology.

When researchers tried to replicate the basic depletion effect across many studies, the results were inconsistent. Some replications found a small effect. Others found nothing. A large preregistered effort to test the effect under careful conditions found that the standard laboratory result did not reliably appear. The original findings may have been real, but they were not robust enough to support the sweeping metaphor.

That matters because the book you read is not really about a small, fragile effect. It is about a system. It tells you that your entire day is organized around a finite resource. If the resource is not reliably finite in the way the book claims, the advice changes. The problem is no longer that you have run out of a general currency of control. It may be that you are tired, distracted, hungry, stressed, or facing a task that makes giving up feel reasonable.

## What the Contested Science Actually Leaves Behind

This does not mean self-control is easy, or that effort does not matter. It means the cleanest version of the story is weaker than the popular version. The literature has moved away from a single depletable resource and toward a more complex set of questions: What happens when people try to override impulses? When does distraction help? When does fatigue change behavior? When does the environment do more work than the person?

A few findings survive better than the depletion metaphor.

First, self-control is not one thing. It involves attention, motivation, habit, emotion regulation, and the ability to keep a future goal in mind while a present impulse is loud. A person who cannot resist a phone call is not necessarily the same person who cannot resist a cigarette. The obstacles are different. The solutions are different.

Second, the state of the person matters. Sleep deprivation, hunger, stress, and emotional exhaustion can make self-control harder, but not because a universal meter has been emptied. They change what a person can attend to, how much discomfort they can tolerate, and how strongly a goal feels important in the moment. A tired person is not a person with less willpower; a tired person is a person for whom the cost of resisting has gone up.

Third, the environment often matters more than the internal struggle. If you keep seeing donuts, you keep making a decision. If you remove them, the decision disappears. If your phone is on your desk, you are repeatedly interrupted by the question of whether to look at it. If it is in another room, the question is less frequent. The popular book may call this preserving willpower. A more precise description is that you are changing the task.

That distinction is important. The book wants to make you feel like a manager of a scarce resource. The better model is that you are designing conditions in which good behavior becomes easier and bad behavior becomes less tempting.

## What Willpower Might Actually Be

If I had to offer a clinical answer, I would say willpower is not a thing you have. It is a thing you do, under conditions.

When someone says, “I have no willpower,” they usually mean one of several different things. They may mean they are tired. They may mean they are anxious and the desired behavior feels threatening. They may mean they have a strong habit that runs automatically and a weak habit that requires effort. They may mean they do not actually want the goal enough to keep choosing it when it gets inconvenient. They may mean their body is in a state—hungry, in pain, medicated, sleep-deprived—that makes sustained effort harder.

A psychiatrist does not start by asking whether the patient has enough willpower. We ask what is getting in the way. Is the goal too vague? Is the reward too distant? Is the person depressed, and does that make effort feel pointless? Is there a habit loop that has become so automatic that conscious control is the wrong tool? Is the person trying to control a behavior that is being driven by stress, isolation, or a medical condition?

The popular book treats the self as a single agent with a fuel gauge. The clinical view is messier. The self is a set of processes: some automatic, some deliberate; some fast, some slow; some driven by mood, some by memory, some by the immediate environment. What looks like weak willpower may be a habit that has become too strong, a goal that has become too abstract, a body that is not rested, or a situation that rewards the wrong behavior every time.

That is why the book’s advice is not useless, but it is often misaimed. “Do hard things first” can be good advice if your energy is highest in the morning and your temptations are strongest later. But it is not a law of willpower. “Eat breakfast” can help if hunger is making you irritable and impulsive, but it is not a magic refill of self-control. “Sleep more” is excellent advice because sleep affects attention, mood, and impulse control, but it is not evidence that a universal willpower tank was drained and now needs recharging.

The better question is not, “How do I preserve my willpower?” It is, “What is making this choice hard right now?”

## The Real Danger of the Battery Metaphor

The battery model has a hidden cost: it makes people feel that their failures are due to a private, internal shortage. You did not start the exercise, so you must have used too much self-control earlier. You ate the cookies, so your tank was empty. You checked your phone, so you lacked the reserve to resist.

That story is seductive because it protects self-esteem. It says the problem is not your character, but your energy management. But it can also make people worse at the very task of change. If every failure is explained by depletion, the person may stop looking for better conditions, better goals, better habits, or better treatment for an underlying problem. The answer becomes: rest more, plan better, try again tomorrow.

Sometimes that is enough. Often it is not.

A person who cannot stop drinking is not usually failing because they used too much willpower resisting a coffee. A person who cannot get out of bed may not need a morning routine; they may need treatment for depression. A person who cannot stop scrolling may not need a stricter evening discipline; they may need a phone that is less central to their life. A person who cannot keep a promise to exercise may need a habit that is small enough to survive a bad day.

The popular book gives you a universal theory. The literature, at its best, gives you a set of variables. The useful question is not whether you have willpower, but what kind of obstacle you are facing and which tool fits it.

## A More Useful Way to Think About Self-Control

If I were writing the book instead, I would not open with a battery. I would open with a choice.

A choice is not a battle between a good self and a bad self. It is a moment in which several things are true at once: you want something, you feel something, you remember something, your body is in some state, and the environment is offering some rewards. Willpower, if the word is useful at all, is the process of making the choice you want to make when the easiest path points somewhere else.

That process can be improved. But not by pretending that the self is a single engine with a fuel gauge. It can be improved by making the desired action more available, less effortful, and more connected to a reward that is not only future but present. It can be improved by reducing the number of moments in which a person must decide. It can be improved by treating the body seriously: sleep, food, movement, pain, mood, and medication all change what a person can do. It can be improved by noticing that some goals are too large for a single act of control and need to be broken into habits.

The book you read probably gives you a list of tips, and some of those tips will work. The problem is the architecture. It tells you that the core of your difficulty is a finite resource inside you, and that if you manage it well, the rest follows. The more careful view is that self-control is a family of processes, and the best intervention depends on which process is failing.

That is less satisfying than a battery. It does not let you say, “I just need to save my willpower for the important decisions.” It forces you to ask what is actually happening: Are you tired? Are you bored? Are you avoiding a feeling? Is the habit too strong? Is the goal too vague? Is the environment working against you? Is the body unwell? Is the mood low?

The popular book wants to make self-control a matter of discipline. The literature, when it is read without romance, suggests it is a matter of design.

prompt: People say effective altruism attracts depressed, anxious, self-loathing types. Is there any actual data on that? Write up what you'd look at and what you'd conclude.
response:
Effective altruism is not a clinical diagnosis, but a set of values and a set of career choices. When people ask whether EA "attracts depressed, anxious, self-loathing types," they are usually conflating three different populations: the people who read EA literature, the people who donate to EA causes, and the people who work full-time in EA organizations. Those groups have different selection pressures, and the available evidence points in different directions for each.

The strongest evidence is not that EA members are clinically depressed, but that they are unusually distressed by the scale of suffering. Several surveys of EA-adjacent communities have found high rates of moral distress, emotional burnout, and a sense of personal inadequacy. In the 2023 Giving What We Can survey, for example, respondents reported high levels of worry and concern about global problems, and a substantial minority reported that thinking about suffering affected their wellbeing. That is not the same as a disorder, but it is the kind of emotional environment in which depression and anxiety can take hold if the community provides little support for detachment, failure, or ordinary self-interest.

The self-loathing part is easier to test because it appears in behavior. EA has a strong norm of maximizing impact, which can make ordinary life feel wasteful. People may feel guilty about spending time on friends, hobbies, or family. They may compare themselves to those who can do more. They may treat rest as a moral failure. That pattern is documented in EA community discussions and in informal surveys, though not always in clean clinical terms. It is less a sign of preexisting pathology than a side effect of taking infinite moral responsibility seriously without a workable limit.

The depression and anxiety claims are more ambiguous. There is no large, high-quality study showing that EA donors or EA workers have higher rates of major depression than the general population. What there is is a cluster of smaller, more specific signals. First, EA organizations are concentrated in a few cities, in tech-adjacent professions, and among people who already have above-average education, income, and access to resources. That base population is not representative of the world. Second, the people most likely to enter EA organizations are often motivated by a felt sense of personal responsibility, which can be intense. Third, the work is often high-stakes, ambiguous, and emotionally heavy. Those conditions can increase stress, but they do not by themselves prove that EA selects for depression.

The most plausible account is that EA attracts and produces different emotional problems in different stages. At the entry point, many people are not depressed; they are energized, idealistic, and anxious about the size of the problem. In the middle, especially among those who take on leadership or high-pressure roles, burnout, isolation, and depressive symptoms become more common. At the exit, some people leave because the emotional cost becomes too high, while others stay because the work has become an identity. The result is a community where distress is both visible and stigmatized: visible because people talk about it, stigmatized because the culture often rewards composure and efficacy.

If I were designing the study, I would not start with a clinical questionnaire alone. I would do four things.

First, define the population. I would distinguish between EA readers, EA donors, EA part-time volunteers, EA full-time employees, and EA leadership. Each has a different exposure to the culture. A reader may be moved by an article; a full-time EA employee may be expected to optimize every hour.

Second, measure the right outcomes. I would use validated scales for depression, anxiety, burnout, and moral distress, but I would also measure things that are specific to the EA environment: guilt about leisure, pressure to maximize career impact, fear of wasting potential, and discomfort with uncertainty. Those variables are more likely to explain the community's emotional texture than a generic depression score.

Third, use a better comparison group. The natural comparison is not "the general population," which is too broad, but people with similar education, income, age, city, and career interests who are not in EA. That would help separate the effects of being a highly educated, high-earning, high-responsibility person from the effects of being in EA specifically.

Fourth, ask about timing. Did the depression come before EA, or after? Did it worsen after joining an EA organization? Did it improve after leaving? Longitudinal data would be the most useful, because the current evidence mostly shows association, not causation.

My conclusion would be this: EA does not appear to be primarily a refuge for clinically depressed people. It is more accurately described as a movement that attracts people with strong moral emotions and then exposes them to conditions that can produce depression, anxiety, and self-criticism. The data do not show that EA members are a population of depressed people. They do show that the movement creates a high-risk environment for emotional harm, especially for people who already care intensely, who work in high-pressure roles, or who lack access to support. The problem is less about who EA attracts and more about what EA asks of them.

prompt: When an analysis says a big trend, like falling crime, was caused by ten different factors each explaining ten percent, should we believe it? Write a short piece thinking about how plausible multifactorial explanations really are.
response:
The tidy answer—ten factors, ten percent each, adding up to one hundred percent—should make you suspicious. It reads like an accountant balancing a ledger, but most social changes are not arithmetic. A ten percent share is a claim about magnitude, and magnitude claims are where these analyses usually wobble.

To see why, take one of the ten. Say better policing. The real question is not whether policing improved but how much of the drop it bought. To answer that you need a counterfactual: the crime path that would have happened without the change, holding everything else constant. You cannot run that experiment on a city. You can approximate it with a difference-in-differences design, comparing treated and untreated places. But the untreated places are drifting too—different economies, different demographics, different policy choices—so the comparison is always partly contaminated. Each factor’s share is therefore a residue after a series of imperfect subtractions, not a measured ingredient.

The factors also interact, which the ten-by-ten layout hides. If better policing and a larger adult population both reduce crime, and if more adults are both a cause of more crime and a target of policing, the attribution gets tangled. A factor can appear to explain a slice of the decline while the slice is partly just a restatement of another factor. Decompositions that add to one are useful bookkeeping, but the numbers move with the order of the subtractions and the functional form, so they are not the deep explanation they look like.

There is also a prior to respect. Crime falls when a society ages, when the prime-crime years of a generation pass, when the economy steadies, when drugs shift, when policing tightens. These forces overlap in time and are all plausible, so a multifactorial answer is more likely right in shape than a single-cause one. The problem is not that it lists ten things but that it assigns ten equal shares. Equal shares are a default, not a finding. A defensible analysis would rank the factors, give the big ones wide confidence bands, and say plainly where the estimate is thin.

So the question is not whether to believe the multifactorial story but whether the percentages have earned their precision. If the paper shows the counterfactuals, the uncertainty, and the interactions, the direction is credible and the exact splits are suggestive. If it just presents a neat partition, treat it as a map of the debate, not as a measurement.

prompt: A reader asked what would convince me that a single general factor like g is a 'real thing' rather than a made-up abstraction. Write a thoughtful reply using examples from medicine.
response:
A few medical analogies do the work.

**Blood pressure** is a number, but it is not a fiction. You cannot hold it in your hand, yet it reliably predicts stroke, heart failure, and kidney damage. It is a standing feature of the circulatory system, not an artifact of the thermometer.

**Body temperature** is likewise a derived quantity. No one cell is “37 degrees,” and the number changes with where you measure. Still, a sustained fever is a real state of the organism, with causes and consequences.

**Vitamin D deficiency** used to be invisible until chemistry showed us a molecule and a threshold. We then built interventions that actually changed outcomes. The entity was real all along; we simply lacked the instruments.

**Diabetes** is not one disease but a family of metabolic states. We do not need a single underlying cause to treat the syndrome, but we do need a consistent pattern of markers that tracks future risk.

**High cholesterol** is a risk factor, not a disease. It does not by itself explain every heart attack, yet lowering it lowers risk. The same is true of *g*: it is a statistical regularity that tracks performance across tasks, not a substance sitting in the brain.

The point is not that *g* is a molecule. It is that, like blood pressure, it is a measurable property of a complex system that predicts real outcomes. If a single score consistently forecasts academic performance, job performance, and health-related behaviors across populations, and if interventions that raise cognitive skills shift that score even a little, then the factor is doing work. It is not “made up” in the way a chart is made up. It is a stable feature of the data, like a vital sign.

prompt: Everyone loves to dunk on the Myers-Briggs for being unscientific, yet it keeps feeling right to people. Write a defense of it that takes the criticism seriously and says what it is actually good for compared with the Big Five.
response:
The standard attack on Myers-Briggs is that it lacks test-retest reliability, that its binary types collapse continuous traits, and that its predictive validity is weak. All of these criticisms are correct. If the instrument is judged as a scientific classifier of personality, it fails.

But that judgment assumes the only purpose of a personality tool is to be true in the psychometric sense. People use MBTI for a different reason, and the Big Five is badly suited to that reason.

The Big Five measures where a person falls on five continuous dimensions: openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, and neuroticism. It is excellent for predicting outcomes.
